senses.definition: The exploitation, or opportunity for exploitation, of an unintentional video game mechanic.
senses.example: Players discovered a cheese strategy that let them skip the boss entirely.

senses.definition: A fastball.
senses.example: The pitcher blew a cheese past the batter, who never even moved his bat.

senses.definition: To prepare curds for making cheese.
To make holes in a pattern of circuitry to decrease pattern density.
To smile excessively, as for a camera.
To stop; to refrain from.
senses.example: Cheese it! The cops!

senses.definition: To anger or irritate someone, usually in combination with "off".
senses.example: All this waiting around is really cheesing me off.

senses.definition: To use a controversial or unsporting tactic to gain an advantage (especially in a game.)
senses.example: You can cheese most of the game using certain exploits.

senses.definition: To use an unconventional, all-in strategy to take one's opponent by surprise early in the game (especially for real-time strategy games).
Said while being photographed, to give the impression of smiling.
senses.example: Say "cheese"! ... and there we are!

core.definition: A food made from milk curds that have been pressed and often aged, eaten sliced, grated or melted.

pronunciation.tip: This is a single syllable with a long ee vowel and a voiced z at the end. Do not add a vowel after the z, and do not pronounce it 'chess'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a food word; the adjective 'cheesy' carries a negative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Cheese is one of the most common foods in American homes, restaurants and grocery stores. It is usually uncountable in general use, as in 'some cheese' or 'a slice of cheese', but Americans also say 'cheeses' for varieties. At the deli, you can ask for 'a slice of American cheese' or 'shredded cheddar'.

distinctions.note: Cheddar is one specific variety of cheese, while cheese is the general category.
Dairy is a broad category including milk, butter and yogurt; cheese is one dairy product.

examples.everyday: Can you grab some shredded cheese from the fridge for the tacos?
examples.professional: We changed the catering order to cheese-free options after two guests reported allergies.
examples.analytical: Cheese is a useful case for food science because aging changes its texture and flavor through microbial activity.

nuance.analogy: Like milk that bacteria and time have transformed into something firmer and richer.
nuance.etymology: From Old English cyse, from Latin caseus.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'chess' or 'cheez-uh'; it is one syllable, /tʃiz/.
Pluralizing general uncountable cheese; say 'some cheese', but use 'cheeses' for different varieties.

cheese.etymology: From Middle English *chese*, from Anglian Old English *ċēse*, from **kāsī*, borrowed from Latin *cāseus*.

senses.definition: Of or relating to chemistry.
senses.example: chemical experiments

senses.definition: Of or relating to a material or processes not commonly found in nature or in a particular product.
senses.example: Critics say the cereal contains too many chemical additives for a natural product.

senses.definition: An artificial chemical compound.
senses.example: I color my hair with henna, not chemicals.

senses.definition: An addictive drug.
senses.example: He admitted he had been taking a chemical to stay awake during finals week.

senses.definition: Any specific chemical element or chemical compound or alloy.
senses.example: Hydrogen and sulphur are both chemicals.

core.definition: A substance made by or used in chemical processes, such as a cleaning product, fertilizer or industrial material.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, CHEM-ih-cul, not che-MI-cal. The middle vowel is a short, reduced 'ih,' and the ending is a soft 'kul.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; in everyday talk it can sound negative when it suggests artificial or harmful substances, as in 'chemicals in food.'
nuance.usage_note: Americans use chemical for cleaning products, pesticides, industrial materials and anything made in a lab, often with some suspicion that it is artificial. In slang, 'chemicals' can mean illegal drugs, so be careful in casual talk. As an adjective it means relating to chemistry, as in 'chemical reaction.'

distinctions.note: Chemistry is the science itself, while a chemical is a specific substance.
Chemical does not mean harmful; the opposite of chemical in product labels is usually natural, but many natural substances are also chemicals.

examples.everyday: Please keep the bleach and other household chemicals on the top shelf, away from the kids.
examples.professional: The plant needs a safety data sheet for every chemical we ship to the Ohio facility.
examples.analytical: Whether a chemical is safe depends on dose and exposure, not on whether it is labeled natural or artificial.

nuance.analogy: A chemical is like an ingredient in a recipe: its name alone tells you little until you know how much you add and what it does.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin chemicus, relating to alchemy, which later came to mean chemistry.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable and saying che-MI-cal.
Using chemical to mean natural or healthy, when it simply means made from or involving chemistry.
Using chemicals as a slang word for drugs in formal settings, where it may be misunderstood.

senses.definition: The state of being a child.
The time during which one is a child, from between infancy and puberty.
senses.example: Her childhood in Ohio was filled with summers on the lake and long winters.

senses.definition: The early stages of development of something.
senses.example: The project is still in its childhood, so the design will change a lot.

core.definition: The period of life when a person is a child, between infancy and adolescence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, CHILD. The second syllable has a short oo sound like the vowel in 'good,' and it is not a long 'hood' with a strong vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive or nostalgic in most contexts, but it can also be negative when describing difficult or traumatic early years.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use childhood in everyday talk about growing up, such as childhood friends, a childhood home, or childhood memories. Phrases like since childhood or from childhood are very common. In professional and academic writing, childhood can also describe the early stage of a field or technology.

distinctions.note: Youth can mean the young years in general or young people as a group, while childhood refers specifically to the time when a person is a child.
Childhood describes a period of life, while childishness describes immature behavior, often in a negative way.

examples.everyday: I grew up on a farm, and I still remember my childhood summers there.
examples.professional: Our machine learning program is still in its childhood, so we are still setting basic data standards.
examples.analytical: Moral development is often traced through childhood, when a person first learns to tell obligation apart from personal preference.

nuance.analogy: Childhood is like the foundation of a house: what is built there shapes everything that goes up afterward.
nuance.etymology: From child plus the suffix -hood, from Old English -hād, meaning state, condition, or period of life.
common_mistakes: Saying in the childhood instead of in childhood, since the word is used without an article in these phrases.
Confusing childhood with childish, which describes immature behavior rather than a period of life.
nuance.biblical_note: Scripture uses the idea of childhood to describe a person's early life and its place in God's care. In Mark 9:21 a father tells Jesus that his son has had the affliction from childhood, and Jesus heals him. Ecclesiastes 11:10 notes that childhood and youth are vanity, meaning fleeting. The Hebrew word yaldut and the Greek phrase ek paidiothen both describe the time of childhood.

childhood.etymology: From Middle English *childhode*, *childhod*, from Old English *ċildhād* (“childhood”).

senses.definition: Synonym of handwriting or penmanship, one's personal skill at writing.
Synonym of calligraphy, the art of beautiful writing.
Synonym of autograph, writing in one's own hand.
Synonym of palmistry, fortune-telling based on one's hand.

core.definition: Handwriting or penmanship, meaning a person's personal skill or style of writing by hand.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, RAH, and the final syllable is a light fee sound. Keep the r clear and avoid saying 'chirogra-phy' with a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive, but rare and somewhat old-fashioned.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'chirography' in daily life; they say 'handwriting' or 'penmanship' instead. The word appears in paleography, historical studies, and writing about manuscripts. In serious writing, it may be used to contrast an individual's hand with printed text.

distinctions.note: Handwriting is the everyday word; chirography is a more technical or literary term for the same thing.
Calligraphy is decorative and artistic writing; chirography is more general, referring to ordinary handwriting or a person's hand.

examples.professional: The archivist compared the chirography of the two letters to see whether one clerk wrote both.
examples.analytical: Chirography reveals more than legibility, since a writer's stroke and spacing preserve traces of habit, training, and emotional state.

nuance.analogy: Chirography is like a fingerprint of the hand, showing a unique pattern each person leaves on paper.
nuance.etymology: From Greek cheir meaning hand and graphein meaning to write.
common_mistakes: Using 'chirography' in everyday conversation where 'handwriting' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with calligraphy, which is decorative writing as an art form.

chirography.etymology: From *chirograph* + *y* under influence from *geography* &c. from French *chirographe*, from Latin *chirographus* and *chirographum*, from Ancient Greek *χειρόγραφος* and *χειρόγραφον*, from *χειρο-* (“hand-”) + *γραφος* (“writing, written thing”).

senses.definition: The musical director of a choir, who conducts performances and supervises rehearsal.

core.definition: The person who leads and directs a church or school choir, conducting rehearsals and performances.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, 'KWY', with a lighter secondary stress on 'mas'. The 'ch' is silent and sounds like 'kw', and the final '-er' is a reduced American r-sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests skill, patience and dedication to a group.
nuance.usage_note: In American churches, 'choir director' is the more common everyday term, especially in Protestant congregations. 'Choirmaster' sounds more traditional and is used in Anglican, Episcopal and Catholic settings, and by historians. Calling a school music teacher a 'choirmaster' sounds old-fashioned.

distinctions.note: 'Choir director' is the everyday American term and works for any choir; 'choirmaster' is more traditional and often used for church or cathedral choirs.
A conductor leads any ensemble, including orchestras; a choirmaster specifically leads singers.
A cantor is a singer who leads prayers or chants in a synagogue, or a song leader in some churches; a cantor is not the same as a choir director.

examples.everyday: Our choirmaster has been directing the church choir for twenty years.
examples.professional: The choirmaster asked everyone to arrive ten minutes early for the sectional rehearsal.
examples.analytical: The choirmaster shapes the sound of the congregation, so his musical decisions also become pastoral ones.

nuance.analogy: Like an orchestra conductor who leads with a baton, but for voices.
nuance.etymology: 'Choir' from Old French quer, from Latin chorus; 'master' from Latin magister.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'choir' as 'choy-er' or 'chore'; it sounds like 'kwire'.
Writing it as two words, 'choir master'; the standard form is one word.

senses.definition: The Christian sacrament at which someone, usually a child, is baptized and given a Christian name.
Any instance of someone's or something's being christened.

core.definition: The Christian ceremony in which a baby or child is baptized and given a Christian name, often followed by a family party.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is reduced to a weak 'uh', and the ending '-ing' is a short 'ih-ng' sound, not 'eeng'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests family celebration and new beginnings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'christening' mainly for infant baptism, especially in Episcopal, Lutheran, Catholic and some Methodist families. Baptist and other believers' churches usually say 'baptism' instead. Americans also use it playfully for launching a ship or opening something new. A natural reply to an invitation is 'Sure, what time is it?'

distinctions.note: Baptism is the formal theological term for the rite, while christening is more popular and often refers to infant baptism with a family party.
A dedication is a non-sacramental ceremony for a child in some churches, while a christening is an actual baptism.

examples.everyday: We're going to a christening on Sunday for my coworker's new baby.
examples.professional: The christening of the new data pipeline is scheduled for Friday's release, so the team should bring their notes.
examples.analytical: The christening of infants raises the theological question of whether faith must precede the sacrament, or whether grace comes first.

nuance.analogy: A christening is like a grand opening for a newborn: the family publicly welcomes the child into the community.
nuance.etymology: From christen, Old English cristnian 'to make Christian', from Christ, plus the noun ending -ing.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'christening' with 'christened' in conversation; 'christening' is the noun for the ceremony.
Saying 'CHRIS-ten-ing' with a full vowel in the middle syllable instead of a reduced 'uh'.

traditions.view: Christening is baptism with chrismation and communion, administered as a single initiation rite, most often to infants.
Christening is infant baptism, which removes original sin and makes the child a member of the Church.
Christening is practiced by Lutherans, Reformed, Anglicans and Methodists for infants, while Baptists and many evangelicals reserve baptism for believers who confess faith.

christening.etymology: From Middle English *cristenynge*, from Old English *cristnung*; compare *christen* + *-ing*.

senses.definition: A patch of land adjoining a church, often used as a graveyard.

core.definition: The land around a church, often used as a graveyard for the church's members.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, church. Don't stress yard. The r in yard is a strong American r, and the vowel in yard is the open ahr sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to solemn. In stories or poems it evokes quiet, age and history.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say cemetery or graveyard for a burial ground. Churchyard is used for the grounds around an old church, especially in small towns, New England and the South, and in literature. In casual talk it may sound slightly quaint, so people often say the cemetery behind the church.

distinctions.note: A cemetery is usually a larger, separate burial ground; a churchyard is the land next to a church and is usually smaller.
Graveyard is the plain everyday word and can sound slightly spooky; churchyard stresses the connection to a church.

examples.everyday: We walked through the old churchyard on the way back from the farmers market.
examples.professional: The preservation team said the churchyard wall needs repairs before the next season.
examples.analytical: The gravestones in the rural churchyard record the families who shaped the town's religious life.

nuance.analogy: A churchyard is like a backyard that belongs to the church: it sits right next to the building.
nuance.etymology: Church plus yard, an enclosed piece of land, combined in English.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on yard (church-YARD).
Confusing churchyard with cemetery; a churchyard is smaller and attached to a church.

senses.definition: Having no claws.

core.definition: Having no claws, especially an animal or body part that lacks the sharp nails found in similar species.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the -less ending is a reduced syllable pronounced lus, not les. Keep the aw vowel from 'paw'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term, mostly used in biology or zoology.
nuance.usage_note: Clawless is used mainly for animals in zoology or nature writing, and occasionally for fictional creatures. For a cat that has had its claws removed, Americans say 'declawed'. For weakened power in general, people use 'defanged' rather than 'clawless'.

distinctions.note: Defanged is mostly figurative for weakened power, while clawless is usually literal and describes an animal's physical structure.

examples.everyday: That little frog is clawless, so it can't climb up the glass the way the lizard did.
examples.professional: The 2010 study used a clawless toad species to test grip mechanics on smooth surfaces without nail-based gripping.
examples.analytical: A clawless creature must rely on pads and suction to move, which reshapes how biologists define locomotion itself.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand with smooth fingertips, where grip depends on the palm and friction rather than hooks.
nuance.etymology: From claw, from Old English clawu, plus the suffix -less, meaning without.
common_mistakes: Using clawless for a declawed cat; the American word for surgical removal is 'declawed'.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'klaw-LESS'.

senses.definition: Lenient or merciful; charitable.
senses.example: The judge was clement toward the young man who had confessed to the crime.

senses.definition: Mild.

core.definition: Showing mercy or leniency toward someone, or, in literary English, describing pleasantly mild weather.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -ent is weak, closer to 'uhnt' than to a strong 'ent'.

nuance.connotation: Positive but rare. It suggests gentle, merciful judgment; the weather sense is literary.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use clement in everyday speech, so you will mostly see it in formal or literary writing. In legal and political news, people say 'lenient' or 'merciful' instead. For weather, everyday speakers say 'mild' or 'pleasant'.

distinctions.note: Lenient is common and means less strict; clement is more formal and suggests mercy from a position of power.
Merciful describes showing compassion; clement often describes someone who could punish but chooses not to.
Mild is the everyday word for weather; clement is literary and used mainly for pleasant weather.

examples.everyday: My landlord was surprisingly clement about the late rent, which I didn't expect.
examples.professional: The director was clement toward the team after the failed launch and focused on lessons learned.
examples.analytical: A clement reading of the text would stress mercy, but the law itself offers no such clemency.

nuance.analogy: Like a teacher who grades the essay with an open hand, leaving room for mistakes.
nuance.etymology: From Latin clemens, mild or merciful.
common_mistakes: Using clement for 'clean' or 'clever' because of the similar sound; it means merciful or mild.
Using clement as a noun for a pardon; the noun is clemency.

senses.definition: Of or relating to clerks or their work.
Of or relating to the clergy.
Clerical garments.
senses.example: He wore his clerical to the funeral, black collar and all.

senses.definition: (uncommon) A member of the clergy.
senses.example: The retired clerical from our diocese spoke at the youth meeting.
senses.label: uncommon

core.definition: Relating to the clergy or ordained ministers; also relating to the routine office work of clerks, such as filing, copying, and recording information.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the second to a quick 'uh.' The 'er' is r-colored, and 'clerk' in American English is pronounced 'klurk,' so do not say 'clay-ri-cal.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most uses; in 'clerical error,' it suggests a small, careless mistake that is usually easy to fix.
nuance.usage_note: In American offices, 'clerical' usually describes routine paperwork, as in 'clerical staff' or 'clerical work,' and 'clerical error' is a common phrase for a minor mistake in records or billing. In religious contexts, it means relating to the clergy, as in 'clerical collar.' Context makes the sense clear, so listen for the setting before you assume.

distinctions.note: Ecclesiastical is more formal and refers to the church as an institution or its affairs, while clerical focuses on clergy or on office clerks.
Clerk is the noun for the person doing office or record work; clerical is the adjective describing that work or the clergy.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I think that was just a clerical error on the bill, so I'll get it fixed.
examples.professional: Most of the data problems were clerical, such as typos in date fields and duplicate customer records.
examples.analytical: The clerical establishment resisted reform, arguing that the church's authority came from its ordained ministers alone.

nuance.analogy: Clerical is like a small typo in a paper form: it is easy to make, easy to notice, and easy to correct.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin clericalis, from clericus (cleric), from Greek klērikos; see clergy.
common_mistakes: Using 'clerical' to mean 'clerk-like' in general speech, when 'clerical error' or 'clerical work' is the usual phrase.
Pronouncing 'clerk' with a long 'a' ('klayrk'); American speakers say 'klurk.'
Assuming 'clerical' always refers to priests; in American offices it more often means paperwork.

senses.definition: In a clinical manner: dispassionately or analytically.
In the setting of a medical clinic; in a clinical setting; (of a health condition) to a degree high enough to be relevant to clinical practice.
senses.example: clinically apparent

senses.definition: At a person's bedside.
senses.example: a person baptized clinically

core.definition: In a medical sense, to a degree relevant to diagnosis or treatment; or in a cool, detached and analytical manner.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the last syllable is often reduced to a light sound that sounds like 'lee'. Many Americans say the middle as 'ih-kuh', so avoid giving each syllable equal weight.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative. In medical contexts it is neutral, but describing someone as acting clinically can suggest coldness or lack of warmth.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'clinically' in medical talk, such as 'clinically proven' or 'clinically depressed', and also in casual talk to describe a cold, precise manner. Saying 'clinically proven' in an ad is common. A natural reply to a cold, analytical remark might be 'You said that so clinically.'

distinctions.note: Medically is the broad term for relating to medicine, while clinically refers specifically to patient care or diagnosis.
Coldly describes an unfriendly manner, while clinically describes a detached, objective manner, often without intending harm.

examples.everyday: My doctor said I'm not clinically depressed, just really stressed out.
examples.professional: The model's results are clinically significant only if they change the treatment decision.
examples.analytical: The essay treats grief clinically, and that detachment is precisely what makes its argument hard to accept.

nuance.analogy: Clinically is like looking at a patient through an X-ray: you see the structure without the warmth of the person.
nuance.etymology: From clinical, from Greek klinikos, of a bed, from klinē, bed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the middle syllable as a full 'eye' sound, as in 'KLIN-eye-kuh-lee'.
Using 'clinically' to mean 'in a clinic' for everyday places; it is mainly for medical or analytical contexts.

senses.definition: Scattered with a disorderly mixture of objects that occupies space; littered.

core.definition: Full of many objects scattered in a messy way, so that the space feels crowded and disorganized.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short, reduced 'er' sound, and the final 'd' is pronounced as a 'd' sound with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Mildly negative. It suggests disorder and can sound like a criticism of someone's home or desk, though people often use it casually about themselves.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cluttered often in everyday talk about rooms, desks, or inboxes, sometimes with a light apology: 'Sorry, my place is a little cluttered.' It is polite and common, so you can use it when inviting people over. A stronger, more informal alternative is 'a total mess.'

distinctions.note: Messy describes a state of disorder in general, including dirt or spills, while cluttered specifically refers to too many objects in a space.
Crowded refers to too many people or things filling a space; cluttered suggests disorganized objects, not necessarily a lack of room.

examples.everyday: Sorry the living room is so cluttered, we've been moving stuff around all week.
examples.professional: Her inbox is so cluttered that she missed the deadline reminder twice this month.
examples.analytical: The author argues that a cluttered prose style obscures the argument, forcing readers to hunt for the thesis.

nuance.analogy: Like a backpack stuffed with too many things: every item is useful, but there is no room to find anything.
nuance.etymology: From clutter, a variant of clotter, related to clot; the past participle ending -ed makes it an adjective.
common_mistakes: Using cluttered for a single messy object, where 'a mess' is more natural.
Confusing the adjective cluttered with the noun clutter, as in 'a cluttered' instead of 'a clutter of objects'.

conversation.text: The counters are so cluttered that I don't have room to cook.
His desk is always cluttered with papers and coffee cups.
The garage is too cluttered to park the car inside.

senses.definition: The shape, outline, or boundary of a coast. (The term coastline is generally used to describe the approximate boundaries at relatively large spatial scales.)
senses.example: The sweep of the rocky Southern California coastline off Point Fermin.

core.definition: The outline or shape of a coast, meaning the boundary where land meets the sea, as seen on a map.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, which is 'coast', and give 'line' a light secondary stress. The vowel in 'line' is a full diphthong, like 'line' in English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and descriptive. It can sound poetic when describing scenery.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coastline to describe the shape of a shore, especially on maps or in travel writing. In everyday talk, 'the coastline' is often used to describe scenery, such as 'the rugged coastline of Oregon'. Shoreline is a close alternative in everyday talk, but coastline suggests a larger geographic scale.

distinctions.note: Coast refers to the land region along the sea, while coastline is the line or outline where land meets water.
Shoreline is the edge of a body of water at a local scale, while coastline covers larger geographic boundaries.

examples.everyday: From the plane you could see the whole coastline curving south.
examples.professional: Our satellite data tracks how the coastline shifts after each storm season.
examples.analytical: A coastline's apparent length depends on the scale of measurement, which is why the boundary is hard to pin down.

nuance.analogy: A coastline is like the edge of a torn piece of paper: its shape is clear, but its exact length depends on how closely you look.
nuance.etymology: From 'coast' plus 'line', meaning the line along which the coast runs.
common_mistakes: Using 'coastline' to mean the whole region of a country, when it refers to the boundary line.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound unnatural.

conversation.text: The coastline in Maine is gorgeous, but the water is freezing.
We took a boat tour along the coastline and saw some seals.
That part of the coastline is mostly cliffs, so there's no real beach.

senses.definition: Of two or more objects: being in the same location.
senses.example: The two survey markers were coincident, so the land records showed one boundary.

senses.definition: Of two or more events: occurring at the same time; contemporaneous.
senses.example: The power outage was coincident with the storm, which made the cause hard to pinpoint.

senses.definition: Of two or more things: having the same qualities; being in accordance; consonant, matching.
senses.example: Her account of the accident was coincident with the police report in every detail.

core.definition: Happening at the same time as something else, or occupying the same place. Also used of things that match or agree closely.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, IN, not on the last. The middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa, and the final -ent is weak, so say it as one soft unit.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. The word describes timing or position without judging the events.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coincident mainly in writing, science and formal analysis. In conversation they say 'at the same time' or 'right when' instead. The standard construction is coincident with, as in 'coincident with the storm.'

distinctions.note: Coincident describes things that happen together or overlap; coincidental describes a chance occurrence that may seem meaningful.
Simultaneous stresses the exact same moment and is used for actions; coincident is broader and often used for overlap or matching in formal or technical writing.
Concurrent describes things that run alongside each other over a period of time, such as concurrent processes or concurrent lawsuits.

examples.everyday: The power went out, coincident with the start of the storm, which is why I missed your call.
examples.professional: The latency spike was coincident with the deployment, so we will check the release logs before blaming the database.
examples.analytical: Hume argued that two events, however tightly coincident in time, do not by themselves establish a causal connection.

nuance.analogy: Like two lines drawn on the same spot of paper, they sit exactly on top of each other.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin coincidens, from Latin coincidere, to fall together (com-, together, plus incidere, to fall upon).
common_mistakes: Confusing coincident (occurring together) with coincidental (happening by chance).
Putting the stress on the third syllable: coh-in-SIH-dent is wrong; the stress is on IN.
Using coincident to + object instead of coincident with.

coincident.etymology: The adjective is borrowed from French *coïncident*, from Medieval Latin *coincidentem*, an accusative singular form of Latin *coincidēns* (“coinciding”), the present active participle of *coincidō* (“to coincide”), from *co-* (variant of *con-*) + *incidō*…

senses.definition: Having an unregulated body temperature; ectothermic.
senses.example: Lizards are cold-blooded, so they bask on rocks in the sun to warm up.

senses.definition: Lacking emotion or compunction.
senses.example: The villain's cold-blooded decision to abandon the children shocked everyone in the courtroom.

senses.definition: Of a type of horse: tall and muscular, usually good-natured and suitable for heavy work.
senses.example: The farmer bought a cold-blooded draft horse, tall and muscular, to pull the heavy plow.

senses.definition: Of an engine or vehicle: difficult to start; runs poorly until warmed up.
senses.example: My old pickup is cold-blooded in winter, so I let it idle for ten minutes before driving.

core.definition: Showing no emotion or pity, especially when doing something cruel or violent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on COLD, with a lighter secondary stress on BLOOD. The vowel in blood is the uh of 'cut', and the -ed is a separate short syllable, id.

nuance.connotation: Negative when describing cruel, unemotional behavior; neutral in biology.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cold-blooded for a calculated, unemotional act, especially a murder or betrayal, as in 'a cold-blooded killer.' In biology, scientists prefer ectothermic to describe animals whose body temperature follows their surroundings. Don't use it casually for someone who is simply calm or reserved.

distinctions.note: Cold-blooded stresses a deliberate, calculated act, while cold-hearted describes a general lack of warmth or compassion.
Callous is a formal word for being insensitive to others' suffering; cold-blooded implies a deliberate act done without emotion.

examples.everyday: He dumped her by text after three years, which was honestly cold-blooded.
examples.professional: Laying off the whole team by email without warning was a cold-blooded decision.
examples.analytical: Cold-blooded cruelty differs from ordinary harm because it reflects deliberate detachment rather than rage or impulse.

nuance.analogy: Like a reptile whose body temperature follows the room, cold-blooded behavior follows calculation rather than feeling.
nuance.etymology: Cold from Old English ceald; blood from Old English blōd.
common_mistakes: Using cold-blooded for someone who is merely calm or reserved
Stressing blood as strongly as cold, which weakens the compound stress pattern

senses.definition: To give an appearance or impression; to project a certain image; to seem or appear (to be some way). [ with as; or with like]
senses.example: How did she come across when you met with her?

senses.definition: To find, usually by accident.
senses.example: In the dark he came across an old box by accident.

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see come,‎ across.
senses.example: He came across the street towards me.

senses.definition: To change sides; to cross over to work for the opposition.
senses.example: You argued well in court but your firm doesn't pay its lawyers well, so why don't you come across to ours?

senses.definition: To produce what was desired; to come up with the goods. [with with]
senses.example: He came across with the rest of the money when we mentioned our lawyer.

senses.definition: To give in and do what is wanted or expected; to acquiesce to something.
senses.example: He finally came across after hours of arguing, agreeing to the plan his wife wanted.

senses.definition: To have sex; to give in to seduction.
senses.example: She refused his advances for weeks, but eventually she came across.

senses.definition: To confess to something.
senses.example: After hours of questioning, the suspect finally came across and admitted the robbery.

core.definition: To make a particular impression on others; to seem a certain way to people who see or hear you.

pronunciation.tip: Come gets light secondary stress and across gets the main stress, so the two words blend in speech. The vowel in KRAWS is the rounded 'aw' of 'caught', which many Americans say the same as 'cot'.

nuance.connotation: Depends on context: come across as friendly is positive, and come across as arrogant is negative. It describes how someone is perceived.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use come across to describe how a person, message or email seems to others, often in feedback: 'You came across as really confident in the interview.' The other everyday sense, to find something by chance, is also common: 'I came across an old photo while cleaning.' Use come across as followed by an adjective or noun, or come across like followed by a noun phrase.

distinctions.note: Seem is neutral and describes a general impression; come across as often describes the impression a person makes through how they speak or act.
Run into usually means meeting a person by chance, while come across is more often used for finding things or information by chance.

examples.everyday: I think I came across as rude in that text, so I'm sorry about it.
examples.professional: In the review meeting, your slides came across as more confident than the data really supports.
examples.analytical: Her argument comes across as a plea for compassion, yet its logic is quite rigorous.

nuance.analogy: Your tone is like a radio signal: it reaches the listener whether or not you meant to send it.
nuance.etymology: Combines come, from Old English cuman, with across, from Middle English on cros 'crosswise'.
common_mistakes: Writing 'I came across him' when you mean he made an impression; use 'He came across as' for impressions, and 'I came across him' only for chance meetings.
Forgetting the past tense 'came across' in narratives, as in 'I come across an old photo yesterday.'

conversation.text: I came across some old photos while cleaning the attic.
He comes across as shy, but he's really funny.
Did my point come across clearly in the email?

senses.definition: Suitable to be eaten; edible.
senses.example: The picnic basket held only comestible items, nothing that would spoil in the summer heat.

senses.definition: Anything that can be eaten; food.

core.definition: Something that can be eaten; a food item, usually used in the plural for groceries or edible goods sold in a store.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable, MES. The final '-ible' is weakened to a syllabic 'l', so it sounds like 'bul', not 'bull' with a long vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly old-fashioned. It sounds formal or literary compared with food or groceries.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use comestible in everyday speech; they say food, groceries, or snacks. The plural comestibles appears in older shops, delis, or formal writing, such as 'fine comestibles' on a store sign. In modern use, edibles often means cannabis products, so avoid edible when you mean ordinary food.

distinctions.note: Edible is an adjective meaning safe or fit to eat, while comestible is a noun for the food itself and sounds more formal.
Groceries is the everyday American word for food bought at a store, while comestibles sounds old-fashioned or formal.

examples.everyday: We grabbed some comestibles at the little deli downtown, and the sandwiches were great.
examples.professional: Our food safety audit covers every comestible sold in the cafeteria, including packaged goods.
examples.analytical: The philosopher distinguishes comestibles from nourishment, since not everything edible actually sustains the body.

nuance.analogy: Like the word provisions, which means supplies, but more formal and less used today.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin comestibilis, from Latin comedere, meaning to eat up or consume.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with combustible, which means able to catch fire.
Using comestible as an everyday word; Americans usually say food or groceries, so comestibles sounds stiff in casual conversation.

comestible.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *comestible*, or its source, Late Latin *comestibilis*, from Latin *comedō* (“to eat”), from *com-* (English *com-*) + *edo* (“I eat”) (as in English *edible*), from Proto-Indo-European (whence also English *eat*).

senses.definition: To provide a commentary; to act as a commentator; to maintain a stream of comments about some event.
senses.example: For the radio audience he will commentate on the match.

core.definition: To give a spoken commentary on an event, such as a game or a news story, while it is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on KAH, and the middle syllable is a reduced 'mun'. The final -ate rhymes with 'eight', not with 'it'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a job or activity rather than an attitude.
nuance.usage_note: Americans commentate mainly on sports and live broadcasts, and the person doing it is a commentator, with a 'color commentator' adding analysis beside the play-by-play announcer. For play-by-play, Americans more often say 'call the game'. Use 'comment on' for a short remark or written analysis instead of commentate.

distinctions.note: To announce is to call the play-by-play, while commentating usually adds explanation and opinion alongside the action.
Comment on is used for a remark or written reaction, while commentate describes an ongoing spoken account of a live event.

examples.everyday: My dad always commentates on the game out loud, even when nobody in the room is listening.
examples.professional: The producer asked her to commentate on the replay for the internal training video.
examples.analytical: A historian who commentates on events as they unfold must judge without hindsight, a constraint that later written analysis does not face.

nuance.analogy: To commentate is like narrating a movie while you watch it, turning the action into a story as it happens.
nuance.etymology: Back-formation from commentator, from commentary, from Latin commentari 'to consider, think over'.
common_mistakes: Using commentate as a noun, as in 'He is a commentate'; the person is a commentator.
Stressing the last syllable; the stress belongs on KAH, the first syllable.

senses.definition: A formal denunciation; especially one threatening divine punishment.

core.definition: In theology, a formal public denunciation of sinners that threatens divine punishment; the term is used especially for the Anglican Commination service.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on NAY, with a lighter stress on the first syllable. The first vowel is an 'ah,' and the middle syllables are short and weak. Do not confuse the sound with 'communion' or 'commiseration.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes a harsh public condemnation that threatens punishment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans seldom use commination outside church history, liturgy, or theology. In the Episcopal and Anglican tradition, the Commination service from the Book of Common Prayer was historically read on Ash Wednesday. In ordinary speech, people would say 'condemnation,' 'curse,' or 'denunciation.'

distinctions.note: Condemnation is the general word for strong disapproval. Commination specifically involves a threat of divine punishment and a liturgical or formal setting.
An imprecation is a curse called down on someone. A commination is a formal public threat or denunciation, often read as part of a service.

examples.everyday: Our pastor read a commination at the Ash Wednesday service, and it felt pretty grim to the kids.
examples.professional: The synod's commination against the heretical doctrine was printed in the church bulletin.
examples.analytical: The medieval commination psalms reveal a theology in which public curses were a form of moral instruction.

nuance.analogy: Like a judge reading a sentence aloud in a courtroom of souls, announcing the consequences before the whole congregation.
nuance.etymology: From Latin comminatio 'threat,' from comminari 'to threaten.'
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'commiseration' or 'communion' because the spelling and sound are similar.
Using it in ordinary speech where 'condemnation' is the natural word.
Stressing the first syllable too strongly, as in 'KAH-mih-nay-shun.'

senses.definition: A state or quality.
senses.example: National reports on the condition of public education are dismal.

senses.definition: A particular state of being.
senses.example: Hypnosis is a peculiar condition of the nervous system.

senses.definition: The health status of a medical patient.
senses.example: My aunt couldn’t walk up the stairs in her condition.

senses.definition: A certain abnormal state of health; a malady or sickness.
senses.example: My grandfather's heart condition kept him from traveling after his seventieth birthday.

senses.definition: A requirement or prerequisite.
senses.example: Environmental protection is a condition for sustainability.

senses.definition: A logical clause or phrase that a conditional statement uses. The phrase can either be true or false.
senses.example: In the proof, the second condition must be true whenever the first hypothesis holds.

senses.definition: A clause in a contract or agreement indicating that a certain contingency may modify the principal obligation in some way.
senses.example: The lease includes a condition that the landlord may terminate the agreement if rent is late.

senses.definition: To subject to the process of acclimation.
senses.example: I became conditioned to the absence of seasons in San Diego.

senses.definition: To subject to different conditions, especially as an exercise.
senses.example: They were conditioning their shins in their karate class.

senses.definition: To make dependent on a condition to be fulfilled; to make conditional on.
senses.example: The bank conditioned the loan on proof of steady income and a clean credit history.

senses.definition: To place conditions or limitations upon.
senses.example: The judge conditioned his release on weekly check-ins with a parole officer.

senses.definition: To shape the behavior of someone to do something.
senses.example: The children were conditioned to speak up if they had any disagreements.

senses.definition: To treat, especially hair with hair conditioner.
senses.example: She conditions her curly hair every week to keep it soft and manageable.

senses.definition: To contract; to stipulate; to agree.
senses.example: The parties conditioned that payment would be made within thirty days of delivery.

senses.definition: To test or assay, as silk (to ascertain the proportion of moisture it contains).
senses.example: Textile inspectors conditioned the silk samples in a humidity chamber before weighing them.

senses.definition: To put under conditions; to require to pass a new examination or to make up a specified study, as a condition of remaining in one's class or in college.
senses.example: to condition a student who has failed in some branch of study

senses.definition: To impose upon an object those relations or conditions without which knowledge and thought are alleged to be impossible.
senses.example: Kant argued that the mind conditions every object we perceive, so knowledge becomes possible.

core.definition: Something that must hold before something else can hold; in logic, a requirement, or the 'if' part of a conditional statement.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DISH. The first and last syllables are reduced, so the ending sounds like 'shun' rather than 'tee-on'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In logic and math the word is purely technical, with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: In logic, mathematics and statistics, Americans use condition for any requirement that must be met, such as a necessary or sufficient condition. In everyday speech the word is more often used for a stipulation, as in 'on one condition'. Physical or medical uses, such as 'in good condition' or 'a heart condition', are also common, but they are separate senses.

distinctions.note: A circumstance is a fact about the situation that may be relevant, while a condition is a requirement that must be satisfied.
A premise is a statement assumed as the starting point of an argument, whereas a condition limits when something else is true.
A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation, while a condition is a constraint under which a claim holds.

examples.everyday: My mom said I can go to the party on one condition: I finish my homework first.
examples.professional: Before we deploy, we need to confirm that the condition on the input data holds, or the model's predictions won't be valid.
examples.analytical: The implication holds only under the condition that the set is finite, so the general claim does not follow without that assumption.

nuance.analogy: A condition is like a gate: nothing passes through until the requirement is met.
nuance.etymology: From Latin condicio, 'agreement, stipulation', from condicere, 'to agree together'.
common_mistakes: Using 'condition' as a verb meaning 'a requirement' (in the verb sense it means to train or prepare, so say 'set a condition').
Saying 'on condition' followed by a noun without 'that' or a clause: say 'on condition that you finish' or 'on one condition'.

condition.etymology: From Middle English *condicioun*, from Old French *condicion* (French *condition*), from Latin *condicio*.

senses.definition: The process of conniving or conspiring.
senses.example: The scandal came to light because of the manager's connivance with the suppliers.

core.definition: Secret cooperation with wrongdoing, or deliberately ignoring it so that it can continue.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on 'NYVE', the second syllable. The final -vance is a reduced 'vuns', without a clear 'ah' sound, so don't say 'kuh-NIV-ance'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It always implies wrongdoing or deliberate tolerance of it.
nuance.usage_note: You will see 'connivance' in news, legal and literary writing, but rarely in casual speech. Common phrases are 'with the connivance of' and 'without the connivance of'. If you just mean someone is sneaky, use 'scheming' or 'sly' instead.

distinctions.note: Collusion is a secret agreement to cooperate for an unfair or illegal goal; connivance can be passive, simply ignoring a wrong on purpose.
Complicity is involvement in wrongdoing and is broader; connivance specifically refers to knowingly allowing or overlooking it.

examples.everyday: My sister covered for me when I got home late, with a little connivance from Dad.
examples.professional: The audit found that some managers tolerated the vendor fraud through quiet connivance.
examples.analytical: Moral responsibility extends beyond the perpetrators to those whose connivance made the abuses possible.

nuance.analogy: Like a lifeguard who sees a swimmer struggling and looks away, connivance is wrongdoing made possible by deliberate silence.
nuance.etymology: From Latin connivere, 'to close the eyes' or 'wink at', used of tolerating wrongdoing.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun 'connivance' with the adjective 'conniving'; say 'with his connivance', not 'with his conniving'.
Assuming it means cleverness; it always implies wrongdoing or deliberate tolerance.

connivance.etymology: From early, replaced earlier form *connivence*, from Latin *connīventia*, from *connīvēns* (“winking”).

senses.definition: An act of conquest.
senses.example: The conquering of the island by the empire took several bloody decades.

core.definition: The act of taking control of a place or people by force, or of overcoming a difficult thing such as a fear.

pronunciation.tip: The -nk- before the k is pronounced as the velar nasal /ŋk/, not /nk/ with an n sound. The second syllable is a weak, r-colored 'ker'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in personal contexts such as conquering a fear, but negative when it describes military or colonial takeovers of people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans normally use 'conquest' for the noun, as in 'the conquest of Mexico'. 'The conquering of' sounds literary or historical. In everyday talk, say 'winning', 'taking over' or 'beating', for example 'conquering my fear of heights'. For a people or nation, the word carries colonial associations, so consider the context.

distinctions.note: Conquest is the usual noun and can name the result; conquering names the act or process.
Defeating only means winning against an opponent; conquering suggests taking control afterward.
Overcoming is common for obstacles and problems; conquering suggests a stronger, more decisive struggle.

examples.everyday: Learning to ride a bike was a big deal for her, a real conquering of her fear of falling.
examples.professional: The conquering of the new market took two years and a dedicated sales team.
examples.analytical: Gibbon's account of the conquering of Rome's provinces shows how military success reshaped their administration and their loyalties.

nuance.analogy: Like a flag planted on a summit: the climb is the conquering, and the flag is the claim.
nuance.etymology: From conquer, from Old French conquerre and Latin conquaerere, with the English suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the -nk- as /nk/ rather than /ŋk/ in KONG.
Using 'conquering' as a formal name for a single event; historical events use 'Conquest', as in 'the Norman Conquest'.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or depending on the context of information; relating to the situation or location in which the information was found.
senses.example: Contextual clues in the article helped me guess the meaning of the word.

core.definition: Depending on or related to the surrounding situation, background, or circumstances in which something appears.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on TEKST, the second syllable. The -tual ending is pronounced choo-ul, with the t becoming ch.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contextual in academic, professional, and technical writing, especially in discussions of meaning, data, or search. It is less common in casual speech, where people usually say depends on the situation. The adjective is often paired with information or advertising.

distinctions.note: Situational is more general and everyday, while contextual often refers to information or meaning around a specific item.
Contextualized is the past participle form used as an adjective to describe something already placed in a context.

examples.everyday: I didn't know the word, but the contextual clues in the sentence helped me guess it.
examples.professional: The recommendation engine uses contextual signals like time of day and device type to rank results.
examples.analytical: A proposition's truth is often contextual, depending on the assumptions and purposes of the speaker.

nuance.analogy: Contextual meaning is like a single note in music: it sounds different depending on the chords around it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contextus, a weaving together, with the suffix -al.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the ch sound as k, saying kun-TEKST-kwul.
Using contextual for context in a noun phrase, as in saying a contextual of the word.

senses.definition: To act contrary to an order; to fail to conform to a regulation or obligation.
senses.example: The landlord contravened the city housing code by renting out an unsafe basement apartment.

core.definition: To go against a law, rule, regulation, or agreement, breaking or violating it.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on VEEN, the final syllable. Americans often make the second syllable weak, so avoid stressing the first syllable as KAHN-truh-veen.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It implies breaking a rule or law, often in a serious or official way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use contravene in legal, regulatory, and official writing, such as 'the policy contravenes state law.' In everyday speech, they would say 'break,' 'go against,' or 'violate' instead. In a workplace, it sounds appropriately formal in a compliance memo or an HR policy discussion.

distinctions.note: Violate is the common everyday word for breaking a rule; contravene is more formal and often used for laws, policies, or official orders.
Contradict means to say the opposite of something; contravene means to act against a rule or obligation.

examples.everyday: The landlord can't raise the rent that way, because it contravenes the city's housing rules.
examples.professional: This data-sharing plan contravenes our privacy policy, so legal needs to review it before launch.
examples.analytical: A government act that contravenes a constitutional principle is void, whatever its political support.

nuance.analogy: Like driving through a red light, which goes directly against what the sign requires.
nuance.etymology: From Latin contra, against, and venire, to come.
common_mistakes: Using contravene for ordinary small mistakes; it implies a formal breach of a rule.
Stressing the first syllable, as in KAHN-trah-veen.

senses.definition: To convene, to cause to assemble for a meeting.
To call together.

core.definition: To formally call people together for a meeting, assembly, or council.

pronunciation.tip: The single stressed syllable is -VOKE, with the long 'oh' vowel. The k at the end is clearly pronounced, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It suggests an official or formal summons, often by a leader or governing body.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this verb in ordinary speech; they say 'call a meeting' or 'bring everyone together.' It appears in formal, legal, religious, or political writing, such as when a council or board is officially summoned. Using it casually would sound stiff or pretentious.

distinctions.note: Convene is the more common and everyday formal verb in American English, while convoke is rarer and more literary.
Summon suggests calling someone with authority to come, while convoke focuses on bringing a group together for an assembly.

examples.everyday: The homeowners' association president wants to convoke a quick meeting about the parking problem.
examples.professional: The board chair will convoke a special session next week to review the budget proposal.
examples.analytical: The emperor had the authority to convoke the council, and the decision to gather the bishops marked a turning point in the church's governance.

nuance.analogy: To convoke is like ringing a bell that brings every member of a community to the same room at the same time.
nuance.etymology: From Latin convocare, 'to call together,' from con- 'together' and vocare 'to call.'
common_mistakes: Using it when you mean 'invoke,' which means to call upon something, such as a law or a name.
Pronouncing the final k too softly or dropping it.

convoke.etymology: Borrowed from Middle French *convoquer*, from Latin *convocare*, from *con-* (“with”) + *vocō* (“to call”).

senses.definition: A book or an encyclopedia of recipes and cookery tips.
senses.example: They inherited an interesting nineteenth-century cookbook from their grandparents. It tells how to render lard.

senses.definition: Any book or set of strategies and tips.
senses.example: The Anarchist Cookbook

core.definition: A book of recipes and cooking instructions, often with tips on preparing and serving food.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on cook, and book has a weaker secondary stress. Both vowels are short, so avoid stretching them or saying kook-book.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests practical help, creativity, or family tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use cookbook for any book of recipes, from a family's spiral-bound collection to a famous chef's bestseller. You can say 'I'm looking for a vegetarian cookbook' in a bookstore or library. Figuratively, 'a cookbook for managers' means a practical how-to guide, but this use is informal. British speakers may say cookery book, but Americans say cookbook.

distinctions.note: A recipe is one set of instructions for one dish, while a cookbook is a collection of many recipes.
Cookery book is the British term; Americans say cookbook, so use it in American English.

examples.everyday: My aunt gave me her old cookbook, and the pages are covered in handwritten notes.
examples.professional: Our platform team wrote a cookbook of standard deployment steps for new engineers.
examples.analytical: The essay treats the early American cookbook as a document of household knowledge, economics, and gender.

nuance.analogy: A cookbook is like a map: it shows the route, but you still have to drive it.
nuance.etymology: A compound of cook and book, formed in English.
common_mistakes: Saying cookery book in an American store or library; ask for a cookbook.
Placing the main stress on book: say KUK-buk, not kuk-BUK.

cookbook.etymology: From *cook* + *book*; possibly also a German *Kochbuch*, from *kochen* (“cook”) + *Buch* (“book”).

senses.definition: Having no positive integer factors in common, aside from 1.
senses.example: 24 and 35 are coprime.

senses.definition: Having no positive integer factors, aside from 1, in common with one or more specified other positive integers.
senses.example: 24 is coprime to 35.

senses.definition: Whose greatest common divisor is a nonzero constant (i.e. polynomial of degree 0).
senses.example: Two polynomials are coprime when their greatest common divisor is a nonzero constant.

senses.definition: Whose sum is the whole ring; generating the whole ring.
senses.example: Two ideals I and J are coprime when their sum is the whole ring.

core.definition: In mathematics, having no positive common factor other than 1; two integers are coprime if their greatest common divisor is 1.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, prime. The first syllable is koh, not kop, and it carries a light secondary stress.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and precise. It is a standard term in mathematics and computing, with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coprime in mathematics classes, number theory, cryptography, and computer science. It is a technical adjective used in statements about integers, and it is often paired with relatively prime in textbooks. Outside technical settings, you will rarely hear it.

distinctions.note: Relatively prime is a synonym in standard usage, and textbooks use both terms for the same idea.
A prime number has exactly two divisors; coprime describes a relationship between two numbers that share no common factor.

examples.everyday: My kid asked whether 8 and 15 are coprime, and I had to check my notes to be sure.
examples.professional: The step size must be coprime to the modulus, so the sequence covers every residue before repeating.
examples.analytical: If a and n are coprime, then a has a multiplicative inverse modulo n, which is the basis of the cryptographic argument.

nuance.analogy: Two coprime numbers are like two dance partners who share no steps: they move independently and never repeat the same pattern together.
nuance.etymology: From co-, meaning together, plus prime, meaning having no divisors except one and itself.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first syllable as kop, as in cop; the correct vowel is oh, as in co-worker.
Confusing coprime with prime; two numbers can be coprime even if neither is prime, such as 8 and 15.

senses.definition: Of, relating to or pertaining to or resembling red algae of the family Corallinaceae.
Of, pertaining to, or resembling the material coral.
Describing rock formed from the skeletons of such algae.
Any calcareous species of red algae of the family Corallinaceae.
senses.example: Coralline algae coat the reef's rocky surfaces, giving them a pinkish crust under the water.

senses.definition: An animal that resembles such a coral.
senses.example: Under the microscope, the coralline looked like coral but was actually a bryozoan colony.

core.definition: Resembling coral, or describing red algae that build hard calcium carbonate skeletons, or rock formed from them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KOR, and keep the middle -uh- weak. The ending is usually said as 'line' or 'lin', and both are used by American scientists.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise scientific term, though it can also describe something pinkish or branching in a poetic way.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coralline mainly in marine biology, geology, and paleoclimate research. In everyday speech people say coral or pink algae instead. When a scientist says coralline algae, they mean a group of red algae with hard calcareous structures, not the animal coral.

distinctions.note: Coral is the animal or its skeleton, while coralline describes algae or rock with a coral-like structure.
Calcareous describes anything containing calcium carbonate, while coralline specifically refers to coral-like algae or the material they form.
Limestone is a general sedimentary rock, while coralline limestone is formed specifically from coralline algae or coral skeletons.

examples.everyday: Those pink crusty patches on the rocks are coralline algae, not actual coral.
examples.professional: The core samples contain coralline sediment that suggests the water was warmer during that period.
examples.analytical: Coralline algae record past sea temperatures in their calcium carbonate layers, which is why geologists use them as climate proxies.

nuance.analogy: Coralline algae are like the bricks of a seawall built by tiny gardeners: their hard layers accumulate over time and preserve a record of the water around them.
nuance.etymology: From coral plus the suffix -ine, meaning resembling or pertaining to.
common_mistakes: Using coralline to mean the animal coral, when it refers to algae or coral-like material.
Confusing the two ways of pronouncing the ending, which is acceptable in both forms, and then changing the stress.
Dropping the r in the first syllable; it is clearly pronounced in American English.

coralline.etymology: From French *corallin*, from Latin *corallinus*, from *corallium* (“coral”), via Greek probably of Semitic origin.

senses.definition: Fitted with a cord.
Having the appearance of cords or furrows.
senses.example: the hard, corded upper arms of a bodybuilder

senses.definition: Of wood: piled in cords.
senses.example: The firewood was corded neatly along the fence, ready for winter.

senses.definition: Wound about with a cord or cords of a specified tincture.
senses.example: The package was corded in red twine and sealed with wax.

core.definition: Having a cord attached, such as a corded phone or drill that plugs into the wall instead of running on batteries.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, KORD. The final -ed after a d sounds like 'id', and the r is clearly pronounced, so it does not sound like 'cord-d'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical description of how a device is powered or how a fabric looks.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use corded in everyday shopping and home talk, for example comparing corded and cordless vacuums or drills. For fabric, corded describes a ribbed texture, such as corded velvet. In the lumber trade, corded refers to firewood stacked in cords, a standard unit of volume.

distinctions.note: Corded means it plugs into power through a cord, while cordless means it runs on a battery or wireless power.
Ribbed is a general term for raised lines, while corded specifically describes raised cords or ridges, often in fabric.
Wired is used for connected electronics and networks, while corded describes a device with a power cord, especially appliances and tools.

examples.everyday: I'd rather get the corded drill, since it never runs out of battery in the middle of a project.
examples.professional: We're ordering corded headsets for the call center because they're more reliable than wireless ones.
examples.analytical: The corded texture of the fabric, with its raised ribs, changes how it reflects light under raking illumination.

nuance.analogy: A corded device is like a garden hose: it stays connected to the source, so you never run out of water, but you're limited by how far the hose reaches.
nuance.etymology: From cord plus the past-participle ending -ed.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the final -ed as a separate syllable like 'cord-ed' in the wrong place, or dropping the d sound.
Confusing corded with cordless when shopping; check which one you need before buying.
Using corded to describe a plain fabric; it refers specifically to a ribbed or corded texture.

senses.definition: A body corporate, created by law or under authority of law, having a continuous existence independent of the existences of its members, and powers and liabilities distinct from those of its members.
senses.example: The corporation filed its annual report with the state and paid its taxes.

senses.definition: The municipal governing body of a borough or city.
senses.example: The city corporation voted to approve the new budget for road repairs.

senses.definition: (historical) In Fascist Italy, a joint association of employers' and workers' representatives.
senses.example: Under Mussolini, each corporation brought employers and unions together under state supervision.
senses.label: historical

senses.definition: (dated) A protruding belly.
senses.example: After the holidays, his corporation was impossible to hide under the tight shirt.
senses.label: dated

core.definition: A business or organization legally treated as a separate entity from its owners, able to own property, sign contracts, and be sued.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the third syllable, 'RAY', and say the -tion ending as 'shun'. The middle vowel is a reduced 'uh'; don't say 'kor-por-ation' with full vowels.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a legal and business term. It can sound impersonal or powerful, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'corporation' in business, law, finance, and news, and they often abbreviate it as 'Corp.' in company names. Everyday conversation usually uses 'company' or 'business' instead. In US municipal law, a 'municipal corporation' refers to a city government, which is a rare but correct use.

distinctions.note: Company is the everyday word for any business, while corporation is the legal form of a business that is formally incorporated.
Incorporation is the process of forming a corporation, while corporation is the entity that results from that process.

examples.everyday: My neighbor works for a big corporation, but his small bakery is just a sole proprietorship.
examples.professional: The vendor is a Delaware corporation, so the contract should list its registered agent for legal notices.
examples.analytical: A corporation is a legal person, able to hold rights and duties apart from the people who own it.

nuance.analogy: A corporation is like a legal person created by paperwork: it can sign, own, and be sued, even though no single human is the whole company.
nuance.etymology: From Latin corporatio, from corporare 'to form into a body,' from corpus 'body.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'corporation' for every business, even a small shop that is not incorporated.
Confusing 'corporation' with 'incorporation', the process of forming a corporation.

corporation.etymology: From Middle English *corporacion*, *corporation*, from Late Latin *corporatio* (“assumption of a body”), from Latin *corporatus*, past participle of *corporō* (“to form into a body”); see *corporate*.

senses.definition: In a coterminous manner; ending together.

core.definition: In a way that shares the same boundaries or extent, so that two things begin and end together.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on the middle syllable 'ter.' Don't drop the extra syllables in 'mi-nous-ly,' and reduce the final syllables to a quick 'nuhs-lee.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise, technical word with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mainly in legal, administrative, geographic or academic writing, for example when a school district runs coterminously with a town. The adverb is rare in speech, so in everyday talk people usually say the district 'lines up exactly with' the town. For a plain alternative, use 'at the same boundaries' or 'coextensively.'

distinctions.note: Contiguous means touching or adjacent, but the areas need not have the same boundaries, while coterminous means the boundaries match exactly.
Concurrent means happening at the same time, while coterminous refers to shared spatial or temporal limits, so the two words are not interchangeable.
Coextensive is a close synonym that means having the same extent, and it is more common in everyday academic writing than coterminously.

examples.professional: The new data layer is defined coterminously with the census tract, so the two datasets should join cleanly.
examples.analytical: The nation's moral claims and its legal jurisdiction run coterminously, a conflation the essay carefully critiques.

nuance.analogy: Like two shadows that start and stop at exactly the same place.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin coterminus (having the same boundary), from co- (together) plus terminus (boundary, end).
common_mistakes: Confusing coterminous with contiguous, which means only that two areas touch.
Stressing the first syllable, as in 'KOH-tur-mi-nus-lee,' rather than the middle syllable.
Spelling it conterminous; the spelling coterminous is far more common in American writing.

senses.definition: A cough; the act of coughing.
senses.example: Her persistent coughing kept me awake all night, so I finally bought cough syrup.

senses.definition: A repetitive vocalisation of a bird or other animal that resembles human coughing.
senses.example: Early each morning, the pheasant's coughing call echoed across the wooded ravine behind our cabin.

core.definition: The act of forcing air out of the lungs with a sudden, harsh sound, often a sign of illness or irritation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, KAH. The gh is silent and the ng is one nasal sound, so avoid adding an extra vowel like KAH-fee-ing.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in most settings, but a persistent or loud cough can sound worrying, so a short apology is polite.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use coughing as a noun for the act or sound, often in phrases like a coughing fit or a coughing spell. In a meeting or restaurant, turn away, cover your mouth, and say Sorry or Excuse me. Americans rarely comment on someone else's coughing except to ask if they are okay or to offer water.

distinctions.note: Cough is the basic verb and noun; coughing usually names the ongoing act or the repeated sound.
A sneeze is a sudden forceful expulsion through the nose and mouth, not a repeated sound from the throat.
Informal for a dry, rough, repeated cough; it suggests a persistent, unpleasant cough.

examples.everyday: Sorry about the coughing, it's just a tickle and I'm fine.
examples.professional: Sorry for the coughing earlier; I'll mute my mic if it starts again during the call.
examples.analytical: Persistent coughing is a symptom doctors use to narrow a diagnosis, but by itself it rarely identifies a single cause.

nuance.analogy: Coughing is the body's emergency exhaust valve, forcing out whatever is blocking the airway.
nuance.etymology: Coughing is the -ing form of cough, from Middle English coughen, probably imitative.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the gh as a hard g or k as in through; in cough the gh is pronounced f, so the word is kahf.
Using coughing as a verb; the verb is cough, while coughing is the gerund or noun.

senses.definition: A plan; a set of intended actions, through which one intends to achieve a goal.
senses.example: After weighing the risks, the team agreed on a course of action for the server migration.

core.definition: A plan or set of steps someone decides to take to reach a goal or solve a problem.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AK in action, and of reduces to a weak uhv. The -tion ending is shuhn, so say kors-uhv-AK-shuhn, linking the words smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and businesslike. It sounds appropriate for meetings and decisions, but can sound stiff in casual talk.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use course of action often in meetings, emails and discussions of problems, as in 'What's the best course of action here?' For casual talk, people say What should we do? or What's our plan? A natural reply is 'Let's go with option B' or 'I'd recommend we wait a week.'

distinctions.note: A plan is a general idea or schedule, while a course of action emphasizes a chosen set of steps among alternatives.
A strategy is a broad, long-term approach, while a course of action is a specific set of steps taken now.
An option is a possible choice before you decide, while a course of action is the choice you commit to.

collocations: the most prudent course of action
agree on a course of action

examples.everyday: The landlord won't fix the heat, so what's our best course of action?
examples.professional: Let's agree on a course of action before Friday's release so the team knows what to do.
examples.analytical: Aristotle's account of deliberation treats a course of action as the means chosen to reach an end already accepted.

nuance.analogy: A course of action is a route on a map: you know the destination, and you choose which road to take.
nuance.etymology: Course is from Latin cursus, 'running'; action is from Latin actio, 'a doing'.
common_mistakes: Using course of action for a single small step; it refers to an overall plan.
Pluralizing it as courses of action when you mean a single plan; the singular is usually correct.

senses.definition: One who is highly skilled at one's trade; an artisan or artificer.
senses.example: My grandfather was a craftsman who could build a staircase without drawing a single plan.

senses.definition: A person who makes or creates material objects partly or entirely by hand.
senses.example: The potter is a craftsman who throws and glazes every bowl herself.

senses.definition: A person who produces arts and crafts.
senses.example: At the county fair, the craftsman sold woven baskets and hand-carved wooden spoons.

core.definition: A person who is highly skilled at making things by hand, such as a carpenter, potter, or woodworker.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced schwa, so it sounds like 'KRAFTS-mun', not 'man' with a full vowel. The ts cluster is one smooth sound.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises skill, patience, and pride in work, and it is often used to honor workers in traditional trades.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'craftsman' for skilled artisans in woodworking, furniture, jewelry, and building trades, and it is often used with respect. Modern American speech increasingly uses 'craftsperson' or 'artisan,' especially in formal writing. A natural reply to praise for a craftsman's work is 'Thanks, I put a lot of time into it.'

distinctions.note: Artisan suggests a small-scale maker often with artistic emphasis; craftsman focuses more on technical skill in a trade.
An artist emphasizes creative expression, while a craftsman emphasizes technical mastery and functional work.

examples.everyday: That old guy at the hardware store is a real craftsman, and he can fix almost any wooden chair.
examples.professional: We hired a local craftsman to restore the lobby's oak paneling for the company's new headquarters.
examples.analytical: The Protestant Reformers often praised the craftsman's vocation as a form of service, though the medieval guild system shaped how that dignity was understood.

nuance.analogy: A craftsman is like a sculptor of daily life, shaping wood or metal with patience until the object is both useful and beautiful.
nuance.etymology: Craft from Old English craeft, skill, plus man.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'man' with a full vowel instead of the reduced 'mun'.
Using craftsman for a general worker; it implies skilled, handmade work.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, the word craftsman translates several terms. The Hebrew 'charash' refers to a skilled worker in metal, wood, or stone, and the Greek 'technites' appears in Acts 19:24 and 19:25, describing silversmiths and other craftsmen in Ephesus whose trade was threatened by Paul's preaching. These passages show craftsmen as workers with economic and social standing.

senses.definition: Characterized by rugged, sharp, or coarse features.
senses.example: The goat climbed up the craggy rocks.
