nuance.connotation: Mildly negative or affectionate; it points to a harmless flaw rather than a serious fault.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use foible in writing, speeches, or witty conversation, not in ordinary small talk. It is a polite way to describe a quirk, like 'Everyone has their foibles.' In casual speech Americans more often say 'quirk' or 'weird habit.' Using it can sound slightly bookish, so it works best in a thoughtful remark about someone you know well.

distinctions.note: A quirk is a casual, everyday oddity; foible is more formal and can hint at a character weakness.
A vice is a serious moral fault, while a foible is a minor, forgivable failing.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's foible is that she won't throw anything away, but we love her anyway.
examples.professional: Every manager has a foible or two, so it helps to know how your boss likes to communicate.
examples.analytical: The novel treats its hero's vanity as a foible rather than a vice, which lets the reader sympathize with him.

nuance.analogy: A foible is like a dent in a well-loved car: it is part of its character and does not stop it from running.
nuance.etymology: From French 'foible,' meaning weak, from 'faible,' weak, ultimately from Latin 'flebilis,' tearful; the sword sense developed from the weaker part of a blade.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it 'fo-BEEL' or 'FOY-bul' with a long, stressed final syllable.
Confusing it with 'fable' in speech, since they sound similar.

senses.definition: A very thin sheet of metal.
Thin aluminum/aluminum (or, formerly, tin) used for wrapping food.
senses.example: wrap the sandwich up in foil

senses.definition: A thin layer of metal put between a jewel and its setting to make it seem more brilliant.
senses.example: The jeweler placed a thin silver foil beneath the diamond to make it sparkle more.

senses.definition: In literature, theater/theater, etc. a character who helps emphasize the traits of the main character and who usually acts as an opponent or antagonist, but can also serve as the sidekick of the protagonist.
senses.example: Her quiet sister was the perfect foil for her loud, dramatic personality.

senses.definition: Anything that acts by contrast to emphasize the characteristics of something.
senses.example: The calm, patient teacher was a foil to the students' restless energy.

senses.definition: A very thin sword with a blunted (or foiled) tip.
senses.example: She practiced lunges with her foil at the fencing club every Tuesday evening.

senses.definition: A thin, transparent plastic material on which marks are made and projected for the purposes of presentation. See transparency.
senses.example: The overhead projector showed her charts on clear plastic foils during the lecture.

senses.definition: A premium trading card with a glossy finish.
senses.example: He pulled a rare holographic foil card from the pack of baseball cards.

senses.definition: A stylized flower or leaf.
senses.example: The architect carved a stylized foil pattern into the stone arch above the doorway.

senses.definition: Clipping of hydrofoil.
senses.example: The boat began to foil as its hull lifted above the water.

senses.definition: Clipping of aerofoil/airfoil.
senses.example: Engineers redesigned the wing's foil to reduce drag at high altitudes.

senses.definition: Failure when on the point of attainment; defeat; frustration; miscarriage.
senses.example: Just as victory seemed certain, a last-minute fumble brought a painful foil.

senses.definition: One of the incorrect answers presented in a multiple-choice test.
senses.example: (This entry needs quotations to illustrate usage. If you come across any interesting, durably archived quotes, then please add them!)

senses.definition: The track of an animal.
senses.example: The hunter followed the deer's foil through the wet snow for two miles.

senses.definition: A small arc in the tracery of a window, etc.
senses.example: The cathedral window's stone tracery included a delicate foil between each pointed arch.

senses.definition: To cover or wrap with foil.
senses.example: Before baking, she foiled the leftover potatoes to keep them warm.

senses.definition: Clipping of hydrofoil.
senses.example: The boat began to foil as its hull lifted above the water.

senses.definition: To prevent (something) from being accomplished.
senses.example: They foiled my plans.

senses.definition: To prevent (someone) from accomplishing something.
senses.example: I was foiled by my superior.

senses.definition: To blunt; to dull; to spoil.
senses.example: Her carefully planned surprise party was foiled when someone revealed the secret early.

senses.definition: To expand a product of two or more algebraic expressions, typically binomials.
senses.example: To simplify the product, first foil the two binomials in the expression.

core.definition: A very thin sheet of metal, most often aluminum, used for wrapping or covering food; also a person or thing that contrasts with another.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the diphthong 'oy,' sounding like 'boy.' Keep the final 'l' clear and do not add a vowel after it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; the everyday sense is purely practical.
nuance.usage_note: In American kitchens, foil almost always means aluminum foil, and people say 'cover it with foil' or 'wrap it in foil.' Americans sometimes shorten it casually, but 'aluminum foil' is clearest in a store. In literature, foil describes a character who contrasts with a main character and makes that character's traits stand out.

distinctions.note: Tinfoil is an older term for foil made from tin; Americans now usually say aluminum foil, and tinfoil often sounds old-fashioned.
Plastic wrap is clingy film for covering bowls; foil is metal and can go in the oven.

examples.everyday: Can you grab the foil? I want to wrap the leftovers before we put them in the fridge.
examples.professional: We'll bake the chicken in a foil pan so cleanup at the potluck is easy.
examples.analytical: The sidekick serves as a foil to the detective, sharpening our sense of his brilliance by contrast.

nuance.analogy: Foil is like a thin skin of metal: light enough to crumple in your hand, but strong enough to keep heat and air out.
nuance.etymology: From Old French 'foille,' from Latin 'folium,' leaf, in the sense of a thin metal leaf.
common_mistakes: Saying 'the foil' for all wrapping: Americans say 'plastic wrap' or 'wax paper' for other materials.
Using foil as a verb in conversation without an object, such as 'foil the food'; the phrase is 'wrap it in foil.'

foil.etymology: From Middle English *foyle*, from Middle French *fueille*, from Old French *fueille* (“plant leaf”), from Late Latin *folia*, the plural of *folium*, mistaken as a singular feminine.

senses.definition: Mathematical logic.
A particular logical calculus.

core.definition: The study of valid reasoning using symbols and strict rules, so that the structure of an argument can be tested apart from its content.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LAH in 'logic,' and the 'o' is the cot vowel, which Americans pronounce the same as 'caught' in many regions. Say the g softly, like the 'j' in 'jet.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in philosophy, mathematics, and computer science.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use formal logic in university courses, computer science, and philosophy. Ordinary speakers might say 'logic' or 'reasoning' instead. The term covers systems like propositional and predicate logic, which are central to mathematical proof and programming.

distinctions.note: Informal logic evaluates everyday arguments using judgment and examples; formal logic uses symbols and strict rules.
Mathematical logic is a branch of mathematics that studies formal systems; formal logic is a broader term that can include other calculi.
Symbolic logic emphasizes the use of symbols; formal logic emphasizes structure and rules, and the two overlap heavily.

examples.everyday: My niece is taking a formal logic class this semester and keeps quizzing me on truth tables.
examples.professional: Our data validation rules were designed using formal logic, so each check can be verified mechanically.
examples.analytical: Formal logic makes explicit the inferential structure of an argument, allowing us to separate validity from the truth of its premises.

nuance.analogy: Like a grammar for arguments: it tells you whether the sentence is well built, regardless of what it says.
nuance.etymology: Formal comes from Latin formalis; logic comes from Greek logikē, meaning the art of reasoning.
common_mistakes: Using formal logic to mean any careful thinking; it refers to a specific symbolic system.
Assuming all formal logic uses only one notation, when many systems exist.

senses.definition: (archaic) Forward in time, place or degree.
senses.example: From that day forth, she never spoke of her brother again.
senses.label: archaic

senses.definition: (archaic) Out into view; from a particular place or position.
senses.example: The plants in spring put forth leaves.
senses.label: archaic

senses.definition: (obsolete) Beyond a (certain) boundary; away; abroad; out.
senses.example: He sent his servants forth across the land to gather the harvest.
senses.label: obsolete

senses.definition: (obsolete) Forth from; out of.
senses.example: Forth the gate the knight rode, his armor shining in the dawn.
senses.label: obsolete

senses.definition: Misspelling of fourth.
Misspelling of fourth.

core.definition: Forward or out into view; used mainly in fixed phrases such as 'back and forth', 'and so forth' and 'from this day forth'.

pronunciation.tip: In General American, forth sounds exactly like fourth, with an r after the vowel and a voiceless th at the end. Do not add a vowel after the r or pronounce the th as a 't' or 'd'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In set phrases it is ordinary, while in older forms like 'go forth' it can sound solemn or ceremonial.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use forth in everyday speech mainly in fixed phrases: 'back and forth', 'and so forth' and 'bring forth'. Alone, it sounds old-fashioned, so 'forward' is the everyday choice. 'From this day forth' is used in ceremonies or formal announcements. Don't write forth when you mean fourth.

distinctions.note: Forward is the everyday word for moving ahead or toward the front; forth is mostly literary or used in fixed phrases.
Forth and fourth sound the same in General American, but forth means forward or out, while fourth is the ordinal number 4th.

examples.everyday: We went back and forth about the dinner plans until we finally picked a place near the park.
examples.professional: We'll go back and forth on the budget numbers and send the final draft to finance by Friday.
examples.analytical: The Psalmist's picture of people going forth to their work frames human labor as a movement outward into the world.

nuance.analogy: Forth is like a door swinging open: it points outward, away from where you started.
nuance.etymology: From Old English forð, meaning forward or onward.
common_mistakes: Writing 'forth' when you mean 'fourth', since they sound the same but have different meanings.
Using 'forth' alone in everyday speech where 'forward' is natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb yatsa, to go out, or come out, is often translated with forth in the RSV, as when people go forth to their work in Psalm 104:23. Genesis 1:11 describes the earth putting forth vegetation, using a Hebrew verb for bringing forth growth. These passages show forth as a way of describing movement or growth outward.

forth.etymology: From Middle English *forth*, from Old English *forþ*, from **forþ*, from Proto-Germanic **furþą*, from Proto-Indo-European, from **per-*.

senses.definition: Reasoning from known facts forward through rules to reach new conclusions.
senses.example: Our expert system uses forward chaining, applying the rules to the facts until no new conclusions appear.

core.definition: A reasoning method that starts with known facts and applies rules forward to reach new conclusions.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on CHAIN, and forward is a secondary-stress word with a reduced final syllable. The d in forward is often nearly silent before a consonant, so it sounds like FOR-werd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise technical term.
nuance.usage_note: In American AI, data science, and logic courses, forward chaining is standard terminology for data-driven inference in rule-based systems. Engineers contrast it with backward chaining, which starts from a goal. Outside technical contexts, people would just say reasoning from the facts.

distinctions.note: Backward chaining starts from a goal and works backward to see which facts would support it; forward chaining starts from facts and works toward conclusions.
Inference is the general process of drawing conclusions; forward chaining is one specific method of doing it in rule systems.

examples.everyday: I told my nephew that forward chaining means starting with the facts and seeing where they lead.
examples.professional: We used forward chaining in the rules engine to flag suspicious transactions as soon as the data arrived.
examples.analytical: Forward chaining derives conclusions from given premises, whereas backward chaining starts from a goal and works back to the facts it needs.

nuance.analogy: Like following a recipe from the ingredients you already have to see what dish you can make.
common_mistakes: Confusing forward chaining with backward chaining
Stressing forward instead of chaining
Using it for general forward planning outside AI and logic

conversation.text: Forward chaining starts from known facts and applies rules until no new facts can be derived.
We use forward chaining because new sensor readings arrive continuously and should trigger alerts.

senses.definition: In a state of fossilization; preserved in rock.
senses.example: The hikers found a fossilized shell embedded in the limestone cliff above the creek.

senses.definition: Old-fashioned, outmoded, or rigidly fixed in a way that is resistant to change.
senses.example: Our manager's fossilized habits made it impossible to try any new software.

senses.definition: Having become a fossil; no longer productive.
senses.example: The fossilized committee had met for decades without producing a single useful recommendation.

core.definition: Rigidly stuck in old ways and out of date, or turned into a fossil over long periods of time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final -d is silent after z, so the word ends in a single sound like 'FAH-suh-lyzd' with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it criticizes ideas, rules, or people as rigid and out of date.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use fossilized to describe old rules, systems, or beliefs that refuse to change, often with a sigh of frustration. Calling a person fossilized can sound rude, so use it carefully about people. For neutral talk about old objects or remains, use 'fossilized' only in science contexts.

distinctions.note: Outdated simply means no longer current, while fossilized suggests something has become rigid and unable to change.
Old-fashioned can be affectionate or nostalgic, while fossilized is usually critical.

examples.everyday: My grandmother's ideas about money are fossilized, and she won't even try a banking app.
examples.professional: Our reporting system is fossilized, so every request still requires a manual export from the old database.
examples.analytical: A fossilized doctrine is one repeated word for word without regard to changes in the context it was meant to address.

nuance.analogy: Like a stiff old tree that can no longer bend in the wind.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of fossilize, from fossil.
common_mistakes: Using fossilized as a casual compliment; it usually sounds critical in American English.
Using it for people in a neutral way; calling someone fossilized can sound insulting.

senses.definition: Having four wheels.
Having a transmission that drives all four wheels.

core.definition: Having four wheels; in vehicles, describing a system that drives power to all four wheels for better traction.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on WEEL, with fohr as a secondary stress. Keep the r in fohr and end the word with a clear L, not a vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. In car advertising it signals capability and toughness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say four-wheel drive, which is common for trucks and SUVs, and often abbreviated 4WD. The adjective form is used before nouns, as in a four-wheel-drive truck. In everyday talk, people say four-by-four or 4x4 with the same meaning in many areas.

distinctions.note: Four-wheel drive usually has a selectable low-range gear for off-road use; all-wheel drive is usually automatic and designed for on-road traction.

examples.everyday: We need a four-wheel-drive truck to get up that muddy road to the cabin.
examples.professional: The fleet manager asked for four-wheel models for the field crews, since winter roads are unreliable.
examples.analytical: Four-wheel traction systems distribute torque differently from front-wheel layouts, which changes how vehicles handle on slippery surfaces.

nuance.analogy: Four-wheel traction is like wearing boots with grip on both feet, so the whole vehicle stays steady on slippery ground.
nuance.etymology: Four (from Old English feower) plus wheel (from Old English hweol).
common_mistakes: Dropping drive in four-wheel drive, which makes the phrase unclear to Americans.
Writing four wheel without the hyphen before a noun.

senses.definition: The principles of a freethinker; free thought.
senses.example: Her grandfather's freethinking led him to question every sermon he heard at church.

core.definition: The practice of forming your own opinions by reason rather than accepting authority, especially on religious and traditional beliefs.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on FREE, with a lighter stress on THINK. End with the velar 'ng' sound in both -ing syllables, not an 'n' or a long 'eeng.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive among admirers, who see it as open-minded and independent, and negative among critics, who may see it as irreligious or disrespectful of tradition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use freethinking mostly in discussions of history, philosophy, religion and politics, and they rarely use it for casual personal opinions. It is often applied to Enlightenment thinkers, nineteenth-century American reformers or skeptics. If you call someone a freethinker, be aware that some religious listeners may hear it as a challenge to faith.

distinctions.note: The two words are nearly interchangeable, but freethinking more often names an attitude or practice, while freethought more often names a tradition or movement.
Critical thinking is a general method for evaluating claims, while freethinking carries a stronger stance of independence from authority, especially religious authority.
Skepticism is doubt about specific claims, while freethinking is a broader commitment to reason over inherited beliefs.

examples.everyday: My uncle is a real freethinking type; he never takes anyone's word for anything and loves a good argument.
examples.professional: Our team values freethinking, so challenge the assumptions in the design doc before we commit to the architecture.
examples.analytical: Eighteenth-century freethinking undermined the authority of revealed religion by insisting that reason alone must test every claim.

nuance.analogy: Freethinking is like a cook who tastes the recipe before following it: the ingredients are still there, but each one is checked by the cook's own judgment.
nuance.etymology: An English compound of free (not bound by authority) and thinking.
common_mistakes: Using freethinking as a personal label in casual talk, where a more natural phrase like open-minded or independent-minded might be better.
Confusing freethinking with free-spirited, which describes an easygoing or unconventional personality rather than an intellectual stance.
Stressing the wrong syllable, saying 'free-THINK-ing' instead of 'FREE-think-ing.'

senses.definition: Easily broken into small fragments, crumbled, or reduced to powder.
Of a poison, likely to crumble and become airborne, thus becoming a health risk.
senses.example: The toxin in the old pesticide is so friable that it easily becomes airborne during sanding.

senses.definition: Of a number: smooth, that factors completely into small prime numbers.
senses.example: The sieve program rejected any number that was not friable over the first hundred primes.

senses.definition: Of soil, loose and large-grained in consistency.
senses.example: Sand has been incorporated to make the soil more friable.

core.definition: Easily broken into small pieces or crumbled into powder, such as soil, rock, or baked goods.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, FRY. Many learners say three full syllables, but the middle vowel is weak, so it sounds like 'FRY-uh-buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a descriptive term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly use friable in soil science, geology, chemistry, cooking, and some medical or workplace-safety contexts. In everyday speech they would say 'crumbly' or 'easy to break.' Hazard reports sometimes use it for materials like old insulation that release dust.

distinctions.note: Crumbly is the everyday word for something that falls apart in small pieces. Friable is more technical and is used in soil, mineral, and safety contexts.
Brittle means hard but likely to snap or shatter. Friable means soft or loose and likely to crumble.

examples.everyday: This cake is so friable that it falls apart if you touch it.
examples.professional: The inspector flagged the old ceiling tiles as friable, so the crew needed special containment.
examples.analytical: Gardeners value a loam because its friable structure lets roots spread and water drain freely.

nuance.analogy: Friable material is like a dry sugar cookie that breaks into crumbs the moment you press it.
nuance.etymology: From Latin friabilis, from friare, to crumble or rub to powder.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'fragile,' which describes delicate objects in general rather than crumbling material.
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'bul' instead of a reduced 'buhl'.

senses.definition: A frog.
A French person.
Froglike.
Suffering from a frog in one's throat; hoarse.
Inclined to fight; aggressive.
Energetic or strong.

core.definition: Informal: hoarse or rough-voiced, as if you have a frog in your throat, usually from a cold or from talking too long.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and keep the r rhotic. The g is hard, as in 'frog', and the ending is a light ee sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly playful; it describes a temporary voice problem and is not usually an insult.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say 'I sound froggy' or 'I have a froggy voice' when they are hoarse from a cold or from talking all day. Among adults the phrase 'a frog in my throat' is more common. The noun froggy, meaning a French person, is an old, offensive ethnic slur; do not use it.

distinctions.note: Hoarse is the standard word for a rough voice; froggy is informal and more playful, often used in everyday talk.
Husky means a deep, warm, slightly rough voice that may be attractive; froggy means a voice that sounds unclear or strained from a cold.

examples.everyday: Sorry, I sound froggy this morning; I think I'm getting a cold.
examples.professional: I'm a bit froggy, so I'll keep my remarks short on this call.
examples.analytical: The froggy quality of the recorded voice reduced its clarity, which mattered for accurate transcription.

nuance.analogy: Like a sore throat that makes your voice crackle, as if a small frog were hopping around inside.
nuance.etymology: From frog, from Old English frogga, with the informal suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using froggy for a French person; this is an offensive slur and should be avoided.
Saying 'I have froggy' without a noun; the usual forms are 'I sound froggy' or 'I have a frog in my throat'.

senses.definition: A command to approach the center of attention of an assemblage, as of military personnel or students.
senses.example: Okay, students, front and center, please, so everyone can see the demonstration.

senses.definition: At the center of attention.

core.definition: At the most visible position, in the center of attention; also a command to step forward into the middle of a group.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on CEN in center, with a lighter stress on front. Say the American r clearly in center and reduce and to a quick uhnd.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It highlights someone or something that is getting attention, which can be good (a star performer) or uncomfortable (a problem nobody wants to face), depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom for putting a person, idea, or problem in the spotlight, as in putting a product or issue front and center in a meeting. The command form, used by coaches, teachers, and drill instructors, means 'come up here where everyone can see you.' A natural reply to the command is simply to step forward.

distinctions.note: Center stage is literal (the middle of a theater stage) or figurative for the main role; front and center stresses visibility and can apply to ideas, not only people.
In the spotlight suggests public attention that may be temporary; front and center suggests a deliberate choice to make something the main focus.

collocations: keep an issue front and center

examples.everyday: Our kids are in the school play, so my wife and I got seats front and center.
examples.professional: Let's put customer retention front and center in the Q3 roadmap review.
examples.analytical: The essay places the problem of suffering front and center rather than treating it as an afterthought.

nuance.analogy: Like a performer walking into the spotlight at the front of the stage.
nuance.etymology: From American English usage of front and center, drawn from military drill commands telling soldiers to step forward to the middle of the formation.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in front and center' instead of 'front and center'.
Using it for a neutral location only; it normally implies attention or importance.

senses.definition: An injury suffered as a result of freezing of some part of the body, typically fingers, toes or the nose.
senses.example: After the blizzard, the hiker's fingers showed signs of frostbite and needed a doctor.

senses.definition: To expose to the effect of frost, or a frosty air; to blight or nip with frost. (Can we add an example for this sense?)
senses.example: The unexpected late frost frostbit the apple blossoms before the bees arrived.

senses.definition: To engage in winter sailboating.
senses.example: We frostbit all winter on the lake, bundled in wool and wet gloves.

core.definition: An injury to skin and tissue caused by exposure to freezing cold, usually affecting the fingers, toes, nose or ears.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FROST, with a lighter secondary stress on BITE. The o in frost is the 'aw' vowel as in 'off', not 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it names a serious medical injury, though people also use it loosely for mild cold-weather nipping.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use it in weather reports, winter safety advice, hiking and skiing talk. You typically say 'I got frostbite on my fingers' or 'He has frostbite'. The adjective is 'frostbitten', as in 'frostbitten toes'.

distinctions.note: Hypothermia is dangerously low core body temperature; frostbite is freezing damage to skin and tissue, usually in the extremities.
Frostnip is a mild, reversible cold injury with no lasting tissue damage; frostbite involves actual freezing of tissue.

examples.everyday: I wore gloves all day on the ski slopes, but my fingers still got a little frostbite.
examples.professional: Our field crews need better cold-weather gear, since two technicians came back last winter with frostbite.
examples.analytical: Frostbite depends less on temperature alone than on wind, moisture and exposure time, which together determine how quickly tissue freezes.

nuance.analogy: Like a sunburn from the cold: the damage comes from skin and tissue freezing, not just from feeling chilly.
nuance.etymology: Compound of frost (Old English forst) and bite (Old English bītan, to bite).
common_mistakes: Treating frostbite as just feeling very cold; it is actual tissue injury.
Pronouncing the o as in 'oh' instead of the 'aw' sound.

senses.definition: To go to hell; to disappear or go away; to screw oneself.
senses.example: I wish you'd just fuck off.

senses.definition: To leave unexpectedly.
senses.example: Haven't seen John for years. Someone said he had fucked off to Australia.

senses.definition: To fritter; to fuck around.
senses.example: Quit fucking off and get back to work before your boss notices.

senses.definition: To annoy, irritate.
senses.example: It really fucks me off when you do that.

senses.definition: To abandon.
senses.example: I'm bored. Shall we just fuck this off and go home?

senses.definition: Used other than figuratively or idiomatically: see fuck,‎ off.
Go away! Get lost!
senses.example: Leave me alone and fuck off, I'm trying to finish this proof.

senses.definition: An expression of disagreement or disbelief.
senses.example: Fuck off! You're joking, aren't you?

core.definition: A vulgar, rude way to tell someone to go away or leave you alone; also to waste time.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on off, pronounced AWF with the aw vowel, which many Americans pronounce like the a in cot. Do not give the main stress to fuck, because the particle carries the emphasis.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and rude; a hostile dismissal that can escalate arguments.
nuance.usage_note: This is one of the most aggressive phrases in American English, and using it at someone can start a fight or get you in trouble at work. Americans say it among friends, jokingly, or in anger. Polite alternatives are go away or leave me alone, while get lost is still informal. Never use it with a stranger, customer or boss.

distinctions.note: Go away is neutral and can be polite or firm, while fuck off is vulgar and insulting.
Get lost is informal and rude but much milder than fuck off, and Americans sometimes say it playfully among friends.

examples.everyday: When my neighbor started yelling at my kids over a ball, I just told him to fuck off and went inside.
examples.professional: If a vendor starts yelling in the meeting, do not tell them to fuck off; escalate it to the account manager.
examples.analytical: The phrase works as a social boundary and a power move, so its rudeness depends on who says it, to whom, and in what tone.

nuance.analogy: It is a door slammed hard rather than a polite knock.
nuance.etymology: Built from fuck, of uncertain origin, plus the adverb off.
common_mistakes: Using it as a brush-off with a boss or customer, where it can end a relationship.
Stressing fuck instead of off, which reverses the natural emphasis.

senses.definition: A theorem (or, in non-mathematical fields, a commonly accepted hypothesis) considered to be of central importance to a specified field.

core.definition: A theorem of central importance to a field, or in other fields, a widely accepted principle that organizes everything else in that field.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on MEN in fundamental, and the second word is stressed on the first syllable, THIR. The given stress on the first syllable of fundamental is wrong for American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals importance and central status.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and scientists use the term for a named result, such as the fundamental theorem of arithmetic or of calculus. In other fields, speakers use it for a principle everything else depends on, as in 'The fundamental theorem of economics is that incentives matter.' Americans say 'the fundamental theorem of X' with a definite article and a field name.

distinctions.note: A lemma is a helper result proved on the way to a larger theorem, while a fundamental theorem is a major result in its own right.
An axiom is assumed without proof, while a fundamental theorem is proved from more basic principles.

examples.everyday: My dad says the fundamental theorem of home repair is to turn off the power first.
examples.professional: Before we debug the model, let's review the fundamental theorem of statistics, the law of large numbers, which our results depend on.
examples.analytical: Whether the fundamental theorem of the field can bear the weight placed on it is a question the author never really answers.

nuance.analogy: A fundamental theorem is like the foundation of a house; the rooms may be different, but they all rest on it.
nuance.etymology: Fundamental comes from Late Latin fundamentalis, from Latin fundamentum, foundation; theorem comes from Greek theōrēma, a spectacle or thing contemplated.
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable of fundamental, as in FUN-duh-men-tal.
Forgetting the article 'the' in names like 'the fundamental theorem of calculus'.

senses.definition: Incapable of producing results, useless; doomed not to be successful; not worth attempting.
Insignificant; frivolous.
senses.example: He filled the meeting with futile remarks about trivial details that nobody needed.

core.definition: Useless and certain to fail; not worth trying because it cannot produce a result.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable is a reduced, weak 'uhl' sound. Do not pronounce it as 'FYOO-tile', which sounds like 'futile' and 'tile' blended.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes efforts that cannot succeed.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'futile' in both everyday and formal speech to describe efforts that are hopeless. It often appears in phrases like 'a futile attempt' or 'futile effort'. In casual talk, people might say 'pointless' or 'a waste of time', but 'futile' sounds natural in serious contexts.

distinctions.note: Useless is casual and general; futile suggests a struggle that is doomed to fail even with effort.
Pointless is more casual and can mean meaningless; futile emphasizes that the effort will not succeed.

examples.everyday: Trying to fix the old printer by myself was futile, so I just called the repair guy.
examples.professional: Continuing to patch the legacy system was futile, so the team proposed a full rewrite.
examples.analytical: Camus argues that the search for final meaning may be futile, yet humans still choose to live fully.

nuance.analogy: A futile effort is like trying to fill a bucket with a hole in the bottom: you keep pouring, but nothing stays.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'futilis' (pouring out easily, leaky, worthless), from 'fundere' (to pour).
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'FYOO-tile', which blends it with 'tile'.
Confusing it with 'fertile', which means productive, the opposite meaning.
patterns: it is futile to do sth

senses.definition: Initialism of for your information.
senses.example: FYI, there are donuts in the break room. [sentence adverbial use]

core.definition: Short for 'for your information'; used to pass along useful facts without asking for a response.

pronunciation.tip: Say each letter: F, Y, I. The stress falls on the final 'eye', and the 'Y' is a long 'eye' sound, so it is 'ef-wy-EYE' rather than a word like 'fy'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is polite in work email and chat, but it can sound blunt or slightly condescending if you use it to correct someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use FYI in email, Slack, and meetings to share information that does not require action, such as 'FYI, the meeting moved to 3 pm'. Often you see it in the subject line. In speech people usually say 'just so you know' or 'heads up'. A natural reply is 'thanks' or 'got it'.

distinctions.note: Heads up is spoken and warns about something coming; FYI is mainly written and simply passes along information.
Just so you know is friendlier and more casual in conversation; FYI is brisker and common in writing.

collocations: FYI in case you missed it

examples.everyday: FYI, the pharmacy closes at six today, so you'll need to pick up the prescription early.
examples.professional: FYI, the release freeze starts Thursday, so please merge anything you need before then.
examples.analytical: In the email, FYI signals that the information is offered for context and does not require a decision from the recipient.

nuance.analogy: Like a sticky note left on the fridge: it's useful to know, and you don't have to do anything about it right away.
nuance.etymology: Initialism of 'for your information', from the 1930s onward in American English.
common_mistakes: Saying 'fai-eye' or 'fee-eye' instead of spelling out each letter.
Using FYI when you are asking for a reply; in that case, write 'please let me know' instead.

conversation.text: FYI, the meeting moved to Conference Room B.
I'm forwarding this to you as an FYI; no action needed.
Just FYI, Tom is out sick today.

senses.definition: A chief lighting technician for a motion-picture or television production.
A glassblower.
Someone aboard a boat whose duty is to gaff a (large) fish once the angler has reeled it in.
An old person, usually a man.
A sailor.
The baby in the house.

core.definition: The chief lighting technician on a film or television set, who designs and supervises the lighting.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The double f is one long 'f' sound, and the final syllable is a light, reduced 'er' with an American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional, used with respect in the film industry.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gaffer mainly in film, television, and video production, such as 'the gaffer set up the lights for the interview.' Outside that industry, the word is rare, though it can mean an older man in British or older English. In the US, you might also say 'lighting director,' but on a set the title gaffer is standard.

distinctions.note: The lighting director is more common in theater and live broadcasting, while gaffer is the usual film and TV term.
A grip handles rigging, equipment, and camera support, while a gaffer is responsible for the lights.

examples.everyday: My cousin works as a gaffer on TV shows, so she is always setting up lights in some strange place.
examples.professional: Please confirm with the gaffer that we have enough power for the three lights in the studio before the shoot.
examples.analytical: The gaffer's role is technical, but its artistic function shapes the mood and meaning of every scene.

nuance.analogy: A gaffer is the chief painter of light on a set, deciding how every scene looks.
nuance.etymology: From gaffer, an old term for an old man or foreman, a contraction of godfather.
common_mistakes: Confusing gaffer with gaffe, which is a social mistake.
Using gaffer for a camera operator; the camera job is a director of photography or cinematographer.

senses.definition: A (normally) complete range.
All the colors that can be presented by a device such as a monitor or printer.
All the notes in a musical scale.

core.definition: The complete range or full extent of something, such as emotions, options, or colors that a device can show.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the final syllable a short, unstressed uh. Learners often pronounce it as gam-OOT or add a long vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes a full range and can be positive or negative depending on what the range covers.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gamut in writing and speech about a full range of emotions, options, or experiences, such as run the gamut. It sounds somewhat formal, so in casual talk you might say the whole range or everything. The phrase run the gamut is very common in American English.

distinctions.note: Range is neutral and everyday, while gamut emphasizes the full set from one extreme to the other.
Spectrum is often used for a continuous range of opinions or light, whereas gamut suggests a complete set that has been covered.

examples.everyday: Our group chat covered the whole gamut of topics, from dinner plans to a movie we all hated.
examples.professional: The monitor's color gamut covers most of the standard sRGB range, so the images look accurate in our design review.
examples.analytical: Her novel runs the gamut of human experience, moving from grief to joy without losing its moral clarity.

nuance.analogy: A gamut is like a piano keyboard: it contains every key from the lowest note to the highest, and you can play anything within that span.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin gamma ut, the name for the lowest note of the medieval musical scale, later extended to mean a whole scale or range.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable as ga-MUT.
Using gamut to mean a small range; it means a full or complete range.
Saying run the gamut as run the gamute.
patterns: run the gamut from A to B

gamut.etymology: 1520s, original sense “lowest note of musical scale”, contraction of Medieval Latin *gamma ut*, from *gamma* (“Greek letter, corresponding to the musical note G”) + *ut* (“first solfège syllable, now replaced by do”).

senses.definition: Any specific kind of this fuel.
senses.example: He was trying to invent a cleaner-burning gasoline.

senses.definition: Marijuana, especially very potent or of high quality.
senses.example: He told me the dispensary had gasoline strains that hit hard within minutes.

senses.definition: An alcoholic beverage made of vodka and energy drink.
senses.example: Our bartender warned us that the gasoline was basically vodka mixed with energy drink.

senses.definition: Made from or using gasoline.
senses.example: The gasoline generator kept the cabin lights on during the three-day power outage.

core.definition: A liquid fuel refined from petroleum that powers cars, trucks and other engines; Americans often shorten it to gas.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and reduce the middle syllable to a weak 'uh.' Many learners pronounce the final -line as 'line' with a long i, but Americans say 'leen' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a practical, everyday word for a product people buy regularly, though its price can make it a source of complaint.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'gas' far more often in conversation, as in 'I need to get gas,' but 'gasoline' appears on signs, in news reports and in formal writing. Do not say 'petrol,' which is mainly British. Slang senses such as marijuana or a cocktail are informal and not used in ordinary talk.

distinctions.note: Gas is the everyday American short form and is used in nearly all casual speech, while gasoline is the full, more formal or technical name.
Petrol is the British word for the same fuel, so Americans would say gasoline or gas instead.
Diesel is a different fuel used in many trucks and buses, so it is wrong to call diesel gasoline, even though both come from petroleum.

examples.everyday: We need to stop for gasoline before the drive to the lake, because the tank is almost empty.
examples.professional: Our fleet's fuel budget went up this quarter because gasoline prices rose again in March.
examples.analytical: Gasoline demand, as economists have argued, depends as much on where people live and how they commute as on the price at the pump.

nuance.analogy: Gasoline is to a car what coffee is to a sleepy morning: the thing that gets it moving.
nuance.etymology: Formed from gas, with the chemical ending -ine; the word entered English in the later 1800s.
common_mistakes: Using the British word petrol at an American gas station, where people will not understand it
Pronouncing the final syllable as 'line' with a long i instead of 'leen'
Treating gasoline as a countable noun, as in 'a gasoline' instead of 'a gallon of gasoline'

senses.definition: A cheap showy trinket.
To sport or keep festival.
senses.example: On the feast day, the townsfolk would gaud in the square, as their grandparents had done.

core.definition: A cheap, showy ornament or trinket, usually of little real value.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable, with the vowel of 'caught' in General American, which merges with the vowel of 'cot' for many speakers. Don't add a diphthong like 'gowd'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies that something is flashy and cheap.
nuance.usage_note: Gaud is rare in modern American speech, and most Americans would not recognize its noun sense. You are more likely to meet gaudy or gaudily in writing. In conversation, say cheap trinket, knickknack or bauble. The verb and older senses meaning trick or jest are obsolete.

distinctions.note: A bauble is a showy trinket that may be lovely; gaud stresses cheapness and tasteless display.
Trinket is neutral and common; gaud is negative and literary.
Knickknack is an everyday word for a small decorative object in a home; gaud implies more glitter and vulgarity.

examples.everyday: The gift shop near the pier was full of cheap gauds for kids.
examples.professional: The conference swag was mostly gauds that nobody wanted to keep.
examples.analytical: Critics dismissed the monument's ornament as gauds that concealed a hollow design.

nuance.analogy: Like sugar-coated pennies sold as treasure.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; possibly from Latin gaudium 'joy', through Middle English.
common_mistakes: Using gaud as an adjective; the adjective is gaudy.
Pronouncing it like 'gowd' with a diphthong; the vowel is the short /ɔ/ of 'caught'.

gaud.etymology: From Middle English *gaude*, *gawde* (“jest, prank, trick; ornamental bead in a rosary, trinket, bauble”).

core.definition: An ancient Philistine city on the Mediterranean coast in southwestern Canaan, later a major trading and military town.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable. The 'a' sounds like the vowel in 'father' and the final vowel is a soft 'uh.' Americans don't pronounce it as 'GAY-zuh' as in the modern Gaza Strip news usage, which is the same name.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In American speech 'Gaza' most often refers to the modern Gaza Strip, a territory in the news. When discussing the Bible, say it is the ancient city, and be clear which meaning you mean. Americans are sensitive to political framing, so a neutral description is best.
word_family: Gazan (adjective or noun, relating to the modern Gaza Strip)

distinctions.note: 'Gaza Strip' is the modern territory on the coast; 'Gaza' alone can mean the ancient city or the modern area, so context is important.
'Gazara' is a different ancient place, probably the same as Gezer, not the Philistine coastal city Gaza.

examples.everyday: My pastor mentioned that Samson died in Gaza, and I had to look it up on a map.
examples.professional: In the seminar slides, we marked Gaza as one of the five major Philistine cities on the coastal plain.
examples.analytical: Zephaniah's oracle against Gaza reads as a judgment on a Philistine city that had been powerful for centuries.

nuance.analogy: Gaza in the Bible is like Jericho in modern storytelling: a famous old city whose name carries a long history.
nuance.etymology: From the Hebrew 'Azzah, a name for the Philistine city; the meaning is uncertain, though it is often connected to 'strong.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'GAY-zuh' when speaking about the ancient city; the first vowel is closer to 'father.'
Confusing the ancient city with the modern Gaza Strip without making the context clear.
nuance.biblical_note: Gaza (Hebrew 'Azzah) was one of the five chief cities of the Philistines, located on the Mediterranean coast in the southern coastal plain. Key passages: Judges 16:21-30, where Samson is taken to Gaza, blinded, and dies when he pulls down the temple of Dagon. Deuteronomy 2:23 mentions the Caphtorim who destroyed the Avvim living in villages as far as Gaza. Zephaniah 2:4 foretells that Gaza will be forsaken. Acts 8:26 refers to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza, where Philip meets the Ethiopian eunuch.

senses.definition: The term of office of a military general.
senses.example: George Washington's generalship was marked by both amazing victories and stunning blunders, neither of which would have happened to someone with more formal officer training.

senses.definition: The skills or performance of a good general; military leadership, strategy.
senses.example: The captain's generalship during the ambush saved the platoon from certain destruction.

senses.definition: By extension, leadership, good management.
senses.example: Under my generalship my fine troop of brats picked up every scrap of litter in that lot.

senses.definition: The position or office of a general.
senses.example: After ten years of service, he finally won the generalship of the western division.

core.definition: Skill in planning and directing military operations, or in leading a group through strategic decisions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on JEN. The -al- is a weak syllable, so say it as ul rather than AL. The initial sound is the soft j of gentle, not a hard g.

nuance.connotation: Positive when praising skilled leadership; can be negative if it suggests manipulation or a tactic that hurts people.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mainly use generalship in military history, historical writing, and sometimes in sports or business to praise sharp tactical leadership. In daily speech they would say 'good strategy' or 'he knows how to run a campaign.' The older sense of a general's term of office is rare in American English.

distinctions.note: Leadership is the broad ability to guide people; generalship is specifically strategic and tactical command skill, usually in war or a major campaign.
Strategy is a plan; generalship is the skill of carrying out and adapting plans under pressure.

examples.everyday: My grandfather loved reading about the generalship behind the D-Day landings.
examples.professional: Her generalship during the product launch kept three teams aligned even when the timeline slipped.
examples.analytical: Historians still debate how much a commander's generalship, rather than supply and morale, decided the outcome of major battles.

nuance.analogy: Generalship is like a chess master's plan for the whole board, not just a single move.
nuance.etymology: From general, from Latin generalis, plus -ship, meaning office, skill, or state.
common_mistakes: Using generalship for a general practitioner or a general manager; it strictly refers to the skill or command of a military general.
Stressing the final syllable; the stress is on the first syllable, JEN.
Confusing it with generality or generalization, which are different nouns.

senses.definition: Tastelessness.

core.definition: Cheap, showy decorations or trinkets that look valuable but lack real worth or good taste.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the first syllable, JIM. The final -ery is reduced to a quick uh-ree with an American r, and the middle vowel often disappears in fast speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it mildly insults the taste or cheapness of the decorations.
nuance.usage_note: This is a literary or critical word that Americans use in reviews of architecture, interior design, or gift shops. In everyday talk people say tacky, cheesy, or knickknacks. Using it about a friend's home can sound snobbish, though it works well in witty writing.

distinctions.note: Kitsch is sentimental, mass-produced art that is often knowingly appealing, while gimcrackery is cheap showy ornament with no real value.
Tacky is common informal American English, whereas gimcrackery is more literary and formal.
Bric-a-brac is a neutral term for small collectible objects, while gimcrackery is a judgment about cheapness and poor taste.

examples.everyday: The gift shop by the pier is full of seashell gimcrackery that nobody really needs.
examples.professional: The hotel renovation removed the gilded gimcrackery from the lobby and let the original architecture show.
examples.analytical: Critics of Victorian design often treated ornamental gimcrackery as evidence of a moral failing, not merely bad taste.

nuance.analogy: Like a hotel lobby full of plastic flowers, gimcrackery looks like abundance but has no real life in it.
nuance.etymology: Origin uncertain; first recorded in the 1600s, probably from gimcrack, a showy but worthless trifle.
common_mistakes: Stressing the middle syllable, as in gim-KRACK-er-ee; the stress belongs on the first syllable.
Using it for anything merely old or small; it means cheap and showy, so it is an insult.

senses.definition: An evening out with female friends.

core.definition: An evening out or in with female friends, usually for fun and conversation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on night, the second word. The possessive girls' sounds like gurlz, with one syllable, and the two words link smoothly.

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly. It suggests fun, relaxation and female friendship, and it can sound exclusive when used in a mixed group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use girls' night for a casual evening with female friends, such as dinner, drinks or a movie. A natural reply is Sounds fun, or Count me in. Women of all ages say it, and it is often playful. Mixed-gender groups usually say something like a night out with friends, to be more inclusive.

distinctions.note: Girls' night out is slightly fuller and implies going out somewhere; girls' night can happen at home.
A girls' trip is a longer outing involving travel; girls' night is a single evening.

examples.everyday: We're having girls' night at Maria's on Friday, so come join us if you can.
examples.professional: Our team's girls' night after the conference was a good way to reconnect, though we kept it separate from work.
examples.analytical: The phrase girls' night marks a social category that is partly friendship and partly a claim to leisure outside the household.

nuance.analogy: Girls' night is like a standing appointment with friends: a regular break that belongs to you.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing girls' with an extra syllable, saying GUR-lulz
Using girls' night in a mixed group without considering whether it sounds exclusive

conversation.text: It's girls' night tonight, so the guys are on their own.
We do a girls' night once a month, usually wine and a movie.
"Where's Mom?" "She's at girls' night with her book club friends."

senses.definition: Ellipsis of glans penis or penile glans.
Ellipsis of glans clitoridis or clitoral glans.
The acorn or mast of the oak and similar fruits.
senses.example: In autumn, the squirrels buried the glans of the old oak across the backyard.

senses.definition: Synonym of goiter.
senses.example: Her grandmother's medical chart mentioned a glans that had grown visibly around her neck over the years.

senses.definition: Synonym of pessary.
senses.example: The 1890s medical manual recommended a glans, a rubber device inserted to support a prolapsed uterus.

senses.definition: A structure at the extremity of the penis and of the clitoris in humans and other mammals.
senses.example: The urologist explained that the glans is highly sensitive and can be affected by infection.

core.definition: In anatomy, the rounded, sensitive tip of the penis or clitoris, part of the external genitalia.

pronunciation.tip: It is one syllable with the short vowel of 'cat'. End with a voiced z sound, so it sounds like 'glanz', not 'glanss' or 'glan-uhz'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical in medical contexts. In casual conversation it can feel awkward or embarrassing, so people often avoid it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use glans mainly in medicine, sexual health education, urology, and anatomy classes. In a doctor's office it is a neutral clinical term. Outside those settings, most people say 'the head' or 'the tip' instead. The word sounds similar to 'gland' but has a different meaning.

distinctions.note: A gland is an organ that produces secretions, such as the thyroid. Glans is unrelated in meaning, despite the similar sound.
The prepuce is the fold of skin that covers the glans, not the glans itself.

examples.everyday: My doctor explained that the irritation was on the glans, not the shaft.
examples.professional: The clinic's sexual health handout uses the term glans throughout, so patients see the same word in every section.
examples.analytical: Clinically, the glans is distinguished from the prepuce, though the two are often discussed together in circumcision research.

nuance.etymology: From Latin glans, meaning acorn, because the anatomical structure was named for its resemblance to an acorn.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with 'gland' because of the similar sound.
Using the clinical term in casual conversation, where Americans usually say 'the head' or 'the tip'.

senses.definition: Something learned by gleaning.
The act of collecting leftover crops from farmers' fields after they have been commercially harvested or on fields where it is not economically profitable to harvest.
senses.example: Volunteers spent the morning gleaning potatoes from the field after the commercial harvest ended.

senses.definition: Dumpster diving.
senses.example: On weekends, he goes gleaning behind the grocery store for bread and produce that was tossed.

senses.definition: The catching of insects and other invertebrates by plucking them from within foliage, or sometimes from the ground. It may also be applied to where prey is picked off, or from within, natural and man-made surfaces such as rock faces and under the eaves of houses.
senses.example: The warbler spends hours gleaning caterpillars from the undersides of oak leaves.

core.definition: The act of collecting leftover crops from a field after the main harvest, or something learned bit by bit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The final '-ing' is a reduced 'ing', not 'eeng'. In speech the vowel of the second syllable is a short 'i'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests humility, thrift, and helping people in need.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gleaning mainly for farm volunteer programs, food banks, or Bible study. Informal speakers might say 'dumpster diving' for taking discarded food or goods, which carries a more casual or negative tone.

distinctions.note: Harvesting is the main, planned collection of crops. Gleaning is the secondary collection of what was left behind.
Scavenging means searching through discarded things, often for food or value, and can sound negative. Gleaning sounds more organized and charitable.

examples.everyday: Our church youth group went gleaning at a local farm after the apples were picked.
examples.professional: Our food bank runs a gleaning program that collects surplus produce from farms and delivers it to shelters.
examples.analytical: In the Book of Ruth, gleaning is a legal right of the poor, which turns a field's leftovers into a form of dignity.

nuance.analogy: Like picking up the coins a crowd leaves behind after the main event is over.
nuance.etymology: From glean (verb), from Old French glener.
common_mistakes: Using gleaning for any kind of picking up. In agriculture it means collecting what is left after the harvest.
Mispronouncing the stress as GLEE-ning with a long final vowel. The ending is a light 'ing'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word leqet means gleanings, the grain or fruit left behind after harvest. Leviticus 19:9-10 commands owners not to harvest every corner of the field or pick up every fallen grape, leaving those gleanings for the poor and the stranger. Deuteronomy 24:19-21 repeats this rule and adds that a forgotten sheaf should be left in the field. The Book of Ruth 2 shows Ruth gleaning in the field of Boaz, a concrete case of this law in action.

senses.definition: Concerning all parts of the world.
senses.example: Pollution is a global problem.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the whole of something; total, universal:
senses.example: Global variables keep support engineers employed.

senses.definition: Of a variable, accessible by all parts of a program.
senses.example: Global variables keep support engineers employed.

senses.definition: Which has to be considered in its entirety.
senses.example: Before we fix the bug, we need a global understanding of how the system behaves.

senses.definition: Spherical, ball-shaped.
senses.example: In the center was a small, global mass.

senses.definition: Of or relating to a globe or sphere.
senses.example: The museum displayed a global model of the Earth made in 1492.

senses.definition: A globally scoped identifier.
senses.example: Declare the counter as a global so every function can update it.

senses.definition: In the global manner; world-wide.
senses.example: The company must compete globally, so every product launch is planned worldwide.

core.definition: Relating to the whole world; affecting or involving every country, region, or part of the planet.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, GLOH. The final -al is a reduced, unstressed syllable that sounds like 'buhl,' not 'BAL' with a strong a.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes scale and scope, so it can be positive for reach or negative when it signals a problem that affects everyone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'global' widely in news, business, and science: 'global economy,' 'global warming,' 'global market.' For products or services that are sold everywhere, 'worldwide' is also common and sounds slightly more everyday. In computing, 'global' refers to a variable accessible throughout a program.

distinctions.note: Worldwide often describes how far something has spread; global more often describes a whole system or issue that affects the entire planet.
International concerns relations between nations; global covers the whole world as one unit, including effects that cross all borders.
Universal means applying to everyone without exception; global means across the world but may still have exceptions.

examples.everyday: Gas prices keep going up because of what is happening in the global oil market.
examples.professional: We need a global view of customer data before we roll out the new dashboard to every region.
examples.analytical: Any global theory of justice has to account for how resources are distributed unequally across nations.

nuance.analogy: A global map shows the whole coastline, not just the harbor you happen to be standing in.
nuance.etymology: From 'globe,' from Latin globus, meaning ball or sphere.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the second syllable as 'bal' with a strong vowel; the final syllable is reduced to 'buhl.'
Confusing the adjective 'global' with the noun 'globe' or with the adverb 'globally' in sentences.

senses.definition: A list of difficult words or specialized terms used in a particular book or document, or in a particular domain of knowledge, with their definitions; a list of glosses (explanatory annotations).
senses.example: At the back of the book you can find the glossary.

core.definition: A list at the end of a book or document that defines difficult or specialized words, usually in alphabetical order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and make the middle syllable a reduced 'uh' that is almost silent. Don't pronounce a separate 'gloss-ah-ree'; the word has three syllables. The final syllable is 'ree' with a clear American r.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and helpful.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'glossary' for a short list of terms in a textbook, technical manual, or report, and they expect it at the back of the document. In a business setting, people also refer to a 'project glossary' or 'data dictionary' for shared definitions. Calling a simple list of words a glossary is normal, while a full dictionary is a different thing.

distinctions.note: A dictionary covers the whole language, while a glossary covers only the words in one text or field.
An index lists topics and page numbers, while a glossary explains the meaning of terms.

examples.everyday: The cookbook has a glossary at the back that explains terms like roux and blanch.
examples.professional: Please add a glossary to the requirements document so the team agrees on what 'active user' means.
examples.analytical: A glossary can make a theological argument more transparent by fixing the meanings of key terms before the argument begins.

nuance.analogy: Like a pocket guide to a foreign city: you carry it to decode the signs you do not understand.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin glossarium, from Latin glossa, a difficult word needing explanation, from Greek glōssa (tongue, word).
common_mistakes: Using glossary for a complete dictionary of a language; a glossary is limited to one text or subject.
Stressing the middle syllable, as in 'glo-SAR-ee'; the stress is on GLOSS.

glossary.etymology: From Middle English *glosarie*, from Latin *glossārium*, from Ancient Greek *γλῶσσα* (“tongue”).

core.definition: The hill outside Jerusalem where Jesus was crucified, its name meaning place of the skull.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to a schwa, and the th is voiceless as in think, followed by a reduced final vowel. Do not pronounce the h, which is silent.

nuance.connotation: Solemn and religious. The name carries deep emotional weight for Christians.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use Golgotha in church, Bible study, preaching and literary writing about the crucifixion. In everyday talk people usually say Calvary, the Latin name, or simply the crucifixion site. Using the name casually would sound unusual.

distinctions.note: Calvary is the Latin-based name for the same place, used more often in English hymns and devotional writing; Golgotha is the Aramaic name used in the Gospels.

examples.everyday: When we visited Jerusalem, our guide took us to the church that marks the site of Golgotha.
examples.professional: In the sermon series, the pastor traced the journey from the upper room to Golgotha.
examples.analytical: The Gospel writers name the place Golgotha, a term in Aramaic, and explain it as the place of the skull.

nuance.analogy: Golgotha is like a landmark on a map of faith: a single hill that carries the weight of the whole story.
nuance.etymology: From Aramaic gulgulta, meaning skull, related to the Greek kranion and the Latin calvaria; the origin of the name for the hill is debated.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the h, as in GOHL-gah-thuh, instead of the silent h at the end, which is a reduced vowel.
Using Golgotha for any execution site; it refers to the specific hill in Jerusalem.
nuance.biblical_note: Golgotha is the Aramaic name for the place of Jesus' crucifixion outside Jerusalem. The Greek Gospels translate it as the place of the skull, Greek kraniou topos. In Matthew 27:33 the soldiers lead Jesus to the place called Golgotha. Mark 15:22 gives the same location and the translation. John 19:17 describes Jesus carrying his cross to the place called the place of the skull.

golgotha.etymology: * From the Ancient Greek *Γολγοθᾶ* from the Aramaic *גּוּלְגּוּלְתָּא*.

senses.definition: A good, cheerful mood.
senses.example: His good spirits were contagious.

core.definition: A cheerful, positive mood; a happy, lively state of mind that shows in how someone acts.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SPIR. The final ts is a clear t and s sound, and the r in spirits is pronounced in American speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive and cheerful; it describes a pleasant mood that others notice.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often say in good spirits, as in 'She's in good spirits today,' rather than good spirits alone. Spirits is plural here and does not mean alcohol. A natural reply to a cheerful greeting is 'You too, I'm glad things are going well.'

distinctions.note: Good mood is more casual and everyday; good spirits sounds a little warmer and more lively.
High spirits suggests energetic, noisy happiness, while good spirits is calmer and more general.
Good humor describes a mood of pleasant joking, while good spirits covers a wider sense of cheerfulness.

examples.everyday: You seem to be in good spirits today, did something nice happen?
examples.professional: The team is in good spirits after shipping the release on time, so let's keep the momentum going.
examples.analytical: Being in good spirits reflects a mood that can change, but it may also reveal a deeper settled character over time.

nuance.analogy: Good spirits are like sunlight through a window: they brighten everything in the room, even on a gray day.
common_mistakes: Saying I'm in a good spirits, with a before spirits; the usual form is in good spirits with no article.
Confusing spirits in this sense with alcoholic drinks, which is a different meaning.

senses.definition: Ready for use or normal operation, especially after repair or renewal.
senses.example: I replaced the broken spring and now the toaster is good to go.

senses.definition: Ready for some specific task or ready for normal activity, especially after preparation or recovery.
senses.example: The doctor examined me and says I'm good to go.

core.definition: Ready to start, use or continue, especially after repair, approval, checking or preparation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on GOH, and 'to' often reduces to 'tuh' in fast speech, so the phrase sounds like 'good-tuh-GOH'. Keep the 'oh' vowel long and clear.

nuance.connotation: Positive: it signals that everything is finished and clear, so you can move ahead.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this at repair shops, airports, medical offices and online checkouts when something is ready. For example, a mechanic might say 'You're good to go.' A natural reply is 'Great, thanks!' Do not say 'I'm good' alone to accept an offer, since in American English that often means 'No, thanks'.

distinctions.note: Ready is neutral and general, while good to go is informal and often means cleared or approved to move on.
All set is also informal and suggests that all steps are finished, often used when something has been arranged or completed.

collocations: all set and good to go
the car is good to go
good to go for the flight

examples.everyday: The mechanic finished the brakes, so you're good to go.
examples.professional: The new build passed QA, so it's good to go for Friday's release.
examples.analytical: Once the validation checks pass, the model is good to go, though the authors caution about data drift.

nuance.analogy: Like a race car when the green flag waves, it is prepared and cleared to start.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am good to go' when you mean 'No, thanks', which confuses Americans.
Using it for people who are merely willing, when it more often refers to things being cleared or ready.

conversation.text: I've packed the car, so we're good to go.
The code passed review, so it's good to go for release.
"Do you need anything else from me?" "Nope, you're good to go."

senses.definition: A person of East or Southeast Asian descent, but now especially:
A Korean person.
A Vietnamese person.
A black insurgent in the Rhodesian Bush War.
Grime or mud.
senses.example: He came in from the fields covered in gook from head to toe.

senses.definition: A dull or hapless person.
senses.example: Don't be such a gook; come to the party and have some fun.

senses.definition: A bonnet (headwear).
senses.example: Grandma tied on her gook before walking to church on the cold Sunday morning.

senses.definition: (dated) A foreigner (to the speaker), especially the (enemy) natives of a place the speaker's military is at war with or in.
senses.label: dated

senses.definition: Synonym of look.
senses.example: Gook at those clouds rolling over the mountains, we might get rain.

core.definition: A deeply offensive racial slur for a person of East or Southeast Asian descent, especially Korean or Vietnamese.

pronunciation.tip: It has the short oo of book, not the long oo of goo. Because it is a slur, do not use it at all; learn it only to recognize and avoid it.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative and offensive; it is a racial slur that dehumanizes people and is never neutral.
nuance.usage_note: This is a racial slur that came into American military slang during the Korean and Vietnam wars. Never use it, even as a joke or in casual conversation. If you need to discuss it, say 'a racial slur' and name the group in neutral terms like Korean or Vietnamese. The verb sense 'to look' is rare and dialectal, so you can ignore it.

distinctions.note: A respectful umbrella term for Americans of Asian descent, though it is better to name a specific background such as Korean or Vietnamese when that is relevant.
The accurate, neutral terms to use when you need to refer to someone's nationality or ethnicity.

examples.everyday: Please don't ever say that word around me, because it's a racial slur.
examples.professional: HR asked us to remove that word from all internal documents and training slides.
examples.analytical: The word's history in wartime slang shows how slurs turn ethnic groups into enemies.

nuance.analogy: Like a weapon disguised as a nickname: it sounds casual, but it hurts deeply.
nuance.etymology: Origin disputed; it spread in American military slang in the twentieth century.
common_mistakes: Using it as a casual or joking word; it is a slur and causes real harm.
Assuming it is a neutral term for Asian people; it is not, and it should never be used.

gook.etymology: First attested in the 1890s, US military slang in reference to Filipinos (in particular, it is defined in an 1893 citation in Slang and Its Analogues as referring to prostitutes who followed army camps; it is defined similarly in a 1914 work).

senses.definition: The state of being graceful.

core.definition: The quality of moving, behaving, or looking smooth, balanced, and pleasing, without awkwardness.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, GRAYS. The -ful ending reduces to a short, unstressed fuhl, and the final -ness is a quiet nus, not nes.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises a person's movement, manners, or style, and can also describe writing or design.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use gracefulness mostly for physical movement, such as dancing, skating, or an athlete's motion, and for manners or style in writing or art. In casual talk people more often say she moves so gracefully or she's so graceful. The noun sounds a bit formal, so use it in writing or a thoughtful comment.

distinctions.note: Grace is the broader word and can mean a quality, a favor, or a prayer of thanks, while gracefulness refers specifically to smooth, pleasing movement or form.
Elegance suggests refined style and sophistication, while gracefulness focuses on fluid, easy motion.

examples.everyday: Watching her skate at the rink, I was amazed by her gracefulness.
examples.professional: The design team praised the gracefulness of the new interface, which made complex tasks feel simple.
examples.analytical: Aquinas would locate the gracefulness of a well-ordered act in its fittingness to the agent's nature and purpose.

nuance.analogy: Like a swan gliding across a lake, with no visible effort under the surface.
nuance.etymology: From grace (Latin gratia, favor, charm) plus the suffixes -ful and -ness.
common_mistakes: Saying gracefulness when the adjective graceful is what fits the sentence, as in she was graceful, not she was gracefulness.
Stressing the second syllable, as in grace-FUL-ness, instead of GRAYS-fuhl-nus.

senses.definition: Showing grandiloquence.
senses.example: The mayor spoke grandiloquently about the city's glorious future, though the budget showed otherwise.

core.definition: In a showy, pompous way that uses big, impressive words to make an impression.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the -DIL- syllable, then reduce the -uh- and -kwunt- to quick, light sounds. The final -ly is a clear lee, as in 'quickly.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that the manner of speaking is showy and insincere.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this adverb rarely, mostly in writing about speech or style. In casual talk they would say 'in a showy way' or 'like he was giving a speech.' It is best reserved for critical description, not for everyday compliments.

distinctions.note: Grandly can be neutral or admiring about a dignified style, while grandiloquently specifically criticizes wordy, showy speech.
Eloquently means well and persuasively; grandiloquently means in an inflated, overdone way.

examples.professional: The consultant described our roadmap grandiloquently, and the actual budget decisions got lost in the adjectives.
examples.analytical: The author argues grandiloquently for a providence that the evidence she cites does not quite support.

nuance.analogy: Like a magician who makes a simple card trick look like a cosmic event, using far more drama than the trick needs.
nuance.etymology: From grandiloquent, from Latin grandiloquus, from grandis (grand) and loqui (to speak), plus the adverb suffix -ly.
common_mistakes: Using it as a positive word for dignified speech.
Stressing the last syllable instead of the -DIL- syllable.

senses.definition: Of, related to, or involving local influential figures.
senses.example: Grass tops politics shaped every zoning decision in the county for decades.

senses.definition: People in a position of power or influence at a local level.
senses.example: The grass tops in our town meet privately before every council vote to agree on positions.

core.definition: Influential local leaders, such as business, religious and civic figures, who can mobilize community support for a cause.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first word, GRASS, and keep the two words linked into one unit. The vowel in 'tops' is the open 'ah' of 'hot' in General American, since the cot-caught merger is common.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in political and organizing contexts, but can sound elitist if used to suggest insider influence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'grasstops' mainly in political campaigns, lobbying and advocacy news. It contrasts with 'grassroots,' which means ordinary citizens. In formal writing it is usually spelled as one word, 'grasstops,' and it is rarely used in casual talk.

distinctions.note: Grassroots means ordinary members of the public, while grasstops means well-connected local leaders who can bring others along.
Elites are powerful people at the national or wealthy level, while grasstops are influential people in a local community.
Stakeholders is a broad term for anyone with an interest, while grasstops refers specifically to local influence.

examples.everyday: Our town council always listens to the grasstops people, like the school principal and the bank manager.
examples.professional: The advocacy team plans to combine grassroots volunteers with grasstops meetings with county commissioners.
examples.analytical: Political scientists distinguish grasstops mobilization, which works through local elites, from grassroots mobilization, which works through mass participation.

nuance.analogy: If grassroots is the crowd of ordinary voters, grasstops is the small group of well-connected local leaders who can bring that crowd along.
nuance.etymology: Modeled on 'grassroots,' a US political term; the exact coinage of 'grasstops' is not well documented.
