common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in MAH-noh-SIL-uh-bik; the main stress is on LAB.
Using the adjective where a noun is needed: say 'a monosyllable' for the word, and 'monosyllabic' only to describe something.

monosyllabic.etymology: Late Latin *monosyllabicus*, from Latin *monosyllabus*, from Hellenistic Ancient Greek *μονοσύλλαβος*.

senses.definition: A structure built for commemorative or symbolic reasons, or as a memorial; a commemoration.
senses.example: There is a monument on the town green to the soldiers who died in World War I.

senses.definition: An important site owned by the community as a whole.
senses.example: The old town square is a monument that belongs to every resident.

senses.definition: A sign of exceptional achievement.
senses.example: Winning the Nobel Prize was a monument to her decades of patient research.

senses.definition: An important burial vault or tomb.
senses.example: Visitors lined up to see the royal tomb, a monument carved deep into the cliffside.

senses.definition: Any grave marker.
senses.example: Her family placed fresh flowers at the monument marking her grandfather's grave.

senses.definition: A legal document.
senses.example: The attorney cited the 1852 charter, a monument of title, in the property dispute.

senses.definition: A surveying reference point marked by a permanently fixed marker (a survey monument).
senses.example: The surveyor found a brass monument set in concrete at the northeast property corner.

senses.definition: A pile of stones left by a prospector to claim ownership of ore etc. found in a mine.
senses.example: Following the old claim, the miner found a stone monument marking the vein.

senses.definition: A natural or artificial object used as a reference point.
senses.example: Hikers use the large granite boulder as a monument for navigating the valley trail.

senses.definition: A surviving record.
senses.example: Those faded letters remain a monument to my great-grandmother's daily life in 1910.

senses.definition: To mark or memorialize with a monument.
senses.example: The city plans to monument the founders' graves with a bronze sculpture in the square.

senses.definition: To place a surveyor's monument at.
senses.example: The crew will monument each corner of the parcel before the boundary survey is filed.

core.definition: A large structure, statue or stone built to honor a person or event, or a site preserved for its historical importance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle vowel is a short 'yoo' sound, and the last syllable is a reduced schwa, so it is not pronounced 'MAHN-yoo-ment'.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral. It suggests honor, permanence and respect.
nuance.usage_note: Americans speak of the Washington Monument, a national monument, or a historic site as a monument. For a small memorial plaque, they usually say memorial or marker. The verb is less common in everyday speech; it appears mostly in formal writing and in land surveying.

distinctions.note: A monument is usually a physical structure; a memorial may be a structure, a site, a ceremony or a day.
A statue is a single figure; a monument may be any large structure built to commemorate something.

examples.everyday: We visited the Lincoln Memorial on our trip, and it is an impressive monument.
examples.professional: The design team proposed a simple stone monument for the plaza, with the names engraved on the base.
examples.analytical: The Hebrew term for a standing stone marks a memorial whose meaning depends on the covenant it commemorates.

nuance.analogy: A bookmark in history: a fixed mark that tells people where something important happened.
nuance.etymology: From Latin monumentum, from monere 'to remind, warn'.
common_mistakes: Using monument for any small memorial plaque; Americans usually say memorial or marker for small items.
Stressing the second syllable; the stress is on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The RSV usually renders the Hebrew matstsebah as pillar or standing stone rather than monument. Jacob sets up a stone pillar at Bethel (Genesis 28:18) and later sets a pillar on Rachel's grave (Genesis 35:20), marking a sacred place or a memorial. Moses builds an altar with twelve pillars at Sinai (Exodus 24:4), representing the twelve tribes of Israel. These passages show that stone markers in Scripture commemorate God's acts and promises.

monument.etymology: From Middle English *monument*, from Old French *monument*, from Latin *monumentum* (“memorial, monument, tomb”), from *monēre* (“to remind”).

senses.definition: A personal slogan.
senses.example: You have to be in it to win it — that's my motto.

senses.definition: A sentence, phrase, or word, prefixed to an essay, discourse, chapter, canto, or the like, suggestive of its subject matter; a short, suggestive expression of a guiding principle; a maxim.
senses.example: The school's motto, 'Truth in all things,' was carved above the main entrance.

senses.definition: A sentence, phrase, or word, forming part of an heraldic achievement.
senses.example: The family's coat of arms bore a motto in Latin beneath the shield.

senses.definition: To compose mottos.
senses.example: He mottoes every chapter of his book with a line from Ecclesiastes.

core.definition: A short phrase or saying that expresses a guiding principle, often chosen by a person, family, school, group or state.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final o is a long 'oh' sound. Americans use the 'ah' vowel from the cot-caught merger, so avoid saying 'MAW-toh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it suggests inspiration, personal values and identity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use motto for a personal saying they live by, like a motto of hard work and kindness, or for official mottos such as a state or school motto. In casual conversation, my motto is is a natural way to share your values. A natural reply is simply a common phrase, such as that is a good one.

distinctions.note: A slogan is a catchy advertising phrase for a product or campaign, while a motto expresses lasting values for a person or institution.
A maxim is a general rule of conduct, often formal, while a motto is shorter and often chosen as an identity or emblem.
A proverb is a traditional saying that comes from a culture, while a motto is usually chosen on purpose by a person or group.

collocations: motto on the coat of arms

examples.everyday: My motto is 'Don't sweat the small stuff,' and it has saved me a lot of stress over the years.
examples.professional: Our team motto this quarter is 'Ship small, learn fast,' so we stop perfecting features too early.
examples.analytical: Many medieval coats of arms carried a Latin motto that stated the family's guiding virtue in a few words.

nuance.analogy: A motto is like a compass for a group or person: a short phrase that points you in the same direction every day.
nuance.etymology: From Italian motto, 'a word or saying,' ultimately from Latin muttum, 'a mutter.'
common_mistakes: Using motto for a long rule or paragraph; a motto is short and memorable.
Misspelling the plural; both mottos and mottoes are accepted, but mottos is more common in American writing.

motto.etymology: Borrowed from Italian *motto* (“a word, a saying”), from Latin *muttum* (“a mutter, a grunt”), late.

senses.definition: A hill or mountain.
senses.example: We hiked up the mount to watch the sunrise over the valley.

senses.definition: Any of seven fleshy prominences in the palm of the hand, taken to represent the influences of various heavenly bodies.
senses.example: the mount of Jupiter

senses.definition: A bulwark for offense or defense; a mound.
senses.example: Roman soldiers piled earth into a mount outside the walls to launch their attack.

senses.definition: An animal, usually a horse, used to ride on.
senses.example: The rider climbed onto his mount.

senses.definition: A car, bicycle, or motorcycle used for racing.
senses.example: The team's new mount finished second at Daytona after a late pit stop.

senses.definition: A mounting; an object on which another object is mounted.
senses.example: The post is the mount on which the mailbox is installed.

senses.definition: A step or block to assist in mounting a horse.
senses.example: Before riding, she climbed the wooden mount beside the barn to reach the saddle.

senses.definition: A signal for mounting a horse.
senses.example: At the bugle's sharp mount, the troopers leapt into their saddles.

senses.definition: A dominant ground grappling position, where one combatant sits on the other combatants torso with the face pointing towards the opponent's head.
senses.example: He trapped his opponent with a tight mount and began working for the armbar.

senses.definition: The act of getting onto the apparatus.
senses.example: The gymnast's clean mount onto the balance beam earned a perfect start score.

senses.definition: A green hillock in the base of a shield.
senses.example: The shield bore a green mount at its base beneath three silver stars.

senses.definition: To get upon; to ascend; to climb.
senses.example: to mount stairs

senses.definition: To place oneself on (a horse, a bicycle, etc.); to bestride.
senses.example: The rider mounted his horse.

senses.definition: To cause to mount; to put on horseback; to furnish with animals for riding.
senses.example: The cavalry captain ordered his men to mount their horses before dawn.

senses.definition: To sit on a combatant's torso with the face pointing towards the opponent's head; to assume the mount position in ground grappling.
senses.example: He quickly mounted his opponent and pinned her shoulders to the mat.

senses.definition: To attach (an object) to a support, backing, framework etc.
senses.example: to mount a mailbox on a post

senses.definition: To attach (a drive or device) to the file system in order to make it available to the operating system.
senses.example: Run this command to mount the USB drive so the operating system can read it.

senses.definition: To increase in quantity or intensity.
senses.example: The bills mounted up and the business failed. There is mounting tension in Crimea.

senses.definition: To get on top of (another) for the purpose of copulation.
senses.example: The stallion tried to mount the mare before the handler pulled him away.

senses.definition: To have or begin sexual intercourse with someone.
senses.example: She mounted him last night.

senses.definition: To begin (a campaign, military assault, etc.); to launch.
senses.example: The General gave the order to mount the attack.

senses.definition: To prepare and arrange the scenery, furniture, etc. for use in (a play or production).
senses.example: The crew needed three days to mount the production before opening night.

senses.definition: To incorporate fat, especially butter, into (a dish, especially a sauce to finish it).
senses.example: Mount the sauce with one tablespoon of butter.

senses.definition: (rare) To rise on high; to go up; to be upraised or uplifted; to tower aloft; to ascend; often with up.
senses.example: Smoke began to mount up from the chimney as the storm clouds gathered.
senses.label: rare

core.definition: To climb onto or get on something, such as a horse or bicycle; also to fix something onto a support for display.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the single syllable and keep the final nt clear, without dropping the t. The vowel is the diphthong in how or now.

nuance.connotation: Neutral: a plain, practical verb that carries no emotional weight.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often say get on a horse or get on a bike in casual talk, but mount is natural in writing and in polite speech about riding or displaying things. Mounting a photo or a TV on a wall is a common everyday use. In a formal or military context, mount can also mean to organize or launch something, as in mount a campaign.

distinctions.note: Climb emphasizes going up a surface by effort, while mount emphasizes getting onto something such as a horse, bike or platform.
Install means to set up equipment or software in place, while mount means to fix a single object onto a support such as a bracket or frame.

collocations: mount a TV on the wall

examples.everyday: I can mount the ladder, but I need you to hold it steady while I hang the picture.
examples.professional: The team will mount the new dashboard on the shared display in the conference room by Friday.
examples.analytical: Philosophers have long asked whether a thinker can mount a defense of a position without first accepting its premises.

nuance.analogy: Like getting into a saddle and settling in before the ride, to mount is to get up onto something and be ready to use it.
nuance.etymology: From Old French monter, from Late Latin montare, from Latin mons 'mountain'.
common_mistakes: Saying mount the car, which Americans normally express as get in the car.
Confusing mount with mountain; the verb means get on, not climb a mountain.

mount.etymology: From Middle English *mount*, *munt*, from Old English *munt*, from Latin *mōns* (“a hill, mountain”), from a root seen also in *ēmineō* (“to project, to protrude”) (English *eminent*).

senses.definition: One who sells dubious medicines.
senses.example: The traveling mountebank sold bottles of colored water as a cure for every ailment.

senses.definition: One who sells by deception; a con artist.
senses.example: The mountebank talked the old widow into handing over her savings for a fake investment.

senses.definition: Any boastful, false pretender.
senses.example: Nobody believed the self-proclaimed general, who was just a mountebank with a borrowed uniform.

senses.definition: To act as a mountebank.
senses.example: He spent his twenties mountebanking through county fairs, selling miracle tonics to farmers.

senses.definition: To cheat by boasting and false pretenses.
senses.example: The candidate mountebanked the voters with grand promises and claims he could never keep.

core.definition: A person who cheats people by making false or exaggerated claims, especially to sell something worthless.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a reduced schwa. The final vowel is the short 'a' of 'bank', not the 'ah' of 'father'.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It describes someone who deceives others for profit or fame.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'mountebank' mostly in literary, historical, or critical writing, and sometimes to tease someone who oversells. In everyday speech, people usually say 'con artist', 'fraud', or 'snake oil salesman'. It is a sharp insult, so use it carefully.

distinctions.note: A con artist is a common, everyday term for someone who cheats people, while a mountebank is more literary and often refers to a showman selling false cures.
A charlatan pretends to have knowledge or skill he does not have, while a mountebank is especially a showy seller of quack remedies.

examples.everyday: Don't trust that guy selling miracle cures at the fair; he's a total mountebank.
examples.professional: The vendor was a mountebank who promised instant results and never delivered anything measurable.
examples.analytical: Socrates treats the sophist as a mountebank who sells the appearance of wisdom for a fee.

nuance.analogy: Like a street performer who draws a crowd with loud promises while selling a bottle of colored water.
nuance.etymology: From Italian 'montambanco', from 'monta in banco', literally 'climb on a bench', referring to an itinerant seller who mounted a platform to advertise his wares.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'MOUNT-uh-bank' with the 'mount' spelling taken literally; the word is spelled with 'mounte' but pronounced 'MOUN-tuh-bank'.
Using it as a neutral word for a performer; it is always an insult implying fraud.

mountebank.etymology: From archaic Italian *montambanco* (“quack who mounts a bench to hawk his wares”), contracted from *monta-in-banco* (“mount on bench”).

senses.definition: To continue without being distracted; to keep going.
senses.example: Ignore the noise in the hallway and move ahead with the exam.

senses.definition: To proceed; to make or signify progress.
senses.example: the construction project is moving ahead

senses.definition: To go on to something else.
senses.example: the committee moved ahead to the next item on the agenda

core.definition: To keep making progress and go on to the next step, especially after a delay or distraction.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on AHEAD, while MOVE takes secondary stress. Say the final d clearly and reduce the first vowel of ahead to a quick uh, so it does not sound like 'a-HEAD' with a long stressed vowel.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests momentum and willingness to continue, and it is often used to encourage someone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use move ahead constantly at work and in daily life, for example 'Let's move ahead with the launch on Monday.' You can also say 'move ahead' when a meeting decides to skip a stalled item and continue. A natural reply is 'Sounds good' or 'Let's do it.' Do not confuse it with 'go ahead', which means to give permission.

distinctions.note: Go ahead means to proceed or give permission ('Go ahead, ask your question'); move ahead stresses making progress toward a larger goal.
Move forward is slightly more formal and can be used for both people and plans; move ahead is more conversational.

examples.everyday: The mechanic says the car is fixed, so we can move ahead with the road trip this weekend.
examples.professional: Since the data pipeline passed review, we can move ahead with the model deployment next sprint.
examples.analytical: A theory of progress must explain why societies sometimes move ahead while others remain fixed in their institutions.

nuance.analogy: Like a runner who keeps going after a stumble, moving ahead means you do not stop for every distraction.
nuance.etymology: From move (Old English motian) plus ahead, from a- (on) and head, meaning in front.
common_mistakes: Saying 'move ahead to' when the object is a plan; Americans say 'move ahead with' the plan.
Using 'move ahead' for giving permission; that meaning belongs to 'go ahead'.

senses.definition: Change a meeting to a different time.

core.definition: To change a meeting to a different day or time.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'MEET' in 'meeting', and 'the' reduces to 'thuh' before the consonant. Say 'meeting' with a long 'ee' and no 't' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is routine workplace language, and asking to move a meeting is normally polite if you give a reason.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say 'move the meeting' in email, chat and conversation, often with a time: 'Can we move the meeting to 3?' It is less formal than 'reschedule the meeting'. Typical replies are 'Sure, what time works?' or 'That works for me.'

distinctions.note: 'Reschedule' is more formal and explicit about changing the date, while 'move the meeting' is the everyday spoken form.
'Cancel' means the meeting will not happen at all, while 'move' means it will happen at a different time.

collocations: move the meeting back an hour
move the meeting to next week

examples.everyday: Can we move the meeting to later? I have a dentist appointment.
examples.professional: I'll move the meeting to Thursday so the vendor can join.
examples.analytical: Moving the meeting changes which stakeholders can attend, so the agenda should be reviewed before the new time is confirmed.

nuance.analogy: Like shifting a reservation to a later table, the event stays the same while its slot changes.
nuance.etymology: 'Move' is from Latin movere, 'to move'; 'meeting' is from Old English mētan, 'to meet'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'move the meeting for Thursday'; use 'move the meeting to Thursday'.
Confusing 'move' with 'cancel' when the meeting is still happening.

conversation.text: Can we move the meeting to the afternoon?
I had to move the meeting because of a conflict.
They moved the meeting to Conference Room A.

senses.definition: Short for vegetable mucus.
senses.example: The okra pods release a slippery mucus when they are cut or boiled.

senses.definition: A slippery secretion from the lining of the mucous membranes.
senses.example: The mucus in coryza may vary from runny to viscous.

core.definition: The slippery, clear or yellowish fluid the body makes to keep the nose, throat and other organs moist and protected.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, with a long 'yoo' vowel that starts with a y sound. The final syllable is a reduced 'us', so do not stress the second syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative: it is a plain medical term, but in casual talk it suggests something gross, so people often choose snot or phlegm.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use mucus in everyday talk about colds, allergies and health, and in medical contexts. Casually, people say 'snot' for nasal mucus and 'phlegm' for the thick mucus you cough up. Mucus is the standard neutral word for a doctor, a nurse or a school nurse's note.

distinctions.note: Phlegm is the thick mucus from the lower airways that you cough up; mucus is the general word for the fluid.
Snot is informal and mainly refers to nasal mucus; avoid it in professional settings.
Mucous is the adjective; mucus is the noun, though they are pronounced the same in American English.

examples.everyday: I've got so much mucus that I can't stop blowing my nose.
examples.professional: The patient's lungs were clearing, but there was still thick mucus in the bronchial tubes.
examples.analytical: Mucus traps inhaled particles and bacteria, and the cilia lining the airways move it upward so it can be swallowed or coughed out.

nuance.analogy: Mucus is like the nonstick coating in a pan, keeping surfaces slick and protected from a harsh environment.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mucus, meaning nasal discharge or slime.
common_mistakes: Confusing the noun mucus with the adjective mucous, as in saying 'mucous' for the substance.
Pronouncing it with a short u like 'MUK-us' rather than the long 'yoo' vowel of 'MYOO-kus'.

senses.definition: Synonym of sweet flag.

core.definition: The root of sweet flag, a marsh plant with a sweet, spicy smell, used in some folk herbal remedies. It is not the same as the animal muskrat.

pronunciation.tip: Stress MUSK in the first word and give root a lighter secondary stress. The k in musk is clear, so do not drop it.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a specialized botanical or herbal term.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use this name in everyday life. In botany and herbalism, the plant is usually called sweet flag, Acorus calamus, and muskrat root is an older folk name. If you want to avoid confusion, say sweet flag.

distinctions.note: Sweet flag is the standard name for the whole plant, while muskrat root refers specifically to its root or to the plant under an older folk name.
A muskrat is a small aquatic rodent, and the plant only shares the name with it.

examples.everyday: My grandmother kept a jar of dried muskrat root in the pantry for her tea.
examples.professional: The herbarium lists muskrat root as a synonym of sweet flag, so please check the specimen label before filing it.
examples.analytical: The name muskrat root shows how folk usage can attach a plant to an animal, even when the two are unrelated.

nuance.analogy: Calling it muskrat root is like calling a plant 'bear grass' because it grows where bears live: the name follows a local association, not the actual relationship.
common_mistakes: Thinking muskrat root is a different plant from sweet flag.
Confusing the root with the animal muskrat, which is unrelated.

senses.definition: "I'll pay for this"; said when you offer to pay for someone else.

core.definition: I'll pay for this; said when you offer to pay for someone else's food or drink.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on 'treat', the only word the voice emphasizes, and 'my' is quick and light. The t is not a flap: it is a clear, aspirated t followed by a long vowel, and the 'tr' is said with the tongue slightly farther back than in British speech.

nuance.connotation: Positive and generous; it signals friendliness rather than obligation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this among friends, family and coworkers when paying for a meal, coffee or a small gift. Say it before the bill arrives or while reaching for your wallet. Common replies are 'Thanks, I owe you one' or 'That's really nice of you.' In formal business settings, follow the company's expense rules instead.

distinctions.note: Equally common and slightly more casual; both mean you are paying.
Means each person pays a share of the bill; the opposite of paying for everyone.

collocations: Let me get this, it's my treat

examples.everyday: Don't argue, this one's my treat.
examples.professional: Lunch is my treat today, since you covered the coffee last week.
examples.analytical: Who pays is an ethical question; when one person says 'my treat', the gesture signals generosity rather than debt.

nuance.analogy: Like a host lifting the check at a restaurant, the gesture itself is the gift.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I treat you' to mean paying; use 'it's my treat' or 'I'll get this'.
Confusing the phrase with the noun 'treat' for a snack; here it means the act of paying.

conversation.text: Put your wallet away; dinner is my treat tonight.
It's my treat. You paid last time.
Let's get ice cream after lunch, my treat.

senses.definition: The characteristic of being pessimistic or contrarian.
senses.example: Her negativity about the project made every meeting feel like a funeral.

senses.definition: Negative sentiment.
senses.example: The comment section was full of negativity, so I stopped reading the reviews.

senses.definition: The characteristic of having a negative charge.
senses.example: Students measured the negativity of each ion to predict how the compound would bond.

core.definition: A tendency to focus on the bad side of things, or the expression of pessimistic or critical feelings.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the third syllable, TIV, and the final -ity is a reduced 'ih-tee', not 'eye-tee'. Learners often add an extra vowel after the g, so say 'neg' rather than 'nay-geh'.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It describes an unpleasant mood or attitude, and it is usually a criticism of a person or group.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use negativity for a general gloomy or critical attitude, such as 'the negativity on social media' or 'bad energy in the office'. It is less specific than pessimism, which is a belief that things will turn out badly. In casual talk people often say 'so much negativity' or 'bad vibes'. To avoid sounding harsh, you can respond with 'I hear you, let's look at the options'.

distinctions.note: Pessimism is a belief that outcomes will be bad; negativity is a broader habit of focusing on what is wrong, often in tone or mood.
Cynicism is a distrust of others' motives; negativity can be general and does not need to involve distrust.

examples.everyday: I'm tired of all the negativity in our group chat, so I muted it for a while.
examples.professional: The feedback was useful, but the negativity in the review made it hard for the team to act on it.
examples.analytical: Negativity in a philosophical argument is not always a flaw; Hegel treats the negative as a driving moment in the development of thought.

nuance.analogy: Negativity is like a gray filter on a camera: it does not change the scene, but it makes everything look darker.
nuance.etymology: From negative, from Latin negare 'to deny', plus the suffix -ity.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable as NEG-uh-tiv-i-tee, which makes the word hard to follow.
Using negativity for a single critical comment, where 'criticism' fits better.

senses.definition: To fail to care for or attend to something.
senses.example: to neglect duty or business; to neglect to pay debts

senses.definition: To omit to notice; to forbear to treat with attention or respect; to slight.
senses.example: to neglect strangers

senses.definition: To fail to do or carry out something due to oversight or carelessness.
senses.example: I neglected to renew my library card, so now I owe a fine.

senses.definition: To ignore for the sake of simplifying calculations without significantly affecting accuracy.
senses.example: We can neglect this term, as it approaches zero in the limit anyway.

senses.definition: The act of neglecting.
senses.example: Years of neglect left the historic house with a collapsing roof and rotting floors.

senses.definition: The state of being neglected.
Habitual lack of care.
senses.example: The old barn had fallen into neglect after the family moved to the city.

core.definition: To fail to take care of someone or something, or to not give enough attention to a duty or responsibility.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, 'GLEKT', and the final 'ct' is a clear 't' sound. Don't add an extra vowel between 'g' and 'l' or between 'l' and 'ct'.

nuance.connotation: Negative; it implies carelessness or failure of duty, though sometimes it is unintentional.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'neglect' in everyday speech, for example about pets, plants, or cars, and in formal writing about public services or child welfare. It can sound harsh when applied to a person, so 'I forgot' or 'I didn't get to it' may be softer. 'Neglect' is also a common legal and social term.

distinctions.note: 'Forget' means you did not remember, while 'neglect' suggests you did not give enough care or attention, even if you remembered.
'Ignore' means deliberately paying no attention, while 'neglect' can be careless or accidental.

examples.everyday: I've neglected the lawn all summer, so now the weeds are taller than the grass.
examples.professional: We neglected to update the documentation after the release, so the new team members got confused.
examples.analytical: Aquinas warns that to neglect the duties of charity is to neglect the very love that orders all other virtues.

nuance.analogy: Neglect is like a plant on a windowsill that gets no water: nothing happens at first, but over time it wilts.
nuance.etymology: From Latin 'neglegere', from 'neg-' (not) and 'legere' (to gather or pick up).
common_mistakes: Using 'neglect' with 'to' plus a noun, as in 'neglect to the garden'; the verb takes a direct object: 'neglect the garden'.
Confusing 'neglect' with 'neglecting to do' versus 'neglecting doing'; the pattern 'neglect to do something' means fail to do it.

neglect.etymology: The verb is Middle English *neglecten*, derived from Latin *neglēctus*, perfect passive participle of *neglegō* (“to make light of, disregard, not to pick up”), itself from *nec* (“not”) + *legō* (“to pick up, select”).

senses.definition: An enemy, especially an archenemy.
senses.example: Batman is in constant conflict with his nemesis, The Joker.

senses.definition: A person or character who specifically brings about the downfall of another person or character, as an agent of that character's fate or destiny, especially within a narrative.
senses.example: In the novel, the detective's longtime nemesis is a cunning forger who keeps framing him.

senses.definition: The personification of the "fatal flaw" of a dramatic hero in the style of Greek tragedy.
senses.example: Chocolate chip cookies are my real nemesis.

senses.definition: Polar opposite, especially of a literary character.
senses.example: In the story, the gentle healer is the nemesis of the cruel warlord.

senses.definition: The principle of retributive justice.
senses.example: In her sermon, the pastor warned that nemesis follows every act of cruelty, sooner or later.

senses.definition: A punishment or defeat that is deserved and cannot be avoided; (an instance of) retribution.
senses.example: After years of cheating his partners, his bankruptcy felt like a nemesis he had earned.

core.definition: An enemy or rival who repeatedly defeats you or brings about your downfall; an archenemy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the middle syllable is a weak schwa, so say NEM-uh-sis, not nuh-MEE-sis. The final s is a crisp /s/ sound.

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a serious, persistent opponent, and it can also describe an unavoidable source of ruin, such as a personal weakness.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nemesis in everyday speech for a rival you can never beat, like a sports team's nemesis or a childhood bully who keeps coming back. It is slightly dramatic, so it works well in storytelling and humor but may sound heavy for a minor disagreement. Common replies are simply sympathetic remarks such as 'Oh no, your nemesis again?'

distinctions.note: An enemy is anyone who opposes you; a nemesis is a specific opponent who keeps defeating you or who is destined to bring you down.
A rival competes with you on equal terms, while a nemesis is usually stronger and wins more often.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor's dog has become my nemesis since it keeps digging up the garden.
examples.professional: That legacy database has been our nemesis all quarter, because every migration breaks something.
examples.analytical: In Greek tragedy the hero's nemesis is often his own pride, which the plot turns against him.

nuance.analogy: A nemesis is like a shadow that keeps following you and can never be outrun.
nuance.etymology: From Greek nemesis, 'retribution' or 'divine vengeance', from the verb nemein, 'to allot or distribute'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable (nuh-MEE-sis) instead of the first.
Using nemesis for any ordinary opponent; it implies someone who keeps defeating you.

nemesis.etymology: From the Greek goddess of retribution Nemesis (Ancient Greek *Νέμεσις*); unrelated to *nemes*, which is from Egyptian.

senses.definition: Involving the integration of neural network methods with symbolic reasoning systems.

core.definition: Combining neural network learning with symbolic reasoning, such as logic rules, in one AI system.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'bol' in symbolic, and the first part is a weaker secondary stress. The 'ic' ending is a short 'ik', not 'eek'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: This is an AI research term that is common in technical meetings and papers. Americans say it as one adjective before a noun, like neuro-symbolic approach. Outside AI, people rarely use it.

distinctions.note: Hybrid is a general word for mixing two things; neuro-symbolic specifically means combining neural learning with symbolic logic.

examples.everyday: My cousin says his new chatbot is neuro-symbolic, so it can follow rules as well as learn.
examples.professional: For the design review, I'd like to compare a neuro-symbolic approach with our current model.
examples.analytical: A neuro-symbolic architecture aims to combine the generalization of neural learning with the explicit compositionality of symbolic reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Like a student who learns from examples but also checks the textbook rules before answering.
nuance.etymology: Neuro- comes from Greek neuron, and symbolic comes from Greek symbolon, meaning a token or sign.
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable in 'symbolic' as 'SIM-bol-ik'.
Writing 'neuro symbolic' without a hyphen when used as an adjective.

conversation.text: Neuro-symbolic methods combine neural networks for perception with symbolic reasoning for logic and rules.
A neuro-symbolic pipeline lets us extract entities with a model and then validate them with hard constraints.

senses.definition: The branch of medicine that deals with the disorders of nervous system including the brain and spinal cord of the central nervous system and the nerves, muscles, and neuromuscular junction of the peripheral nervous system.
Focal neurologic signs; focal neurologic deficits.
senses.example: Patient had no neurology.

senses.definition: The results of a neurological examination.
senses.example: Neurology is normal.

core.definition: The branch of medicine that deals with disorders of the brain, spinal cord and nerves, including their diagnosis and treatment.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on RAH, the second syllable. The final -y is a long ee sound, and the middle syllables reduce to quick uh sounds.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It names a medical field and can sound serious when a patient or family member mentions it.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use neurology both for the medical field and for a clinic or department, as in 'She works in neurology' or 'I have a neurology appointment.' Used casually, it refers to a medical specialty, and it is common in hospital and health insurance talk.

distinctions.note: Neurology is clinical medicine that cares for patients, while neuroscience is research into the nervous system, often without treating anyone.
Neurosurgery is the surgical branch that operates on the nervous system, while neurology manages disorders mainly through diagnosis, drugs and therapy.

examples.everyday: I have a neurology appointment on Thursday, so I might be late for lunch.
examples.professional: Neurology wants the EEG results before they change my medication dose, so let's wait until Tuesday.
examples.analytical: Neurology has long sought to map each symptom onto a specific lesion, an ambition that the brain's distributed networks complicate.

nuance.analogy: Neurology is like the mechanic's specialty for the body's wiring: it studies how the signals run and what happens when they break.
nuance.etymology: From neuro-, from Greek neuron meaning nerve, plus -logy, from Greek logos meaning study.
common_mistakes: Using neurology when you mean neuroscience, which is research rather than medical care.
Pronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, which makes the word sound stiff in American speech.

senses.definition: On a traffic sign, indicates that parking a vehicle is not allowed within the area of influence of the sign.

core.definition: A traffic sign or rule meaning that parking a vehicle is not allowed in the marked area.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on PARK, and the r is clearly pronounced, as in 'car'. 'Parking' has a short i in the second syllable, so it does not sound like 'parkeeng'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to negative; it is a prohibition and often comes with a warning of towing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans see 'No Parking' on street signs, often with times such as 'No Parking 8 a.m. to 6 p.m.' Violations can lead to tickets or towing. In some places, 'No Stopping' is a stricter rule that also forbids brief stops.

distinctions.note: 'No stopping' forbids even a brief stop, while 'no parking' may allow a quick drop-off with the driver present.
A 'tow-away zone' describes enforcement, meaning the car will be towed; 'no parking' describes the rule itself.
A 'fire lane' is a designated emergency route with no parking, usually on private property.

collocations: no parking in front of the hydrant

examples.everyday: Don't stop here, there's a no parking sign right behind you.
examples.professional: Facilities put up no parking signs in front of the loading dock so the delivery trucks can get through.
examples.analytical: The no parking restriction in this zone serves public safety more than convenience.

nuance.analogy: Like a stop sign that applies only to parked cars, not to moving traffic.
nuance.etymology: 'No' comes from Old English nā; 'park' comes from Old French parc, 'enclosure'.
common_mistakes: Using 'no parking' as a verb phrase, as in 'don't no parking here'; the correct form is 'no parking' as a sign or rule.
Pronouncing 'park' with the short a of 'hat' instead of the 'ar' sound of 'car'.

senses.definition: Having values whose order is insignificant.
Of, resembling, relating to, or consisting of a name or names.
Assigned to or bearing a person's name.
Existing in name only.
senses.example: a nominal difference

senses.definition: Of or relating to nominalism.
Insignificantly small.
senses.example: He gave me only a nominal sum for my services.

senses.definition: Of or relating to the presumed or approximate value, rather than the actual value.
senses.example: The nominal voltage is 1.5 V, but the actual figure is usually higher.

senses.definition: Of, relating to, or being the amount or face value of a sum of money or a stock certificate, for example, and not the purchasing power or market value.
Of, relating to, or being the rate of interest or return without adjustment for compounding or inflation.
Of or relating to a noun or word group that functions as a noun.
senses.example: This sentence contains a nominal phrase.

senses.definition: According to plan or design.
senses.example: We'll just do a nominal flight check.

senses.definition: Without adjustment to remove the effects of inflation.
senses.example: My employer does not understand how low my nominal wage is.

senses.definition: Of a species, the species name without consideration of whether it is a junior synonym or in reality consists of more than one biological species.
A noun or word group that functions as part of a noun phrase.
senses.example: This sentence contains two nominals.

senses.definition: A part of speech that shares features with nouns and adjectives. (Depending on the language, it may comprise nouns, adjectives, possibly numerals, pronouns, and participles.)
A number (usually natural) used like a name; a numeric code or identifier. (See nominal number on Wikipedia.)
senses.example: Numeric codes of characters used in programming are nominals.

senses.definition: A person listed in the Police National Computer database as having been convicted, cautioned or recently arrested.

core.definition: Existing in name only, or very small in amount; in data, labeling categories without any order.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced vowel, so say 'nul' rather than 'nl' with a separate consonant. The American pronunciation uses an o-like vowel in the first syllable, not a long o.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use; often negative in everyday use, suggesting something small or in name only.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nominal in finance (a nominal fee, nominal interest rate), statistics (nominal data), and everyday talk for a very small amount, like a nominal fee. In a meeting, nominal can mean very small, which is often a polite way to say a cost is minor. In statistics, it names data categories with no inherent order.

distinctions.note: Nominal data has categories with no order; ordinal data has a meaningful order, such as small, medium, large.
Token means symbolic or small in a gesture sense; nominal can refer to a formal, stated amount or name.
Nominative is a grammatical case; nominal refers to nouns or to a name or number in general.

examples.everyday: The gym charges a nominal fee for guests, so it's barely anything.
examples.professional: The consulting fee is nominal, so the real cost is in the implementation hours.
examples.analytical: Nominal categories such as religion or hair color carry no inherent order, so ranking them would distort the analysis.

nuance.analogy: A nominal fee is like a ticket for a free event: you pay something for the record, but the amount is a formality.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nominalis, 'of a name', from nomen, 'name'.
common_mistakes: Confusing nominal with normal, as in 'a nominal amount' versus 'a normal amount'.
Pronouncing the second syllable with a long i sound, as in NAH-mih-NAHL.

nominal.etymology: From the Middle English *nominalle* (“of nouns”), borrowed from Latin *nōminālis* (“of names”), ultimately from oblique stem of Latin *nōmen* (“name”) *-al*.

senses.definition: Synonym of anomia (“the inability to remember names”)
senses.example: After the stroke, her nominal aphasia made it hard to recall her grandson's name.

core.definition: A language disorder, usually from brain damage, in which a person has trouble recalling the names of people, objects, or places.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FAY in 'aphasia,' and the first word has secondary stress on 'nom.' The final 'a' in 'aphasia' is a reduced 'uh' with a 'zh' sound in the middle, not 'uh-FAY-see-uh.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral and clinical. It describes a medical condition without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this term mainly in neurology, speech-language pathology, and medical writing. In U.S. clinics, 'anomia' is the more common term for the same condition. Patients and families usually say 'I can't find the word' or 'I can't remember names.'

distinctions.note: Anomia refers to the same difficulty with names and is the preferred term in most U.S. clinical settings. Nominal aphasia is a less common alternative name.
Aphasia is the broad term for any language loss after brain injury. Nominal aphasia is one specific form of it.
Tip-of-the-tongue describes a brief, temporary lapse in recalling a word that happens to healthy people. Nominal aphasia is a lasting disorder.

collocations: a naming test for nominal aphasia

examples.everyday: After his stroke, my uncle has nominal aphasia, so he often describes an object instead of naming it.
examples.professional: The speech therapist recorded several naming errors that suggested nominal aphasia rather than a general loss of language.
examples.analytical: Cases of nominal aphasia suggest that the brain stores names somewhat separately from other word knowledge.

nuance.analogy: Like a well-organized filing cabinet where a single drawer labeled with names has been jammed shut, so the rest of the files are still there.
nuance.etymology: From Latin nominalis (of names) and, for aphasia, from Greek a- (without) plus phasis (speech).
common_mistakes: Stressing 'aphasia' on the first syllable instead of the second; the main stress is on 'FAY.'
Confusing it with ordinary forgetfulness; the term refers to a medical condition caused by brain damage.

senses.definition: Without distinguishing qualities or characteristics.
senses.example: He drove a nondescript silver sedan.

senses.definition: (rare) Not described (in the academic literature).
senses.label: rare

senses.definition: An undistinguished, unexceptional person or thing.
A species or other type of creature that has not been previously described or identified.

core.definition: Lacking any distinctive features, so plain or ordinary that it is hard to remember or identify.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on SKRIPT, the final syllable. The first syllable is a short ah, and the middle syllable is a reduced ih, not a clear ay.

nuance.connotation: Negative or mildly negative. It usually criticizes something as bland or forgettable.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nondescript to describe a plain building, a car, or a person's appearance that has no memorable features. It is common in both writing and speech, and it is usually a mild insult. Saying a restaurant has a nondescript interior is a polite way of saying it looks dull.

distinctions.note: Ordinary is neutral and says nothing about appeal; nondescript suggests the thing is dull or hard to notice.
Unremarkable is a close synonym but feels more evaluative; nondescript more strongly emphasizes a lack of identifying features.

examples.everyday: We drove past a nondescript office building, and it took us three tries to find the entrance.
examples.professional: The report used a nondescript template that made it hard to tell one project from another.
examples.analytical: Her argument fails because it reduces a complex historical event to a nondescript list of causes.

nuance.analogy: Like a beige wall in a hallway; you pass it a thousand times and never notice it.
nuance.etymology: From non- 'not' and descript, from Latin describere 'to describe'; the sense of 'without distinguishing features' arose in the 1800s.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it as 'non-DES-kript', with the stress on the wrong syllable.
Using it to mean 'not described', which is a specialized sense rarely used in everyday English.
Confusing it with 'indescribable', which means too extraordinary to describe.

senses.definition: Not fictional.
senses.example: The library's nonfictional shelves hold biographies, history books, and science guides.

core.definition: Based on facts and real events rather than invented stories; describing what actually happened or exists.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on NON, with a lighter secondary stress on FIK. The middle syllables reduce to a schwa, so say 'fik-shuh-nul' rather than 'fik-TION-al'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It simply labels a genre or type of writing and carries no judgment about quality.
nuance.usage_note: Americans usually say nonfiction as a noun, as in 'I read mostly nonfiction,' and often use nonfiction as an adjective too, as in 'the nonfiction section.' Nonfictional is more formal and appears mostly in descriptions of writing or film. In everyday talk, 'true story' or 'based on real events' is more natural.

distinctions.note: Factual describes a statement that is accurate; nonfictional describes a whole work's genre, so a nonfictional book can contain errors.
Nonfiction is the usual noun for the category; nonfictional is the adjective and sounds more formal.

examples.everyday: I'd rather read something nonfictional, like a history of the Dust Bowl, than another novel.
examples.professional: Our team reading list this quarter includes two nonfictional books on data ethics.
examples.analytical: The distinction between a nonfictional account and a novel rests less on style than on the author's commitment to verifiable claims.

nuance.analogy: A nonfictional book is like a map drawn from surveys of real land, while a novel is a map of an imagined island.
nuance.etymology: Non- (not) plus fictional, from fiction, from Latin fictio 'a shaping or invention'.
common_mistakes: Using nonfictional as a noun: say 'I read a lot of nonfiction,' not 'I read a lot of nonfictional.'
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'non-fik-SHUN-al'; the stress belongs on NON.

senses.definition: Not infectious, particularly with respect to a disease.
senses.example: Doctors confirmed the rash was noninfectious, so my son could return to school the next day.

core.definition: Not capable of spreading from one person or organism to another; not caused or transmitted by infection.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on FEC, not on the prefix non-, so keep the first syllables light. The ending -tious is pronounced shus, not tee-us.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to reassuring; it tells listeners a condition is not a risk to others, which people usually welcome in health settings.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word mostly in medical, public health and hospital contexts, such as a noninfectious rash or noninfectious inflammation. In everyday talk people more often say the condition is not contagious or it won't spread. Use it when you need the precise technical distinction from infectious causes.

distinctions.note: Contagious is the everyday word for spreading by touch or breath; noninfectious is the more precise medical term for conditions not caused by a pathogen.
Public health uses noncommunicable for chronic diseases such as heart disease, which are noninfectious; the terms overlap but noncommunicable is the standard policy term.

examples.everyday: My doctor said the rash is noninfectious, so I don't have to stay home from work.
examples.professional: Please mark the case as noninfectious in the chart so the nurses don't use isolation precautions.
examples.analytical: The study separated infectious from noninfectious causes of pneumonia to clarify which treatment pathways apply.

nuance.analogy: Like a splinter in your finger: it hurts and needs treatment, but it cannot spread to the next person.
nuance.etymology: From non- ('not') plus infectious, from Latin inficere, 'to put in, stain, infect'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the prefix non- instead of the root fec, which sounds unnatural to American ears.
Using noninfectious to mean harmless; an injury or disease can be noninfectious and still be serious.

senses.definition: Not viable: not capable of independent life; not practicable.
senses.example: The startup's business plan was nonviable, since costs far exceeded any realistic revenue.

core.definition: Unable to survive or succeed, or not practical enough to be workable.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on VY, the second syllable. Keep the 'vi' as 'vy' and make the last syllable a quick 'buhl'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and factual. In medical contexts it is clinical; in business it is a judgment that something will not work.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nonviable in biology, medicine, business and project planning, such as 'That business model is nonviable.' In casual talk, they usually say 'won't work' or 'not realistic'. In medical contexts, the word is more sensitive, so people choose it carefully.

distinctions.note: Impractical means not sensible or easy to use; nonviable means it cannot succeed or sustain itself at all.
Unworkable is more casual and focuses on a plan failing in use; nonviable is more analytical and can apply to organisms or businesses as well.

examples.everyday: We looked at buying the old house, but the repairs made it nonviable for our budget.
examples.professional: After the pilot, leadership decided the product was nonviable at current costs, so the team pivoted.
examples.analytical: A theory that cannot predict anything testable is, in an important sense, nonviable as science.

nuance.analogy: Like a plant that cannot get enough light, it may survive for a while but cannot grow or last.
nuance.etymology: From non- ('not') plus viable, from French viable, from Latin vita ('life').
common_mistakes: Pronouncing 'vi' as 'vee'; the vowel is a long 'i' as in 'vibe'.
Using nonviable for a difficult but possible task; it means the task cannot succeed.

senses.definition: A person involved in providing direct care for the sick:
senses.example: My aunt was my nurse while I recuperated at home from surgery.

senses.definition: Anyone performing this role, regardless of training or profession.
senses.example: My aunt was my nurse while I recuperated at home from surgery.

senses.definition: A medical worker performing this role, typically someone trained to provide such care but having credentials and rank below a doctor or physician assistant.
senses.example: The nurse made her rounds through the hospital ward.

senses.definition: A medical worker, such as a registered nurse, having training, credentials, and rank above a nurse assistant.
senses.example: The night nurse checked my blood pressure and adjusted the IV drip.

senses.definition: One who, or that which, brings up, rears, causes to grow, trains, or fosters.
senses.example: Eton College has been called "the chief nurse of England's statesmen".

senses.definition: A shrub or tree that protects a young plant.
senses.example: The young oak needed a nurse plant, a hardy shrub, to shade it from frost.

senses.definition: A larva of certain trematodes, which produces cercariae by asexual reproduction.
senses.example: The parasitologist found a nurse larva inside the snail, producing cercariae by asexual budding.

senses.definition: A nurse shark or dogfish.
senses.example: A nurse shark rested motionless on the sandy bottom near the reef.

senses.definition: A lieutenant or first officer who takes command when the captain is unfit for his place.
senses.example: When the captain was too ill to command, the nurse took charge of the ship.

senses.definition: To breastfeed: to feed (a baby) at the breast; to suckle.
senses.example: She believes that nursing her baby will make him strong and healthy.

senses.definition: To breastfeed: to be fed at the breast.
senses.example: She tried to nurse the baby in the back seat during the long drive.

senses.definition: To care for (someone), especially in sickness; to tend to.
senses.example: She nursed him back to health.

senses.definition: To tend gently and with extra care.
senses.example: She nursed the rosebush and that season it bloomed.

senses.definition: To manage or oversee (something) with care and economy.
senses.example: She nursed the small business through the recession with careful budgeting.

senses.definition: To drink (a beverage) slowly, so as to make it last.
senses.example: Rob was nursing a small beer.

senses.definition: To cultivate or persistently entertain (an attitude, usually negative) in one's mind; to brood or obsess over.
senses.example: to nurse a grudge

senses.definition: To hold closely to one's chest.
senses.example: Would you like to nurse the puppy?

senses.definition: To strike (billiard balls) gently, so as to keep them in good position during a series of shots.
senses.example: Instead of breaking hard, he nursed the cue ball to leave his next shot open.

core.definition: A trained health professional who cares for sick or injured patients, usually under a doctor's supervision.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is the American r-colored vowel, so the r is pronounced clearly and the word has one syllable. Learners often add a schwa after the r, making it sound like 'nur-suh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive; it signals care, patience, and competence.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use nurse for anyone trained to care for patients, and they often write RN for registered nurse or LPN for licensed practical nurse. The profession is called nursing. As a verb, nurse means to care for someone who is sick or to feed a baby at the breast, and Americans more often say nursing or breastfeeding for the feeding sense. Calling a nurse a nurse lady sounds dated.

distinctions.note: A doctor diagnoses and prescribes treatment; a nurse carries out much of the daily care and monitoring of patients.
A caregiver may be a family member with no medical training; a nurse is a licensed health professional.
A nanny cares for healthy children in a household; a nurse cares for sick or injured patients in a healthcare setting.

examples.everyday: My sister is a nurse at the hospital, so she works twelve-hour shifts and sleeps a lot on her days off.
examples.professional: The charge nurse asked me to update the patient's medication log before my shift ends.
examples.analytical: The nurse's role in the care team depends on clinical judgment that medical literature has often underestimated.

nuance.analogy: Like a navigator who watches the instruments all night while the captain rests, keeping the ship on course through the hours that matter most.
nuance.etymology: From Old French nurice, from Latin nutrix 'one who nourishes', from nutrire 'to nourish'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'I am a nurse of the hospital'; the usual phrase is 'a nurse at the hospital' or 'a nurse in the ICU'.
Assuming nurse as a verb always means feeding; it can also mean to care for someone, or to sip a drink slowly, as in 'nurse a coffee'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture a nurse is a caregiver of infants and children, and the image is used for tender, patient care. The Hebrew word 'omenet means a nurse or foster-mother, related to the root 'aman meaning to nourish or support. The Greek word trophos means one who nourishes or nurses, and it appears in 1 Thessalonians 2:7. Key passages: 1 Thessalonians 2:7 compares Paul's gentle care for the believers to a nurse caring for her own children. Isaiah 49:23 says that kings and queens will serve the restored people as foster fathers and nurses, a picture of honored, devoted care. Numbers 11:12 has Moses asking whether he must carry the people as a nurse carries a nursing child, expressing his burden of leadership.

nurse.etymology: From Middle English *norice*, from Old French *norrice*, from Late Latin *nūtrīcia*, noun based on Latin *nūtrīcius* (“that which nourishes”), from *nūtrīx* (“wet nurse”), from *nūtriō* (“to suckle”).

senses.definition: Undecided or unsure; equivocating; conflicted in one's opinions.
senses.example: I'm of two minds about this approach that the company has chosen to take. I realize why it was chosen, but I question whether it can work adequately.

core.definition: Unsure or undecided about something, with two conflicting opinions or feelings about it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on MINDS, and 'two' keeps a weaker stress. In speech, 'of two' links together, so it sounds like 'uh-v-TOO'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It describes indecision without judging it, so it is a fair way to admit you have not decided yet.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this idiom in everyday conversation and at work to say they have not made up their minds. It is usually followed by 'about', as in 'I'm of two minds about the new schedule'. A natural reply is 'What's holding you back?' or 'Which way are you leaning?'

distinctions.note: 'Undecided' is a plain, neutral word, while 'of two minds' suggests that you can see good points on both sides.
'On the fence' is more informal and often means you have not chosen a side yet, while 'of two minds' focuses on your internal conflict.
'Ambivalent' is more formal and psychological, and it implies mixed feelings, often emotional ones.

examples.everyday: I'm of two minds about going to the lake this weekend, because the forecast looks bad.
examples.professional: The team is of two minds about switching to the new database, so we need more data before we decide.
examples.analytical: The author is of two minds about reason, honoring its power while doubting its ability to reach the heart.

nuance.analogy: Like a coin balanced on its edge: it has not yet fallen to either side.
common_mistakes: Saying 'of two minds with' instead of 'of two minds about' when you talk about a subject.
Thinking it means you are sick or confused, when it simply means you have not decided.

senses.definition: In a direction away from the speaker or other reference point.
senses.example: He drove off in a cloud of smoke.

senses.definition: Into a state of non-operation or non-existence.
senses.example: Please switch off the light when you leave.

senses.definition: So as to remove or separate, or be removed or separated.
senses.example: He bit off the end of the carrot.

senses.definition: Specifying the number of some item in bills, parts lists, etc.
senses.example: 3 off 20 amp fuses

senses.definition: Offstage.
senses.example: noises off

senses.definition: Used in various other ways specific to individual idiomatic phrases, e.g. bring off, show off, put off, tell off, etc. See the entry for the individual phrase.
Inoperative, disabled.
senses.example: All the lights are off.

senses.definition: Canceled; not happening.
senses.example: The party's off because the hostess is sick.

senses.definition: Not fitted; not being worn.
senses.example: Your feet will feel better once those tight boots are off.

senses.definition: Denoting something faulty, unsatisfactory, objectionable etc.
senses.example: This calculation is off: the numbers don't add up.

senses.definition: Not correct; not properly formed; not logical, harmonious, etc.
senses.example: This calculation is off: the numbers don't add up.

senses.definition: Inappropriate; untoward.
senses.example: I felt that his comments were a bit off.

senses.definition: Less than normal, in temperament or in result.
senses.example: sales are off this quarter

senses.definition: Designating a time when one is not performing to the best of one's abilities.
Disgusting, repulsive, abhorrent.
Circumstanced.
senses.example: Our family used to be well off; now we're very badly off.

senses.definition: Started on the way.
senses.example: off to see the wizard

senses.definition: Far; off to the side.
senses.example: He took me down the corridor and into an off room.

senses.definition: Temporarily not attending a usual place, such as work or school, especially owing to illness or holiday.
senses.example: John's off today. He's back on Wednesday.

senses.definition: Designating a time when one is not strictly attentive to business or affairs, or is absent from a post, and, hence, a time when affairs are not urgent.
senses.example: He took an off day for fishing. an off year in politics; the off season

senses.definition: Presently unavailable.
senses.example: I'll have the chicken please. — Sorry, chicken's off today.

senses.definition: Offsuit.
In, or towards the half of the field away from the batsman's legs; the right side for a right-handed batsman.
Not positioned upon; away from a position upon.
senses.example: He's off the roof now.

senses.definition: Detached, separated, excluded or disconnected from; away from a position of attachment or connection to.
senses.example: The phone is off the hook

senses.definition: Outside the area or region of.
senses.example: The suspect is now believed to be off the campus.

senses.definition: Temporarily not attending (a usual place), especially owing to illness or holiday.
senses.example: off work; off school

senses.definition: Used to indicate the location or direction of one thing relative to another, implying adjacency or accessibility via.
senses.example: His office is off this corridor on the right.

senses.definition: Used to express location at sea relative to land or mainland.
senses.example: The island is 23 miles off the cape.

senses.definition: (Can we verify this sense?) Used to indicate separation from a natural home or origin.
senses.example: He used to be gone a lot of the time, off working on an oil rig.

senses.definition: Removed or subtracted from.
senses.example: There's 20% off the list price.

senses.definition: No longer wanting or taking.
senses.example: He's been off his feed since Tuesday.

senses.definition: Out of the possession of.
senses.example: He didn't buy it off him. He stole it off him.

senses.definition: (Should we delete this sense?) Placed after a number (of products or parts, as if a unit), in commerce or engineering.
senses.example: I'd like to re-order those printer cartridges, let's say 5-off.

senses.definition: Under the influence of.
senses.example: The guy was off a perc.

senses.definition: As a result of; resulting from the actions of.
senses.example: The team won off a late-game fumble by an opposing player.

senses.definition: To kill.
Beginning; starting point.
senses.example: He has been very obviously an untrustworthy narrator right from the off.

core.definition: Into a state of not operating, or away from a place or position; for example, 'turn the light off'.

pronunciation.tip: Say one short syllable with a clear final f, and do not add a vowel after it. Many Americans with the cot-caught merger say /ɑf/, so either sound is fine in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a basic, functional word.
nuance.usage_note: 'Off' is very common as an adverb in phrasal verbs such as 'turn off', 'take off', and 'log off'. Americans say 'Turn it off' or 'I'm off' when leaving. It is also used for cancellation, as in 'The game is off'.

distinctions.note: 'Of' is the preposition meaning belonging or part, while 'off' means separated or not operating, so the spellings are easy to confuse.
'Away' stresses distance, as in 'go away', while 'off' stresses separation, detachment, or switching something off.

examples.everyday: Can you turn off the TV before we go to bed?
examples.professional: I'll log off the call now, but send me the slides and I'll review them tonight.
examples.analytical: The argument breaks off abruptly, as if the author has suddenly cut off the line of reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Like a light switch: 'off' is the position where the current stops flowing.
nuance.etymology: A variant of 'of' in Old English, meaning 'away from'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'off' with 'of' in writing, for example writing 'turn of the light'.
Saying 'turn the light off' with the wrong word order, or 'turn off it' instead of 'turn it off'.

off.etymology: From Middle English *of*, from Old English *of*, *af*, *æf* (“, off, away”), from **ab*, from Proto-Germanic **ab* (“from”), from Proto-Indo-European **h₂epo* (“, off, back”).

senses.definition: Delighted; ecstatic; exceptionally pleased, happy, or satisfied.
senses.example: He was on top of the world after she agreed to marry him.

core.definition: Extremely happy, proud, or satisfied; feeling wonderful about one's life or achievements.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on WORLD. Reduce 'of' to 'uhv' and 'the' to 'thuh' before a consonant, and keep the r in 'world' clearly American.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It expresses joy, pride, or a high point in life.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this for a happy moment such as a promotion, a wedding, or a win. You can say 'I'm on top of the world since the baby slept through the night.' A natural reply is 'That's great, you deserve it.' It is warm and casual, so it fits conversation with friends, family, or coworkers rather than formal writing.

distinctions.note: Both mean very happy; over the moon is slightly more informal and often suggests excitement about a specific good event, while on top of the world can describe a broader sense of well-being.
On cloud nine is a bit more playful and emphasizes blissful happiness, often in romance; on top of the world is more about pride and success.

collocations: feel on top of the world
be on top of the world
on top of the world after the win
feel like I'm on top of the world
sound on top of the world

examples.everyday: Ever since I got the job offer, I've felt on top of the world.
examples.professional: After the successful product launch, the whole team was on top of the world.
examples.analytical: Ambition often promises that success will leave us on top of the world, yet many achievers report a strange emptiness.

nuance.analogy: Like standing on a mountain peak, where everything below looks small and the view feels wide.
common_mistakes: Saying 'on the top of the world'; the usual American phrase is 'on top of the world' without 'the'.
Using it for physical height only; it is a figure of speech for happiness.

conversation.text: After the race, I felt on top of the world.
She's on top of the world since she got into college.
With the new job and the new house, they're on top of the world.

senses.definition: Of or pertaining to a specific period of time in the past, not extending to the present.
senses.example: He was the one-time president of the club.

senses.definition: Occurring or used in a single instance and then never again.
senses.example: one-time charge/payment

senses.definition: To shoot (the ball or puck) directly from a teammate's pass.
senses.example: He one-timed the pass from the winger into the top corner.

senses.definition: The police.
senses.example: The one-time arrived within minutes, sirens blaring, and cleared the parking lot.

core.definition: Happening only once, or as a single occurrence not repeated; or describing a former person or role.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on TIME, with 'one' lightly stressed as 'wun'. The hyphen shows a compound adjective, so say it as one smooth phrase.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can imply the thing will not happen again, which may be disappointing in business or shopping contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use one-time in finance, shopping and planning: 'a one-time fee' or 'a one-time payment'. It also describes a former person or role, as in 'my one-time roommate', which is conversational. Hockey players use 'one-timer' for a shot taken directly off a pass.

distinctions.note: Former simply means earlier in position or time, while one-time as a label for a former person is more informal and conversational.
Occasional means happening from time to time and repeating irregularly, which is the opposite of one-time.

examples.everyday: My one-time roommate still sends me Christmas cards.
examples.professional: We're offering a one-time credit to customers affected by the outage.
examples.analytical: The tribunal treated the decree as a one-time act rather than a standing policy, so its precedent value was limited.

nuance.analogy: Like a single shot in a game that cannot be repeated: once it's used, it's gone.
nuance.etymology: Compound of 'one' (Old English ān) and 'time' (Old English tīma).
common_mistakes: Omitting the hyphen before a noun, writing 'one time fee' instead of 'one-time fee'.
Using one-time for something rare but repeating; for that, say occasional.

senses.definition: In an opaque manner.

core.definition: In a way that hides meaning or intentions, so that people cannot easily see or understand what is happening.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the middle syllable, PAYK, which rhymes with 'bake.' The final -ly is a light 'lee.'

nuance.connotation: Negative. It suggests that information is deliberately concealed or made confusing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'opaquely' in journalism, business, government, and academic writing to criticize unclear processes. In conversation they usually say 'not clearly' or 'without explaining.' It can also describe physical opacity, but that use is rare.

distinctions.note: Vaguely means not clearly defined, often by accident; opaquely suggests that the lack of clarity is deliberate.
Ambiguously means something can be understood in two or more ways; opaquely means it is hard to understand at all.
Cryptically suggests a puzzle or code, while opaquely suggests hidden facts or motives.

examples.everyday: My landlord explained the fee so opaquely that I still don't know why it went up.
examples.professional: The budget was presented so opaquely that the team could not tell which costs were fixed and which were variable.
examples.analytical: The treaty is drafted opaquely, leaving key obligations to be settled later in agreements the public never sees.

nuance.analogy: Like a letter written in a code that only the sender can read.
nuance.etymology: From opaque plus the adverb suffix -ly; opaque comes from Latin opacus, meaning shaded.
common_mistakes: Using 'opaquely' only for physical things; in everyday American English it usually means unclear communication.
Pronouncing the vowel as 'ah' instead of the long 'ay' of 'bake.'

senses.definition: A set of principles and practices through which research outputs are distributed online, free of access charges or other barriers.
senses.example: The university requires that all funded research appear in open access journals within a year.

senses.definition: Public access to infrastructure, such as railways.
senses.example: The city council debated open access to the freight railway for independent operators.

core.definition: A system in which research articles and other scholarly publications are free to read online, without subscriptions or paywalls.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of 'open' and the first syllable of 'access,' with the strongest stress on 'AK' in the noun. Keep 'open' light, as in 'OH-pun,' and do not stress the second syllable of 'access.'

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests fairness, public benefit, and the free sharing of knowledge.
nuance.usage_note: In the United States, 'open access' is mainly used in universities, libraries, and science publishing. People talk about 'open access journals' or 'open access articles.' The second sense, public access to infrastructure such as railways, is rare in American English, where people would say 'public access' instead.

distinctions.note: Open source refers to software code that anyone can view or modify; open access refers to publications and research outputs.
A paywall is the barrier that charges money for reading; open access is the removal of that barrier.
A preprint is an early version of a paper that may not be peer reviewed; open access describes free availability, which a preprint may or may not have.

examples.everyday: My sister found an open access article about sleep that she could read for free, so she shared the link with me.
examples.professional: Our data science team publishes its model documentation under open access so partners can review it without a subscription.
examples.analytical: Open access shifts the economic burden of scholarship from readers to authors and funders, raising questions about equity among researchers.

nuance.analogy: Like a public library for research: anyone with a library card can read the book.
nuance.etymology: Open comes from Old English open; access comes from Latin accessus, meaning approach.
common_mistakes: Stressing the second word too strongly; the main stress in the noun phrase is on 'access.'
Writing 'open-access' without a hyphen in a formal document when it comes before a noun; Americans usually hyphenate it as 'open-access journal.'

senses.definition: Unrestricted by definite limits.
senses.example: There will be an open-ended discussion.

senses.definition: Adaptable to change.
senses.example: The topic is definitions, but is open-ended really.

senses.definition: Permitting a spontaneous or unstructured response.
senses.example: I'll ask you an open-ended question.

senses.definition: Of a straight draw, made up of four consecutive cards, thus able to be completed by either of two ranks of card.
senses.example: The flop of 3-6-Q gave Brunson an open-ended straight draw with his 4-5 of hearts.

core.definition: Without fixed limits or a single correct answer; allowing many possible responses, outcomes or directions.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on END, and OPEN is only lightly stressed. The ending is a soft, reduced vowel, so say 'END-id' with almost no separate 'ed' syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It usually praises flexibility or freedom, but a vague open-ended plan can sound like a lack of commitment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use open-ended for questions, contracts, projects, and discussions that have no fixed deadline or single answer. An open-ended question invites a full reply, while a yes-or-no question does not. In business, an open-ended contract or commitment can worry a manager who wants clear limits, so pair the term with a timeline when you need one.

distinctions.note: Open-ended means deliberately unrestricted; vague means unclear or imprecise, often in a negative way.
Unlimited refers to a quantity or amount without a cap; open-ended more often refers to a question, scope, or process.

examples.everyday: My sister asked me an open-ended question about what I want to do this summer, so I just started talking.
examples.professional: Let's keep the scope of the pilot open-ended so we can adjust the features after the first user feedback.
examples.analytical: An open-ended inquiry does not assume its conclusion in advance, which is why it can surprise its own researchers.

nuance.analogy: An open-ended question is like a road with no sign pointing to a destination: you can go in many directions.
nuance.etymology: From open (Old English opan) and -ended, meaning having an end that is not fixed.
common_mistakes: Saying open-end for the adjective; the American adjective is open-ended.
Stressing the first word OPEN instead of END.

senses.definition: Pertaining to the start or beginning of a series of events.
senses.example: The opening theme of Beethoven's Fifth Symphony is, perhaps, the most recognizable in all of European art music.

senses.definition: Of the first period of play, usually up to the fall of the first wicket.
senses.example: After the opening session, the home side was already three wickets down and struggling to score.
