common_mistakes: Adding an extra syllable, such as 'WAY-tuh-ris', which is not standard American speech.
Using waitress for a man, when waiter or server is the correct term.

conversation.text: The waitress brought us extra bread without us asking.
My mom was a waitress at a diner for twenty years.
Our waitress was so sweet; she even remembered our names.

senses.definition: Distorted by warping; twisted out of shape.
Of a person's mind, attitudes, etc, perverse, strange, aberrant or deviant.
senses.example: a warped sense of humor

core.definition: Bent or twisted out of shape, as wood does when it absorbs moisture; also describing a mind or attitude that is strange or distorted.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with the aw vowel of 'law' and a clear r. The -ed ending is pronounced as a plain t with no extra vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral for objects like wood or floors; negative or humorous when describing a person's mind, attitudes or sense of humor.
nuance.usage_note: Describing a floor, door, or record as warped is ordinary American English. Calling a person's sense of humor or thinking warped is informal and can be playful or insulting. For a simply bent object, Americans often say bent or twisted.

distinctions.note: Bent is general, while warped specifically means twisted out of shape, often by heat, moisture or stress.
Twisted can suggest deliberate evil or a sharp turn, while warped suggests a slow, unwanted distortion.
Deformed suggests a physical defect in a body or object, while warped means changed by its environment over time.

examples.everyday: My bedroom door is so warped that it won't close all the way.
examples.professional: The lab bench is warped, so the level readings keep drifting throughout the day.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the ideology has produced a warped picture of human nature, one that ignores grace and responsibility.

nuance.analogy: A warped board is like a sheet of paper left in the rain: it looks flat until it changes shape and stops lying flat.
nuance.etymology: From warp, from Old English weorpan, to throw.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing warped as two syllables; it is one syllable, /wɔɹpt/.
Using warped for an ordinary bent object when bent is more natural.

senses.definition: That can be watched.
That is worth watching; interesting or thrilling to watch.
Something to be watched, or worth watching.
senses.example: The festival programmers picked only a few watchables from a pile of tedious submissions.

core.definition: Worth watching; enjoyable or interesting to watch, such as a movie, show, or game.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WATCH, with a lighter secondary stress on -ay. The final -able is reduced to a quick 'buhl', not 'AY-bull'.

nuance.connotation: Positive but mild. Calling something watchable is a moderate compliment, weaker than 'excellent' or 'gripping'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use watchable for TV shows, movies, videos, and sports, usually to say something is pleasant enough to keep watching. Saying 'It's pretty watchable' sounds relaxed and honest. Do not use it for people; it describes things you watch.

distinctions.note: Entertaining means actively amusing or fun; watchable only means it holds your attention without being bad.
Gripping is a strong word for something that makes you tense with suspense; watchable is much milder.

examples.everyday: That new cooking show is actually pretty watchable, even if the host talks too much.
examples.professional: The demo video is watchable now, but we still need to tighten the transitions before we share it with the client.
examples.analytical: A film can be watchable without being good, since its pacing and images can sustain attention even when its argument is thin.

nuance.analogy: Like a comfortable chair in a waiting room: you are happy to stay in it even if it is not special.
nuance.etymology: From watch plus the suffix -able, 'able to be watched'.
common_mistakes: Using watchable for people, as in 'She is very watchable'; this sounds odd. Use 'compelling' or 'fun to watch' instead.
Stressing the suffix as in 'wat-CHAY-bul'; the main stress is on WATCH.

senses.definition: A horizontal line indicating the shape of an airfoil.
senses.example: The engineer drew a waterline across the wing model to show the airfoil's shape.

senses.definition: A line showing where the water has been.
The line formed by where the water level of a body of water currently is: where the water's surface currently meets the bank; it may move higher or lower depending on the weather, tide, or season.
The inner rim of the eyelid, just behind the lash line; primarily used in reference to the application of eyeliner.
senses.example: She applied a thin line of liner along her waterline to make her eyes look larger.

senses.definition: A water pipeline.
A line formed by the surface of the water on the hull of a ship when she is afloat; any of a series of short lines marked on the hull to show where the waterline would be under different loadings.
senses.example: The old freighter sat so low that the waterline almost touched the harbor's surface.

core.definition: The line where the surface of a body of water meets the shore or bank, which rises and falls with weather, tides and seasons.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and keep the middle syllable light, with a quick flapped t so it sounds like 'WAW-der'. The last word 'line' rhymes with 'fine'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a plain descriptive term used literally in boating, construction and nature talk, and occasionally figuratively for a limit or level.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word often in boating, fishing, home and real estate talk, as in 'the waterline on the dock is three feet lower than last summer.' For a boat, it is the line on the hull where the water sits. Americans also say 'high-water mark' for the highest level water has reached, which is a different idea.

distinctions.note: Shoreline is the general edge of land along a sea or lake, while waterline is the level where water meets the land or hull at a given moment.
A high-water mark is the highest level water has reached, often shown by debris or a stain, while a waterline shifts daily.

examples.everyday: After the drought, you can see the old waterline on the rocks down at the lake.
examples.professional: The contractor said the leak sits below the waterline, so the crew has to pump the basement dry before repairing the wall.
examples.analytical: Hydrologists treat the waterline as a moving boundary, so any measurement of a shoreline must specify the date and water level it describes.

nuance.analogy: Like the tide mark on a bathtub: the ring moves up and down as the water level changes.
nuance.etymology: Compound of water and line; the line where water meets a hull or shore.
common_mistakes: Writing 'water line' as two words in formal American writing; the compound is usually one word.
Confusing it with 'shoreline', which is the land edge rather than the level of the water.

senses.definition: The ability of a person or animal to orientate itself and to navigate; the process used by a person or animal for orienting and navigating.
senses.example: Good wayfinding in the hospital helps anxious families locate the right ward quickly.

core.definition: The process of finding one's way through a space, using signs, maps, landmarks and other cues to reach a destination.

pronunciation.tip: Stress 'WAY' and say the second part as 'fine-ding', with a clear long 'i' and a short 'ing' ending. Do not stress 'find' as strongly as 'way'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and professional. It describes a design or cognitive process without emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: In American English, 'wayfinding' is common in architecture, urban planning, hospital and airport design, and in discussions of signage and user experience. It also appears in animal behavior research about how birds or other animals navigate. In everyday talk, Americans often say 'finding my way around' or 'getting around'.

distinctions.note: 'Navigation' is broader and often technical, used for ships, planes and GPS, while 'wayfinding' focuses on how people orient and move through built spaces.
'Orientation' means knowing where you are, while 'wayfinding' includes the whole process of getting to a destination.

examples.everyday: The hospital's wayfinding is so confusing that I walked in circles for twenty minutes before I found the clinic.
examples.professional: Our wayfinding redesign for the new campus lobby should reduce the number of visitor calls to the help desk.
examples.analytical: Research on animal wayfinding shows that migrating birds combine magnetic, celestial and olfactory cues to keep their course.

nuance.analogy: Good wayfinding is like a well-marked trail: the path tells you where to go without you having to think about it.
nuance.etymology: From 'way' plus 'find', from Old English 'findan', with the suffix -ing.
common_mistakes: Using 'wayfinding' to mean simply knowing directions; it refers to the whole process, including signs and design.
Using 'wayfinding' as a verb; say 'find my way' or 'navigate' instead.

senses.definition: To get (someone) off (an addiction), to rid (someone) of a habit.

core.definition: To gradually reduce someone's dependence on a substance or habit until they no longer need it.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on 'off', and 'wean' gets a weaker secondary stress. Pronounce 'wean' as 'ween', rhyming with 'queen', not 'when'. In fast speech the t and o link smoothly as 'ween-AWF'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It describes a careful, supportive process of reducing dependence, often in medical or family contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'wean off' for medications, drugs, alcohol, sugar, screen time, and other habits, and it usually implies a slow, planned reduction. You can say 'She is weaning herself off caffeine' or 'The doctor is weaning him off the medication.' It is less common for quitting something suddenly, which Americans call 'going cold turkey' or 'quitting cold.'

distinctions.note: 'Quit' means stop completely, often suddenly, while 'wean off' implies a gradual reduction.
'Cut back on' is a general term for reducing any amount of something, while 'wean off' suggests reducing dependence until it stops entirely.
'Give up' is a more casual phrase for stopping a habit or goal, and it doesn't necessarily involve a gradual process.

examples.everyday: I'm trying to wean myself off coffee, so now I only have one cup in the morning.
examples.professional: The clinical team plans to wean the patient off the sedative over several weeks to avoid withdrawal symptoms.
examples.analytical: Public health researchers argue that policymakers should wean communities off dependence on single-industry economies rather than abruptly withdrawing support.

nuance.analogy: Weaning someone off a habit is like slowly loosening a rope rather than cutting it all at once.
nuance.etymology: 'Wean' comes from Old English 'wenian', meaning to accustom; 'off' is the adverb of separation.
common_mistakes: Using 'wean from' instead of 'wean off' for habits or medications, which sounds less natural in American English.
Saying 'wean' so it rhymes with 'when'. The vowel is a long e, as in 'ween'.

senses.definition: To form something by passing lengths or strands of material over and under one another.
senses.example: This loom weaves yarn into cloth.

senses.definition: To spin a cocoon or a web.
senses.example: Spiders weave beautiful but deadly webs.

senses.definition: To unite by close connection or intermixture.
senses.example: The new policy weaves environmental concerns into every decision the company makes.

senses.definition: To compose creatively and intricately; to fabricate.
senses.example: to weave the plot of a story

senses.definition: To move by turning and twisting.
senses.example: The drunk weaved into another bar.

senses.definition: To make (a path or way) by winding in and out or from side to side.
senses.example: The ambulance weaved its way through the heavy traffic.

senses.definition: To move the head back and forth in a stereotyped pattern, typically as a symptom of stress.
senses.example: The horse began to weave back and forth in its stall after being confined for hours.

senses.definition: A type or way of weaving.
senses.example: That rug has a very tight weave.

senses.definition: Human or artificial hair worn to alter one's appearance, either to supplement or to cover the natural hair.
senses.example: She wore a dark weave to cover the thinning patches near her temples.

core.definition: To make cloth, baskets or other things by passing threads or strands over and under one another.

pronunciation.tip: The vowel is a long e, as in 'believe', and the word ends with a v sound. Do not pronounce it like 'wave' or 'weave' as 'wee-ave'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests skill and craft, or combining things into one whole in a figurative sense.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use weave for textiles, baskets and hair extensions, and figuratively for combining stories or ideas. 'Weave a story' or 'weave together threads of evidence' sound natural in writing and speeches. In casual talk, 'I got a weave' refers to hair extensions.

distinctions.note: Knitting loops yarn with needles; weaving interlaces threads at right angles on a loom.
Braiding twists three or more strands in a pattern; weaving passes threads over and under in a fabric grid.

examples.everyday: My grandmother loves to weave baskets on the porch in the summer.
examples.professional: We need to weave the customer feedback into the product roadmap so each team sees its impact.
examples.analytical: Isaiah's image of the weaver suggests a life drawn together in one thread, which the prophet then breaks off.

nuance.analogy: Like a hand pulling thread over and under a loom until a single fabric holds together.
nuance.etymology: From Old English wefan, to weave, with the past form wove.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'weave' with 'we've' in writing; the verb is weave.
Mixing up the past tense: the past is 'wove', and the past participle is 'woven'.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew behind weaving in the Old Testament is 'arag' (to weave). In the Revised Standard Version, Isaiah 38:12 compares a life being cut off to a weaver rolling up his cloth, and Isaiah 59:5 says the wicked weave the spider's web. Job 7:6 describes the speed of days as swifter than a weaver's shuttle. These passages use weaving as an image of human life ending suddenly or of schemes that trap others.

weave.etymology: From Middle English *weven* (“to weave”), from Old English *wefan* (“to weave”), from **weban*, from Proto-Germanic **webaną*, from Proto-Indo-European **webʰ-* (“to weave, braid”).

senses.definition: Abounding with weeds.
senses.example: weedy grounds

senses.definition: Of, relating to or resembling weeds.
senses.example: The abandoned lot was overgrown with weedy plants and tall, scraggly grass.

senses.definition: Consisting of weeds.
Small and weak.
senses.example: a weedy lad

senses.definition: Characteristic of a plant that grows rapidly and spreads invasively, and which grows opportunistically in cracks of sidewalks and disturbed areas.
senses.example: a weedy species

core.definition: Full of weeds; or, of a person, thin and physically weak in appearance.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, WEE, and end with a long ee sound, like 'happy' with a clear final ee. Avoid a short i ending.

nuance.connotation: Negative, especially when describing a person; it can sound insulting.
nuance.usage_note: For gardens and lawns, Americans say 'weedy' for a place full of unwanted plants, such as 'the lawn got weedy while we were away.' Used of a person, 'weedy' means skinny and weak, which can be rude, so avoid it in front of the person. Americans more often say 'scrawny' or 'skinny' for thin bodies.

distinctions.note: Scrawny stresses thinness and bony appearance; weedy adds the sense of being weak or unathletic.
Overgrown means too large or tangled from neglect; weedy means full of weeds.

examples.everyday: The backyard got kind of weedy while we were on vacation, so we spent the weekend fixing it.
examples.professional: The field is weedy after the wet spring, so we need to spray before the crop is planted.
examples.analytical: Her first draft was weedy, with cluttered and unfocused paragraphs that buried the central argument.

nuance.analogy: A weedy lawn is like a neglected inbox: nothing dramatic, but unwanted clutter keeps growing until someone clears it.
nuance.etymology: From weed (noun) plus the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Using 'weedy' to describe a person in a neutral way; it sounds insulting in American English.
Mixing up 'weedy' (full of weeds) with 'weedless' or with 'weeds' as a noun.

senses.definition: To undergo a weigh-in.
senses.example: Two days before the fight, the boxers weigh in with reporters watching.

senses.definition: To subject to a weigh-in.
senses.example: They had to weigh him in at the loading dock.

senses.definition: To weigh.
senses.example: He weighs in at upwards of 250 pounds.

senses.definition: To bring in one's weight, metaphorically speaking, to bear on an issue; frequently construed with on or with.
senses.example: Everyone wanted to weigh in on what kind of car he should buy.

core.definition: To give your opinion on a topic, often in a discussion, debate or decision.

pronunciation.tip: In phrasal verbs the particle usually carries the main stress, so say IN strongly. Weigh has a long a, and the phrase links smoothly as way-IN.

nuance.connotation: Neutral
nuance.usage_note: In meetings Americans often ask Does anyone want to weigh in? or say I'd like to weigh in on this. It is polite and collaborative. Weigh in also describes wrestlers or boxers stepping on a scale before a match, and that sense is familiar in American sports coverage.

distinctions.note: Chime in is more casual and often means interrupting briefly, while weigh in suggests a considered judgment.
Weigh alone means to measure weight, while weigh in means to give an opinion or undergo a weigh-in.

examples.everyday: My sister always has to weigh in on what I wear to parties.
examples.professional: Can the security team weigh in on the proposal before Thursday's review?
examples.analytical: Several philosophers have weighed in on whether moral judgments can be true or false.

nuance.analogy: Weighing in is like adding your stone to a scale that is still balancing.
nuance.etymology: From weigh plus in; the opinion sense extends the idea of adding your weight to a decision.
common_mistakes: Dropping the preposition; say weigh in on the topic, not weigh in the topic.
Separating the particle in a way that sounds awkward, such as weigh the topic in; keep the phrase together.

conversation.text: Does anyone else want to weigh in before we decide?
My mom weighed in on what color we should paint the house.
The baby weighed in at eight pounds.
I'd love for everyone to weigh in before we decide.
James, do you want to weigh in on this?
Legal hasn't weighed in on the contract yet.

senses.definition: A common small-talk question about TV shows.
senses.example: So, what are you watching these days? I'm hooked on a new crime drama.

core.definition: A casual question asking which TV shows, series, or movies someone is currently following.

pronunciation.respelling: wuht ahr yoo wahch-ing theez DAYZ
pronunciation.tip: Stress lands on DAYS, and watching has its main stress on the first syllable, WAHCH, with a secondary stress on -ing reduced. Watch the vowel: the American 'ah' in WAHCH is the same as in 'cot,' not 'caught.'

nuance.connotation: Positive and friendly; it invites conversation without being personal.
nuance.usage_note: Americans ask this in break rooms, at dinner, or with friends, and expect a show name plus a short opinion. Reply with a title and a quick comment, such as 'The Bear, it's intense but really good.' Avoid asking it in a way that suggests you expect someone to watch the same things you do.

distinctions.note: More specific; it refers to online services, while watching covers TV, streaming, and movies.
Asks about broadcast programming now, while these days refers to current viewing habits.

examples.everyday: Hey, what are you watching these days? I need something new for the weekend.
examples.professional: At the team lunch, someone asked what we were watching these days, and the conversation turned into a debate about the new season.
examples.analytical: The phrase 'What are you watching these days?' treats personal entertainment as a window into a person's taste, values, and mood.

nuance.analogy: It is like asking what book is on someone's nightstand: it opens a quick, low-stakes door to talk about what they enjoy.
nuance.etymology: Watch comes from Old English wæccan, to stay awake or observe; these days comes from the phrase 'in these days,' recorded in English from the Middle Ages.
common_mistakes: Saying 'watching' with a long AH sound like 'caught'; American English uses a short open vowel in WAHCH.
Using 'What are you seeing these days' for TV; the correct verb is watch.

conversation.text: What are you watching these days? I need a new show.

senses.definition: The state of being wicked; evil disposition; immorality.
A wicked or sinful thing or act; morally bad or objectionable behavior.

core.definition: The quality or state of being morally evil, sinful, or deeply wrong; an evil act or behavior.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final syllables are reduced, so say '-nus' with a weak vowel, not '-ness' with a strong one. Pronounce the w clearly.

nuance.connotation: Strongly negative. It names serious moral evil and is used in serious moral and religious discussion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wickedness in religious, literary, and serious moral writing, such as sermons, novels, and philosophy. In everyday speech, they would more often say 'evil,' 'cruelty,' or 'wrongdoing.' It is a heavy word, so avoid using it for minor mistakes or unkind remarks.

distinctions.note: Evil is the broader and more common term for moral wrong. Wickedness is slightly more old-fashioned and often refers to deliberate sin or cruelty.
Sin is a religious or moral term for wrongdoing against God or moral law. Wickedness describes the character or conduct of a person who does wrong.

examples.everyday: I could not believe the wickedness of what he did to his brother.
examples.professional: The report documented acts of wickedness in the company, including the deliberate hiding of safety data.
examples.analytical: Genesis 6:5 describes the great wickedness of humanity, which leads to the flood narrative and to the theme of divine judgment.

nuance.analogy: Wickedness is like rot inside a fruit: it may look fine from outside, but it spreads through the whole thing from within.
nuance.etymology: From wicked plus the suffix -ness, meaning the state or quality of being wicked.
common_mistakes: Using 'wickedness' for small mistakes or rudeness, which is too strong for ordinary wrongdoing.
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word ra'ah (evil, wickedness) is often translated as wickedness in Old Testament texts about human sin. Genesis 6:5 says the wickedness of man was great in the earth. Romans 1:18 speaks of the ungodliness and wickedness of men, which provoke God's wrath, in the RSV's rendering of the Greek adikia (unrighteousness).

senses.definition: A very small gift or donation which, however, represents a great sacrifice on the part of the giver.
The lepton coin.
senses.example: In Mark's Gospel, the widow's mite is a lepton, the smallest coin in circulation.

core.definition: A very small gift that is still a great sacrifice, because the giver offers all or nearly all she has.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WID in 'widow's' and on MITE. The 'w' in 'widow' is a clear W, and the final -ow sounds like 'oh', so the word sounds like 'WID-oh'.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises sacrificial generosity, often even when the amount is small.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this phrase mostly in church, in sermons, and in discussions of charity. You might hear it when someone gives a modest amount that cost them a lot, such as 'She gave her widow's mite to the fundraiser.' It is not used for ordinary tipping or casual spending. A natural reply is a simple agreement, such as 'Yes, that was generous of her.'

distinctions.note: A drop in the bucket means an amount too small to matter. The widow's mite is also small, but it is praised because it costs the giver a real sacrifice.

collocations: a widow's mite to the church
the parable of the widow's mite

examples.everyday: My aunt is on a fixed income, but she sent a twenty to the food drive, and it was her widow's mite.
examples.professional: Our small nonprofit gets many donations, but the widow's mite from a retired teacher reminded the board why we do this work.
examples.analytical: The Gospel narratives present the widow's mite not as a measure of monetary value but as a measure of the giver's total commitment.

nuance.analogy: Like a single candle lit in a dark room: the light is small, but it is given completely.
nuance.etymology: From the widow's two copper coins in the Gospel stories, with 'mite' from Middle English 'myte', a small coin.
common_mistakes: Saying 'widow's mite' as if it meant a literal widow, when it is an idiom about giving.
Mispronouncing 'mite' as 'meet'; it rhymes with 'light'.
nuance.biblical_note: In Greek the coin is a lepton (λεπτόν), the smallest copper coin in circulation. Mark 12:41-44 tells how Jesus watches people put money into the temple treasury and says a poor widow who gives two lepta has given more than all the rich people, because she gave out of her need. Luke 21:1-4 gives the same account. The point is that God values the sacrifice behind a gift more than its size.

senses.definition: Deceitful cleverness or shrewdness.

core.definition: Cleverness used to deceive, trick or get one's way, often in a sly and calculating manner.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on WY, the first syllable. The middle syllable is a short, reduced 'lih' and the ending is a weak 'nus'. Avoid pronouncing it as 'wye-lee-ness' with a long e.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it suggests deception and calculated sneakiness, though it can sometimes be admired for skill.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wiliness in writing or serious conversation about people who outmaneuver others, such as politicians, negotiators or characters in novels. In casual speech, people more often say 'sneaky' or 'slick'. It is a fairly strong word, so use it with care when describing a real person.

distinctions.note: Cunning is broader and can be neutral or admired for clever planning, while wiliness more clearly suggests trickery.
Shrewdness suggests sound judgment and is usually positive, while wiliness implies manipulation and is usually negative.
Slyness suggests secrecy and sometimes playful mischief, while wiliness suggests more calculated and effective deception.

examples.everyday: I don't trust him; his wiliness makes me nervous whenever he offers a deal that sounds too good.
examples.professional: Her wiliness in the negotiation got the vendor to absorb the cost of the delay.
examples.analytical: Machiavelli admired a prince's wiliness, but he treated it as a means of preserving power rather than as a virtue in itself.

nuance.analogy: Wiliness is like a chess player who sets traps several moves ahead, hiding the real plan behind innocent-looking moves.
nuance.etymology: From wily, from wile meaning trick, plus the noun suffix -ness; wile traces to Old English wīl.
common_mistakes: Spelling it 'willness' or 'willingness', which mean something else entirely.
Using wiliness for a simple clever idea without any element of deception.

senses.definition: Ready to do something, particularly something that requires change or effort; not objecting.
senses.example: If my boyfriend isn't willing to change his drinking habits, I will split up with him.

core.definition: Ready and happy to do something, especially something that takes effort or change, and not objecting to it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The middle syllable is a light, reduced vowel, so say WIL-ing, not WEE-ling. The final -ing is a short nasal sound, not a long ee.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It suggests cooperation and openness. It is often used with 'to' plus a verb, as in 'willing to help'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use willing constantly at work and at home: 'Are you willing to stay late?' or 'I'm willing to try.' The 'to' is required before a verb. A common reply to thanks is 'Sure, I'm happy to help' rather than 'I am willing.' Willing sounds slightly more formal than 'happy to' in casual speech.

distinctions.note: Ready means prepared or set up for an action; willing means you are open to doing it and have no objection.
Happy describes your emotional attitude; willing focuses on your readiness to act, even if you are not enthusiastic.
Eager is stronger and shows strong desire or impatience; willing is calmer and simply shows you are not resisting.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor is willing to watch the dog if we go out of town next week.
examples.professional: Several engineers are willing to take over the migration project if the timeline changes.
examples.analytical: Kant argues that a morally good act is one done from duty, not merely from an inclination one is willing to follow.

nuance.analogy: Like a door left unlocked: it is open and ready to be pushed, but nobody has pushed it yet.
nuance.etymology: From Old English willende, present participle of willan, to wish or want.
common_mistakes: Saying 'willing to do' without the 'to': correct form is 'willing to help', not 'willing help'.
Confusing willing with wiling, which is a rare noun meaning a trick or enticement.
patterns: (not before a noun in this sense)

conversation.text: Are you willing to drive, or should I?
I'm willing to try anything once.
She's willing to help, but she can't stay late.

senses.definition: A bag, traditionally made from the skin of a goat (a goatskin), used for holding and dispensing wine.

core.definition: A bag made from animal skin, usually a goatskin, used to hold and pour wine.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on 'WINE,' and the word has two short parts. Both 'wine' and 'skin' are one syllable, so do not add an extra vowel between them.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and historical. It mostly appears in Bible study, history, or literature rather than everyday speech.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use 'wineskin' in everyday conversation. It appears in Bible study, church sermons, and discussions of ancient life. In modern American speech, people would say 'wine bottle' or 'wine bag' for a container, not 'wineskin.'

distinctions.note: A wine bottle is glass or plastic; a wineskin is made from animal hide and is flexible.
A wine bag is a modern carrier or cloth bag; a wineskin is traditionally a goatskin container for storage and pouring.

examples.everyday: The museum had an old goatskin wineskin in the ancient history room, and the guide explained how people carried wine.
examples.professional: In our Bible study curriculum, we use the image of the wineskin to explain why new ideas need new structures.
examples.analytical: The wineskin image in the Gospels expresses a theological claim about the incompatibility of new teaching with inherited religious forms.

nuance.analogy: A wineskin is like a leather water bottle for wine: flexible, light, and made from the animal it once belonged to.
nuance.etymology: From wine plus skin, meaning a container made of animal skin.
common_mistakes: Writing 'wine skin' as two words, which is acceptable in older texts but usually 'wineskin' in modern use.
Using 'wineskin' for a glass bottle in everyday conversation.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word is nōʾd (נֹאד), meaning a leather bag or wineskin, and the Greek word is askos (ἀσκός), meaning a wineskin made of skin. In Matthew 9:17, Mark 2:22, and Luke 5:37, Jesus says that new wine is not put into old wineskins, because the old skins would burst and the wine would be lost. In Joshua 9:4 and 9:13, the Gibeonites present old, torn wineskins to show they have traveled far.

senses.definition: A factory or factories, or a similar collection(s) of industrial facilities.
senses.example: The steel works almost fills the valley.

senses.definition: A mechanism or machinery; the means by which something happens.
senses.example: Aged and degraded oil and grease can really gum up the works.

senses.definition: Everything or everything that is available or possible; especially, all available toppings on food.
senses.example: I'll have a Behemoth Burger with the works.

senses.definition: Drastic treatment; abuse; the axe (dismissal).
senses.example: The new manager gave three employees the works on Monday morning.

senses.definition: A heroin or other drug addict's equipment: syringes, needles, etc.
senses.example: Outreach workers at the clinic hand out clean works to reduce needle sharing.

core.definition: Things a person does or makes, such as deeds or creative works; in theology, good deeds done in obedience to God, often contrasted with faith in discussions of salvation.

pronunciation.tip: One syllable with the American r-colored vowel, as in 'work' plus 's.' Don't add a vowel before the r, and keep the final 'ks' cluster crisp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in itself. In 'justification by works,' it points to a flawed view of earning salvation, while 'good works' is positive.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, 'works' is the verb ('it works') or a noun for factories ('steel works'), or 'the works' for everything on a pizza. In theology, 'works' means human deeds as compared with faith or grace. Don't use the theological sense outside of religious discussion.

distinctions.note: Deeds is a broader and more literary term for actions, while works in theology means actions viewed in relation to the law or salvation.
Actions is a neutral everyday word with no theological weight.
Faith is trust in God; works are the deeds that express or are contrasted with it.
Labor is effort, especially physical, with no special meaning of moral or religious deeds.

examples.everyday: I'll take a burger with the works, please.
examples.professional: Today we will compare how Paul and James talk about works.
examples.analytical: Paul rejects 'works of the law' as the basis for justification but never denies that faith produces good works.

nuance.analogy: In the faith-and-works debate, works can be seen as either the price paid for a gift or the fruit that grows on a living tree.
nuance.etymology: From Old English weorc 'deed, action, something done.'
common_mistakes: Mispronouncing it as 'wor-ks' with a separate vowel or an unrounded vowel.
Using the theological 'works' in casual speech to mean 'jobs.'
Forgetting that 'works' with the verb 'works' is third person singular: 'it works' versus 'works' as a noun.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek ergon means deed or work, and the Hebrew ma'aseh means deed or action. Ephesians 2:8-9 says salvation is not a result of works. Romans 3:28 says a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law. James 2:24 says a person is justified by works and not by faith alone, in a context where he insists faith must be active.

traditions.view: Works are the expression of faith and love, with human cooperation in grace. Orthodoxy does not accept the contrast between faith and works as in Western debates.
Good works done in grace are meritorious through God's gift and increase one's growth in holiness. They are not a way to earn the first grace of justification.

Reformation churches teach that works do not justify but are the necessary fruit of true faith. Lutheran and Reformed theologians distinguish justification from the works that follow it, while Anglicans and Methodists emphasize holy living.

senses.definition: The subjective human experience, regarded collectively; human collective existence; existence in general; the reality we live in.
senses.example: In retrospect, the process of economic globalization has meant the end of the world as we knew it.

senses.definition: The subjective human experience, regarded individually.
senses.example: The period immediately following my divorce seemed like the end of my world.

senses.definition: A majority of people.
senses.example: Running after God is the only life worth living. Even though the world believes that living for God is boring, we believe that there is nothing more exciting.

senses.definition: The Universe.
senses.example: Astronomers hope to learn how the world began shortly after the Big Bang.

senses.definition: The Earth, especially in a geopolitical or cultural context, or as the physical planet.
senses.example: People are dying of starvation all over the world.

senses.definition: Any of several possible scenarios concerning The Earth, either as the physical planet, or in a geopolitical, cultural or societal context.
senses.example: Who would want to live in a world like this?

senses.definition: (Several) alternative scenarios concerning The Earth, either as the physical planet, or in a geopolitical, cultural or societal context.
senses.example: Climate scientists warn that the world faces serious risks if emissions keep rising this century.

senses.definition: A distinct realm, capable of containing objects or inhabitants, which does not physically border other similar realms.
senses.example: Our mission is to travel the galaxy and find new worlds.

senses.definition: A planet, especially one which is inhabited or inhabitable.
senses.example: Our mission is to travel the galaxy and find new worlds.

senses.definition: Any other astronomical body which may be inhabitable, such as a natural satellite.
senses.example: Some astronomers wonder whether a moon orbiting Jupiter could be a world with liquid water.

senses.definition: In various mythologies, cosmologies, etc. one of a number of separate realms or regions having different characteristics and occupied by different types of inhabitants.
senses.example: In the old myth, the dead descend to a shadowy world beneath the earth.

senses.definition: A fictional realm, such as a planet, containing one or multiple societies of beings, especially intelligent ones.
senses.example: the world of Narnia

senses.definition: A very large extent of country.
senses.example: the New World

senses.definition: An individual or group perspective or social setting.
senses.example: In the world of boxing, good diet is all-important.

senses.definition: The part of an operating system distributed with the kernel, consisting of the shell and other programs.
senses.example: On FreeBSD, the kernel and world must be upgraded together to avoid library mismatches.

senses.definition: A subdivision of a game, consisting of a series of stages or levels that usually share a similar environment or theme.
senses.example: Have you reached the boss at the end of the ice world?

senses.definition: The twenty-second trump or major arcana card of the tarot.
senses.example: The World card in the tarot deck often represents completion and fulfillment.

senses.definition: A great amount, a lot.
senses.example: Taking a break from work seems to have done her a world of good.

senses.definition: To consider or cause to be considered from a global perspective; to consider as a global whole, rather than making or focusing on national or other distinctions; compare globalize.
senses.example: We should world the problem of plastic waste instead of treating each country separately.

senses.definition: To make real; to make worldly.
senses.example: She tried to world her lofty ideals into something her family could actually live with.

core.definition: The planet Earth with all its people, places and things; the place where we live and everything in it.

pronunciation.tip: This is one syllable with an r-colored vowel, like 'hurl' with a d at the end. It sounds identical to 'word', so context tells listeners which one you mean. Don't insert a vowel between the r and the l.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It can sound positive or negative depending on the phrase, as in 'the best in the world' or 'the cruel world'.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use world constantly in everyday speech: 'around the world', 'what in the world', 'the real world', 'a world of difference'. 'What in the world' is an emphatic idiom for surprise or frustration, and it is informal but very common.

distinctions.note: Earth names the planet itself, while world can also mean human society or a field of activity, as in 'the world of finance'.
A globe is a physical sphere or model of the planet, while world refers to the living human reality on it.

examples.everyday: I've always wanted to see the world, so I'm saving up for a trip to Italy next year.
examples.professional: Once the model goes live, we need to see how it performs in the real world, not just on the test set.
examples.analytical: Heidegger argues that human existence is always being-in-the-world, so we cannot describe a subject apart from its surroundings.

nuance.analogy: Like a map you carry in your head: the planet is the terrain, but your world is the part you walk through every day.
nuance.etymology: From Old English weorold, meaning human existence or the age of man, from wer 'man' and eld 'age'.
common_mistakes: Confusing 'world' with 'word' in spelling or dictation, since they sound the same.
Adding an extra vowel and saying 'wor-uld' instead of one syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the key Greek word is kosmos, meaning the ordered created universe, or humanity as a system organized apart from God. John 3:16 speaks of God loving the world, meaning humanity as a whole, not the earth alone. 1 John 2:15 warns believers not to love the world, meaning its values and desires, and Romans 12:2 tells them not to be conformed to this world.

world.etymology: From Middle English *world*, from Old English *weorold* (“world”), from **weraldi*, from Proto-Germanic **weraldiz* (“lifetime, human existence, world”), equivalent to *wer* + *eld*.

senses.definition: Causing worry; perturbing or vexing.
Inclined to worry.

core.definition: Causing worry; making you feel concerned about what might happen in the future.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the final syllable is a reduced 'sum' with a schwa. Do not pronounce the final sound as 'sohm' or add an extra syllable.

nuance.connotation: Negative, because it describes something that causes concern, such as a trend, a sign, or news.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use worrisome for trends, symptoms, data, or news, as in 'a worrisome trend in the numbers.' It sounds a bit more formal than worrying in speech. A natural follow-up is to say what you will do about it.

distinctions.note: Worrying is the more common everyday word and can describe feelings or people, while worrisome is more often used for signs or trends.
Alarming suggests sudden danger and strong shock, while worrisome describes a steady concern that needs attention.

examples.everyday: The doctor said the test results were not dangerous, but there was one worrisome number.
examples.professional: The uptick in server errors is worrisome, so let's look into it before the release on Friday.
examples.analytical: The model's declining accuracy on rare classes is worrisome, because it suggests the training data underrepresents them.

nuance.analogy: Like a small crack in a windshield that is not yet a problem but could spread.
nuance.etymology: From worry (verb) plus the suffix -some, meaning causing or tending to.
common_mistakes: Saying worrisome for a person's feeling; for feelings, worried or worrying is usually more natural.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound foreign.

senses.definition: The adoration (or latria) owed to God alone, as greater than the hyperdulia that is given to Saint Mary only and the veneration (or dulia) accorded to all other Roman Catholic saints.
senses.example: Christians gather on Sunday to worship God in song, prayer, and scripture reading.

senses.definition: The devotion accorded to a deity or to a sacred object.
senses.example: Polytheistic theology and worship had to go underground.

senses.definition: The religious ceremonies that express this devotion.
senses.example: The church holds evening worship on Wednesdays, with a short service and a community meal.

senses.definition: Voluntary, utter submission; voluntary, utter deference.
senses.example: The courtiers showed their worship of the king by bowing before every word he spoke.

senses.definition: Ardent love.
senses.example: He wrote sonnets expressing his worship of her, the only woman he had ever loved.

senses.definition: An object of worship.
senses.example: The sacred river was the worship of an entire village long before the first church arrived.

senses.definition: Used as a title or term of address for various officials, including magistrates.
senses.example: Yes, your worship, the defendant has been informed of the charges against him.

senses.definition: Honor; respect; civil deference.
senses.example: She was held in great worship by her students for her patience and fairness.

senses.definition: The condition of being worthy; honor, distinction.
The fact of an artist's music heavily drawing influence from some other artist's work in a way that appears too obvious or unapologetic; a piece of music that does this.
senses.example: Critics called the new single pure worship of the band's favorite 1980s synth group.

senses.definition: To reverence (a deity, etc.) with supreme respect and veneration; to perform religious exercises in honor of.
senses.example: Pilgrims travel for days to worship at the shrine of the patron saint.

senses.definition: To honor with extravagant love and extreme submission, as a lover; to adore; to idolize.
senses.example: The fans worshipped the singer, following her tour across three countries.

senses.definition: To participate in religious ceremonies.
senses.example: We worship at the church down the road.

senses.definition: To touch, fondle, or kiss in an intensely sensual way.
senses.example: The lovers worshipped each other's bodies with slow kisses and gentle touches.

core.definition: To honor God or a sacred being with prayer, praise, and ritual; to show deep religious reverence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable with the 'ur' vowel of 'fur.' The ending is a short i, as in 'ship,' not the long ee of 'sheep.'

nuance.connotation: Positive in religious contexts; in casual use about admiration, it is playful or ironic.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English 'worship' mostly means religious devotion. People say 'We worship at a church downtown' or 'attend worship services.' Figurative use, like 'I worship that chef,' is casual and humorous. In ordinary conversation people often say 'pray' or 'go to church' instead.

distinctions.note: Praying is speaking to God; worship is broader and includes praise, song, and ritual.
Adore is strong emotional love and can apply to people; worship is tied to ultimate religious devotion.
Idolize means admire excessively, often negatively; religious worship is considered right only toward God.

examples.everyday: We worship at a small church near our house on Sunday mornings.
examples.professional: The youth pastor is planning a new worship set for the spring retreat.
examples.analytical: The argument asks what one can rightly worship, and whether worship can be given to anything less than God without idolatry.

nuance.analogy: Like tuning an instrument to a single true pitch, so that everything else is heard in relation to it.
nuance.etymology: From Old English weorthscipe, meaning worth or honor, from 'worth' plus '-ship.'
common_mistakes: Using the British spelling 'worshipped' or 'worshipper' in American writing
Pronouncing it with a long o in the first syllable
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek proskynein means to bow down or do homage, and latreuein means to render sacred service. Matthew 4:10 insists that worship belongs to God alone. John 4:23-24 says the Father seeks true worshipers who worship in spirit and truth. Exodus 20:3-5 forbids worshiping images, in the first commandment.

traditions.view: Worship (latreia) is due to God alone. Icons and saints receive veneration (proskynesis) that passes on to the one they represent, which is treated as a different kind of honor from worship.
Latria, the adoration owed to God alone, is distinguished from hyperdulia for Mary and dulia for the saints, who are honored and asked to intercede.

Worship belongs to God alone, and most Protestants reject praying to saints and venerating images as contrary to Scripture. Lutherans retain honor for the saints as examples, while Reformed and Baptist churches differ on liturgical forms.

senses.definition: In the least favorable of all possible circumstances.
senses.example: In a worst-case scenario, according to the ILO, 51 million jobs could be lost in 2009.

core.definition: Describing the most unfavorable outcome that could possibly happen in a given situation.

pronunciation.tip: When worst-case is used before a noun it has stress on worst, and case is secondary. Say WURST-kays with a clear r, and the final s of case sounds like z in other phrases like 'the case is closed'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a planning term that signals caution rather than negativity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use worst-case in business, engineering, finance and everyday planning, as in 'Let's plan for the worst-case scenario.' It is always hyphenated when it comes before a noun. The noun phrase is worst case, as in 'In the worst case, we lose a day.' Pair it with best-case for balanced planning.

distinctions.note: Worst means most unfavorable in general; worst-case is a planning term for a specific, possible scenario used in analysis.
Pessimistic describes a general attitude that expects bad outcomes; worst-case describes a specific, measured scenario used to plan.

examples.everyday: Before we book the hotel, let's think about the worst-case scenario in case the flight is canceled.
examples.professional: Our worst-case estimate shows the migration will take three weeks, even if the vendor delays their part.
examples.analytical: A worst-case analysis of the argument shows that its premises could be true while the conclusion remains false.

nuance.analogy: Like packing an umbrella for a storm that might not come, a worst-case plan prepares you for the least favorable outcome.
nuance.etymology: Worst comes from Old English wierrest, and case from Latin casus, meaning a falling or occurrence.
common_mistakes: Writing worst case as an adjective without a hyphen before a noun; use worst-case scenario.
Using worse-case, which is incorrect; the standard form is worst-case.

senses.definition: Encased in a wrapping.
senses.example: The birthday present was wrapped in silver paper and tied with a red ribbon.

senses.definition: A feature on a website or online service that includes a summary of a user's activity on the service during a given year, created by logging the user's personal data.
senses.example: Our wrappeds this year are so similar.

core.definition: Covered or enclosed completely in paper, cloth, or other material, usually for protection or as a gift.

pronunciation.tip: The w is silent. The word sounds like 'rapt' with a short a and a crisp final t, so do not add an extra syllable or vowel at the end.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing a physical state. In phrases like 'wrapped up in' it can mean absorbed, which is positive or neutral depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wrapped to describe gifts, food, or items in packaging, such as 'the gift was wrapped beautifully.' 'Wrapped up in' means completely absorbed, as in 'she was wrapped up in her work.' Outside the phrase sense, wrapped with a capital W may also refer to a year-end summary feature in apps.

distinctions.note: Packed describes items placed inside a container, while wrapped describes an item covered by material around its outside.
Covered is general and can describe any surface, while wrapped suggests material folded or tightly enclosed around something.

examples.everyday: The sandwich is wrapped in foil, so it should stay warm on the drive.
examples.professional: The delivered servers were wrapped in protective film to avoid damage during shipping.
examples.analytical: Her argument was wrapped in layers of qualification, which made its central claim difficult to locate.

nuance.analogy: A wrapped object is like a present with a bow and paper protecting it.
nuance.etymology: Past participle of wrap, from Middle English 'wrappen'.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the w, which is silent.
Using wrapped for objects in a box instead of packed or placed.
Forgetting the preposition in 'wrapped up in' when using the absorbed sense.

senses.definition: A tough, malleable, ductile form of iron that is forged rather than cast, suitable for welding.
senses.example: The blacksmith explained that wrought iron resists rust better than modern steel, so he used it for the gate.

core.definition: Tough, malleable iron that is shaped by hammering or rolling, used for fences, gates, railings and decorative ironwork.

pronunciation.tip: Wrought sounds like 'rawt', not 'roo-ought' or 'rowt'. The stress falls on the second word, iron, and the final -ron is a reduced 'urn' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive. It suggests sturdiness, craftsmanship and a traditional or classic look.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use wrought iron for fences, gates, balconies and furniture, often in historic neighborhoods or home improvement talk. As an adjective it takes a hyphen, as in 'a wrought-iron gate.' It is different from cast iron, which is poured into molds and is more brittle, so careful speakers avoid mixing them up.
word_family: wrought (past participle of work, used as an adjective)

distinctions.note: Cast iron is poured into molds and is brittle, while wrought iron is hammered or rolled and is tougher and more bendable.
Steel contains a controlled amount of carbon and is mainly produced by a different process, so it is stronger and more uniform than wrought iron.

examples.everyday: We bought a black wrought-iron gate for the backyard, and it looks great with the brick wall.
examples.professional: The historic district requires that the replacement fence match the original wrought-iron profile and finish.
examples.analytical: The fibrous texture of wrought iron, created by repeated hammering that drives out slag, gave it a character that later steel could not reproduce.

nuance.analogy: Like a sword blade that is folded and hammered again and again, so its grain runs in one direction.
nuance.etymology: Wrought is the past participle of work, so wrought iron is iron that has been worked by hammering.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing wrought as 'rought' or 'roo-ought'; it sounds like 'rawt'.
Confusing it with cast iron, which is poured into molds and is more brittle.

related: wrought (past participle of work, used as an adjective)

senses.definition: In a yielding way.

core.definition: In a soft, compliant way, giving way to pressure or to another person's wishes.

pronunciation.tip: The stress is on the first syllable, and the final '-ly' is a light /li/. Keep the middle syllable short and unstressed so it does not sound like 'yeelding-lee' with two strong beats.

nuance.connotation: Neutral, describing manner; it can sound either gentle or weak depending on the surrounding words.
nuance.usage_note: This adverb is rare in everyday American speech and appears mostly in literary writing, formal prose or careful commentary. Americans would normally say 'without resistance,' 'easily' or 'in a compliant way' in conversation. If you hear it, the speaker is usually describing someone's manner in a deliberate or literary tone.

distinctions.note: Submissively implies accepting a lower status or another's authority, which is stronger than yieldingly.
Passively means without taking action; yieldingly suggests a soft, cooperative giving way rather than inaction.

examples.professional: The vendor responded yieldingly to our request for a lower price, which saved the team a second round of negotiations.
examples.analytical: The text accepts every interpretation the reader brings to it, yieldingly, and that is exactly what makes its meaning so hard to pin down.

nuance.analogy: Like water taking the shape of whatever container holds it.
nuance.etymology: From 'yielding' (adjective) plus the adverbial suffix '-ly'; 'yield' comes from Old English gieldan, to pay back.
common_mistakes: Using it in casual conversation where 'easily' or 'without resistance' sounds more natural.
Confusing it with 'unyieldingly,' which means the opposite.
Stressing the second syllable, which makes the word sound foreign.

senses.definition: Telling someone on a call that their microphone is off.

core.definition: A statement telling someone on a call or video meeting that their microphone is turned off, so others cannot hear them.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on MYOOT, and 'on' is reduced to 'ahn' in fast speech. Americans pronounce the r in 'you're' and the 'mute' starts with a clear 'my' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and helpful. It is a standard, polite prompt in virtual meetings, though it can feel abrupt if said without a friendly tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say this during Zoom, Teams or Google Meet calls when someone is speaking but nothing can be heard. Colleagues often add 'Oops, sorry' or 'Thanks, got it.' It is normal and not rude, but in a large meeting a private chat message is more polite.

distinctions.note: 'You're muted' means the same thing and is equally common; 'on mute' is the more idiomatic phrasing among many Americans.
'On speaker' means the call is using a speakerphone, not that the microphone is off.

examples.everyday: Hey, you're on mute, I can't hear a thing.
examples.professional: Hi everyone, quick note: you're on mute, Priya, so please unmute before you present.
examples.analytical: Virtual meetings expose how much communication depends on small technical acts, so 'you're on mute' becomes a reminder that presence needs active participation.

nuance.analogy: Like someone talking behind a closed window: they are speaking, but nothing gets through.
common_mistakes: Saying 'You're in mute' instead of 'on mute.'
Saying 'Turn off mute' rather than 'Unmute yourself.'

conversation.text: Mike, I think you're on mute.
"Can you hear me now?" "No, you're still on mute."
Sarah, you're on mute. Click the microphone icon at the bottom.

senses.definition: The occurrence or discovery of events described as unlucky, unpleasant or expected.
senses.example: Her career was full of zemblanity, as every promising opportunity turned sour at the last minute.

core.definition: The unlucky discovery of something unpleasant that could have been predicted, the opposite of serendipity.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, ZEM. The middle syllables are short, and the final syllable is a weak 'tee', not a long 'tie'.

nuance.connotation: Negative
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in writing, essays and witty conversation about bad luck that seems almost predictable. It is uncommon, so using it with a friend may sound playful. A natural reply is to laugh and say it figures.

distinctions.note: Serendipity means a fortunate discovery by chance, while zemblanity means an unfortunate discovery that was in some sense foreseeable.

examples.everyday: I left my keys in the car again, which is pure zemblanity for a Monday.
examples.professional: The launch failed on the same bug we had flagged last month, a classic case of zemblanity in our project review.
examples.analytical: Boyd's coinage captures a discovery that is unwelcome yet inevitable, in contrast to the chance good fortune named by serendipity.

nuance.analogy: Like a leaky roof that everyone warned you about, the bad news arrives exactly as expected.
nuance.etymology: Coined by the novelist William Boyd in the 1990s as a deliberate opposite of serendipity.
common_mistakes: Using it for any bad luck, when it specifically implies something foreseeable.
Stressing the second syllable, as in zem-BLAN-ih-tee.
